Euler-Bernoulli F L^3 / (3 E I) = 0.864 mm; the reference converges to it (Timoshenko's 2.4% shear is offset by the fully clamped root). Notes: mujoco: linear tetrahedra lock in bending; sofa: linear tetrahedra lock in bending.
  • wang_finger: Cast ribbed pneumatic finger of Wang et al., Actuators 15(9), 488 (2026), CC BY 4.0: geometry from the paper's Abaqus mesh, Yeoh card from its tensile data, plane strain as in the paper; chord angle against the eight measured points, 5-40 kPa (one finger, one ascending sequence; reading uncertainty about 1 deg). Notes: mujoco: does not reproduce this finger at 1-2 mm (8-19 deg RMS, docs/actuation.md); sofa: does not reproduce this finger at 1-2 mm (8-19 deg RMS, docs/actuation.md).

The first release: a validated core, three robot families and the reference solver they are checked against. See docs/roadmap.md for the details of each milestone.

  • Core (M1): YAML configs with units and strict schemas, --set overrides, material presets, soft and rigid geometry, tetrahedral meshing, a backend-neutral scene, capability flags with refusals, pre-run physics checks, sweeps, CLI.
  • SOFA inverse (--method sofa-qp): angle targets (bend_angle, chord_angle) with any actuator, alone or with position targets (Broyden iteration on the effector goals, angle_direction); a pressure and a cable together (scenarios/inflation/bending_cable.yaml); stroke-controlled cables (solved as tensions, stroke read back, stroke bounds iterated). Round trips recover the actuation to 0.5% or better.
  • SOFA cable (fix): tension-controlled cables are springs with per-step rest lengths, so their tangent stiffness is implicit; the two-cable arm no longer swings in a +-0.5 mm limit cycle on SOFA and the repeated inverse solve converges.
  • Backends: MuJoCo flex (M1), SOFA v26.06 (M4), fem, the locking-free 3D reference (quadratic tetrahedra, P2/P0; M5), and rod, slender bodies as SOFA BeamAdapter beams (M8).
  • Self-collision (M9): body.self_collision for the actuation scenario (MuJoCo flex, SOFA); fem and rod refuse.
  • ROS 2 Humble layer (M2): a generic node, interfaces, launch and RViz.
  • Experiments (M3, M5): drop-test video tracking (including tilt), calibration over any observable, softsim fit against any measured table, leave-one-out validation.
  • Materials (M5): physical and effective cards with validity, uncertainty and references; Gent and Arruda-Boyce; homogeneous tests; fit-material on public data (Marechal 2021, Roels 2025); 25 fitted silicone cards; Prony viscoelasticity on every backend; softsim transfer with error bars; sensitivity and sampling.
  • Gymnasium environments (M12 groundwork): softsim.envs (extra rl), softsim/CableBeamReach-v0 and softsim/CableArmReach-v0, YAML-defined reach tasks with domain randomisation over the cards' uncertainty; softsim/PneuNetBend-v0 (pressure-driven bend angle), softsim/ReducedGripperLift-v0 (grasp and lift on the reduced gripper, randomised object mass and friction) and tools/train_baseline.py (numpy CEM baseline vs random actions).
  • Actuation (M6): pressure, cable (tension or stroke), and region-force actuators; material zones with their own density and damping; bodies from STEP/STL/OBJ/msh; moving and rotating mounts; prescribed region motion; closed-loop control from Python.
  • Robots (M7-M10): PneuNet and the Wang et al. ribbed finger (reference within 0.8 deg RMS of the measurements), cable finger and arm, a two-finger gripper with finite-element grasps and a live page, soft-magnetic elastomers (MRE) on the reference.
  • Benchmarks, full tier: docs/benchmarks.md now has the full tier (hard-magnetic cantilever and the Wang finger: the reference is 0.76 deg RMS from the measurement, MuJoCo and SOFA 18-19 deg, listed as known failures). The 10 g finite-element grasp was re-run with the default friction on the 2 mm mesh (unchanged) and on the validated 1.5 mm finger with teeth (grip while holding 13% higher); the 30 g one stops converging at t = 1.04 s.
  • Drop comparisons: calibrations made before the measured landing tilt was applied (28-29 Oct) are re-simulated without it (tilt: false in the calibration file); with the tilt the SOFA 500 g fits blew up and were missing from the figures. The SOFA Ogden fit's 500 g NRMSE is 79% without the rim artefact (it was reported as 58%).
  • SOFA contact: the alarm distance follows the fastest vertex's travel per step (rim flare of the 500 g drop: a vertex went 2.83 mm through the ground, now 0.006 mm; the restitution table is unchanged, +12% CPU time in that run; SOFTSIM_SOFA_ADAPTIVE_ALARM=0 restores the fixed one). The "frictionless plate 7% stiff" artefact was friction: SOFA's single coefficient (0.1 gives about -7%, 0.8 -33%), at 0 the plate agrees with no contact to 0.6%.
  • Friction: a sliding-block benchmark against exact Coulomb sliding (all backends within 0.8-0.94%) and its sticking case; the reference's friction smoothing is now a slip speed (contact.slip_speed, default 1e-5 m/s), so its stick creep no longer depends on the time step (docs/decisions.md, entry 6). This changes finite-element grasps; null restores the old behaviour.
  • SOFA contact: its "58% energy loss" in frictionless impacts was a friction mismatch (one coefficient for every pair); compared like for like it loses 3.4% more than the reference. Runs now warn (single-friction) when a SOFA scene's coefficients differ.
  • Mounts: a rotating mount can turn at a constant rate (waypoints [time, angle, rate]).
  • Magnetic: saturation of the induced magnetisation (a tanh law from the card's saturation_magnetization) and hard-magnetic particles (remanent_magnetization, Zhao et al. 2019), both on the reference; magnetic zones (each element with its own card) and a hard-magnetic U gripper whose oppositely magnetised arms close in a uniform field.
  • Design and control (M11, first pieces): softsim optimize (design optimisation over parametric geometry, a resumable evaluation log, constraints with an honest infeasible flag) and softsim inverse (quasi-static inverse control: the actuator values that reach target outputs), both checked on MuJoCo; values are the backend's own. softsim inverse --method sofa-qp is the SOFA fast path with SoftRobots.Inverse (QPInverseProblemSolver, CableActuator, PositionEffector): same tensions as the repeated solve to 1%, 7-11 times faster on the cantilever, and it solves the two-cable arm where the repeated solve on SOFA does not settle. Pressure actuators too (SurfacePressureActuator on the cavity, jobs/inverse_bending_sofa.yaml): 4 kPa recovered to 0.03% on the bending tube (7 times faster than the repeated solve), 5 kPa to 0.05% on the PneuNet.
  • Surrogates (M11): softsim surrogate fits a polynomial or RBF model of the equilibrium map from seeded samples (resumable log, held-out validation, JSON evaluable from numpy) and softsim inverse --method surrogate solves on it in milliseconds with an optional verifying simulation; optional DMD-with-control dynamic model. MuJoCo arm: the known tensions found to 0.01%, ~1500 times faster per solve than the repeated solve.
  • Closed-loop control (M11): softsim.control.controller.Controller (surrogate feedforward, damped-least-squares integral feedback with anti-windup, optional MPC-lite on the DMD model) and a ROS 2 controller_node; with a stiffness 20 % off, feedback removes the 17 to 33 % (cantilever) and 1 to 3 mm (arm) feedforward error on MuJoCo.
  • Runs: a run that fails partway saves the samples it computed (summary.yaml → metadata.incomplete).
  • Release (M13): softsim bench and the benchmark table, CI, a docs site with tutorials, a test that every command in the README and tutorials parses and its config validates, softsim --version.

docs.title: Contributing
docs.text: Thanks for helping. softsim's rule is validation first: a feature comes with a capability flag (and a refusal where it is unsupported), a test against an analytic solution or the reference, and, where possible, a comparison with published data.

docs.title: Setup
docs.text:
python3 -m venv .venv
.venv/bin/pip install -e ".[dev,fem]"
.venv/bin/python -m pytest -m "not slow"     # the fast suite; drop -m to run everything
.venv/bin/python -m ruff check .

SOFA tests skip unless SOFA_ROOT points at a SOFA v26.06 install. Mark a test @pytest.mark.slow if it takes more than about 30 s.

docs.title: What goes where
docs.text:
• A new material law or preset: docs/adding_a_material.md
  • A new shape: docs/adding_a_body.md
  • A new scenario: docs/adding_a_scenario.md
  • A new physics engine: docs/adding_a_backend.md
  • A new dataset: docs/adding_a_dataset.md
  • A new validated case: a YAML entry in benchmarks/ (see softsim/bench.py), so it shows in docs/benchmarks.md

docs.title: Style
docs.text:
• Line length 120; ruff check . must pass.
  • SI units inside the code; units as strings in YAML ("17 mm", "55 kPa").
  • Docstrings say what a function computes and against what it was checked.
  • Results in the docs give the command that reproduces them.

docs.title: Data
docs.text: Public data only, with DOI and licence. Data that may not be redistributed is downloaded by softsim fetch, never committed.

docs.title: Inverse control (M11, first piece)
docs.text:
Given a scenario with actuators and a target for one or more of its outputs, find the actuator values that reach it at equilibrium. Code: softsim/control/inverse.py; tests: tests/test_inverse.py.

softsim inverse jobs/inverse_cable_cantilever.yaml     # tension for a 2 degree tip tilt
softsim inverse jobs/inverse_cable_arm.yaml            # two cables, tip x and z

from softsim.control.inverse import solve_inverse

res = solve_inverse("scenarios/actuation/cable_cantilever.yaml", {"bend_angle": "2 deg"},
                    ["cable"], {"cable": (0, "0.7 N")}, overrides=["body.mesh.size=4mm"])
res.values, res.status, res.residual, res.simulations

A job file names the config, overrides, backend, targets (any output column of the scenario, such as tip_x, tip_z, bend_angle, chord_angle; values with units), actuators (name: [lower, upper], finite) and optionally tolerance, max_evaluations, initial, scales and the settling options below. The result is printed as JSON: values, the outputs reached, errors, residual, status, at_bounds, simulations, steps, wall_time.

docs.title: How it solves
docs.text:
1. The equilibrium map. The actuators are held at constant values (Simulation.apply_controls), the scene runs until every target output has stopped changing, and the outputs are read. One Simulation is built and reused: each evaluation continues from the previous equilibrium (warm_start; reset() is called only at the start, or for every evaluation with warm_start: false). For an elastic body the equilibrium does not depend on the path, so this only saves time. Actuators that are not unknowns are held at their value at t = 0.
  2. Settling. An elastic body rings forever, so the solve gives the body (and each zone without damping of its own) stiffness-proportional damping: settle_damping, Rayleigh beta, default 10 ms. A damping force vanishes at rest, so the equilibrium is where it was. MuJoCo has no mass-proportional damping, so the damping time scale has to suit the slowest mode: the cantilever (first mode ~20 Hz at 4 mm) settles with 10 ms; the two-segment arm (first mode ~1 Hz) needs 150 ms. The state counts as settled when every target output moves less than settle_tol (default 0.001) of its scale over the last settle_window (default 0.1 s). The window has to be longer than the slowest relaxation: with a 20 ms window the arm was declared settled while it had only just started to move and the finite-difference Jacobian was wrong (found while building this, see the arm job). Hitting max_settle is counted in unsettled.
  3. The solve. Scaled residuals (output - target) / scale (scale: 1 mm for lengths, 0.01 rad for angles, 1 mN for forces, 100 Pa for pressures; override with scales) are minimised by scipy.optimize.least_squares (trust region, bounds) over the actuator values scaled to [0, 1] of their bounds, with a forward-difference Jacobian (step 2% of the range): one extra equilibrium per actuator per iteration. It stops when the largest scaled residual is below tolerance (default 0.05) or after max_evaluations equilibria.
  4. The outcome. status is converged; bounded_best (an actuator sits at a bound and the target is not reached: the bounded best is returned, at_bounds names it, no exception); max_evaluations; or stalled.

Targets that do not determine the actuators are refused (fewer targets than actuators).

docs.title: Measured (MuJoCo, 4 mm cantilever mesh; the machine was shared, times are indicative)
docs.text:
Case Result Simulations Wall time Cantilever, target = angle at a known 0.40 N, start 0.05 N 0.3998 N (-0.06%), residual 0.003 11 28 s same, start 0.65 N 0.4002 N (+0.04%), residual 0.002 7 19 s Job: 2 degrees (0.0349 rad) 0.2716 N, angle error 8.7e-5 rad 5 13 s Unreachable: 0.5 rad with at most 0.3 N 0.3 N (the bound), angle 0.0386 rad, bounded_best 10 24 s Arm (6 mm mesh, 0.5 ms), known 0.45 / 0.15 N, tip x and z 0.4479 / 0.1487 N, errors 22 um in x and 7.5 um in z 13 44 s

Linearity. On the cantilever MuJoCo's own forward map gives 0.01296, 0.02583, 0.05130 rad at 0.1, 0.2, 0.4 N: the slope varies by 1.1% over the range, as Euler-Bernoulli says for small angles (theta = T d L / (E I)), and the inverse of twice the 0.1 N angle is 0.2 N within 4% (tested). MuJoCo's angle is 0.33 times the EB value at 4 mm (the locking documented in actuation.md).

Conditioning. Two cables with the tip position as targets is an ill-posed problem unless the targets carry both degrees of freedom. On the arm, tip x and the tilt bend_angle fail: bend_angle is an unsigned angle, folded at zero, so the map has a kink. Tip x and tip z work, but z moves ~1.5 mm over the whole range of the cables (it carries the "S against C" shape in second order), so it is judged to 0.2 mm (scales); at a loose tolerance (0.3) the solution reached 0.435 / 0.144 N for the true 0.45 / 0.15 N, at 0.1 it reached 0.448 / 0.149 N. The tolerance bounds the residual, not the actuator error.

docs.title: Limits
docs.text:
• Quasi-static only. Each answer is a held value that reaches the target after settling; the path (and the time it takes, which depends on the damping used to settle) is not planned. Transient control is the next M11 piece.
  • The values are the backend's. The MuJoCo flex locks (about 30% too stiff in bending at 2 mm, a factor 3 at the 4 mm used here for speed), so tensions found on it are not physical ones. For physical values use a card transferred to the backend (softsim transfer, actuation.md) and a mesh that has been checked against the reference, or solve on the reference backend, which is much slower.
  • One equilibrium per value. A structure that snaps or buckles can have several equilibria; the one found depends on the start, and the finite-difference Jacobian is wrong across a snap.
  • History-dependent bodies (contact friction, viscoelastic relaxation beyond max_settle) have no single equilibrium map; warm_start: false removes the dependence on the previous value only.
  • Cost. Each iteration costs 1 + n_actuators equilibria, each a settling run of 0.1-1 s of simulated time. Slow bodies (the arm) cost minutes. The SOFA fast path below removes the repeated solves; reduced models are not implemented.
  • Not done: constraints on outputs, bounds on rates, other backends than MuJoCo and SOFA in tests (backend= is passed through, untested here for the reference).

docs.title: SOFA fast path: SoftRobots.Inverse (--method sofa-qp)
docs.text:
softsim inverse jobs/inverse_cable_cantilever_sofa.yaml                  # `method: sofa-qp` in the job
softsim inverse jobs/inverse_cable_cantilever.yaml --method sofa-qp      # or on the command line
softsim inverse jobs/inverse_cable_arm_sofa.yaml                         # two cables, tip x and z, one QP run
softsim inverse jobs/inverse_bending_sofa.yaml                           # a pressure (SurfacePressureActuator)
softsim inverse jobs/inverse_bending_angle_sofa.yaml                     # a tip tilt with a pressure
softsim inverse jobs/inverse_bending_cable_sofa.yaml                     # a pressure and a cable together
softsim inverse jobs/inverse_cable_stroke_sofa.yaml                      # a stroke-controlled cable

from softsim.control.sofa_inverse import solve_inverse_sofa

res = solve_inverse_sofa("scenarios/actuation/cable_cantilever.yaml", {"tip_x": "2 mm"}, ["cable"],
                         {"cable": (0, "0.7 N")}, overrides=["body.mesh.size=4mm"])

Code: softsim/control/sofa_inverse.py; tests: tests/test_sofa_inverse.py (skipped without SOFA). The result is an InverseResult like solve_inverse's (simulations is the number of settled QP runs).

What it is. SOFA's own inverse solver does the inversion inside the constraint solve. The scene is the scenario's body (same mesh, material, fixed vertices) with QPInverseProblemSolver replacing the Gauss-Seidel solver, each cable a CableActuator (the via points a BarycentricMapping child of the body, pullPoint 1 mm behind the first via point) with minForce / maxForce from the job's bounds, and the target a PositionEffector on a barycentric point at the tip face's rest centroid. At each step the QP finds the cable forces that bring the effector to its goal at the end of the step, within the bounds; the run is stepped until forces and outputs have stopped moving (settle_window, settle_tol as above), and the tensions are read.

  • Units. CableActuator's force is the constraint impulse: the bounds are given to it as force * dt and the reported tension is lambda / dt (without the factor the bound is 1/dt times too loose: the 0.7 N limit becomes 7000 N and the tip flies off; a mutation of this makes the tests fail).
  • Targets. tip_x, tip_y, tip_z are the effector's goal (axes chosen with useDirections); there must be at least as many axes as cables. The effector is a barycentric point and the scenario's output is the face's area-weighted centroid, so the goal is corrected by the remaining error after each settled run (up to max_corrections; the cantilever needed none, the error of the point against the centroid being 2 um). bend_angle / chord_angle are not a position: the effector goal is moved along an axis no position target uses (angle_direction, +x by default; -x is tried when +x leaves every actuator at its lower bound, as for a tube that curls to -x) and the goals of all the targets are found by a Broyden iteration on the angle / position read from the vertices (a secant for one angle: 2 QP runs for the 2 degree job). This works with any actuator (a pressure, a cable, both) and with angle and position targets together; each angle needs a free axis (at most three targets in all). It needs no second effector point (a pair of points on the tip face fixes the translation as well as the tilt, and a Rigid3d effector does not exist in this build: PositionEffector, CableEffector, VolumeEffector and BarycentricCenterEffector are the registered ones), so the angle is the scenario's own metric, exactly. Other outputs are refused.
  • Step. SOFA is implicit, so the step is 2 ms (timestep), not the scenario's 0.1 ms; the body gets the same stiffness-proportional damping as the repeated solve (settle_damping, default 10 ms) so that it settles.
  • Pressure actuators. A pneumatic actuator (SurfacePressureActuator) is built on the actuator's cavity region (a child node with the cavity triangles, mapped to the body); bounds are pressures (cavity: [0 kPa, 10 kPa]) and the targets are positions (tip_x, tip_y, tip_z; mind the direction a robot bends: the bending tube curls to -x, the PneuNet to -z). Measured: the solver's lambda is an impulse, pressure * dt, like the cables (the bounds go in as pressure * dt, the pressure is lambda / dt: a run clamped at 2 kPa gives the tip the ordinary backend's explicit follower pressure gives at 2 kPa, -0.1230656 mm, to 7 digits). Two traps, both found by measurement: the cavity triangles need the opposite winding to softsim's (else the volume shrinks and the pressure clamps at 0), and in SI units the QP's matrices are tiny (the pressure's entry is ~4e-12), so qpOASES returns lambda = 0 for every reachable goal and bangs between 0 and the bound for an unreachable one. The effector weight scales the objective: 1e6 (qp_weight) is the default with pressures, 1e5 and 1e7 give the same pressure. Angle targets work with a pressure (below).
  • Mixed actuators. Pressures and cables can be solved together (one QPInverseProblemSolver, each actuator with its own impulse bounds), with qp_weight 1e6 as soon as one is a pressure (it does not hurt the cable's scaling). scenarios/inflation/bending_cable.yaml is the bending tube with a cable in its thin +x wall: the pressure curls the tip to -x and lengthens the tube, the cable pulls it to +x and shortens it, so tip x and z together fix both.
  • Stroke-controlled cables. A cable with control: stroke (tension k (L - L0 + s)) is solved as a tension and the stroke read back as s = T / k - (L - L0) from the final vertices; the bounds are strokes (cable: [0 mm, 3 mm]) and the QP's tension bounds k (s_bound + L - L0) are re-set after each run at the length reached (the length depends on the tension, so the bound is found by a secant: 3 runs when a bound is active; a bound that is not active needs no iteration).
  • Outcome. Same statuses as above. A goal beyond the bounds leaves the cable at its bound (bounded_best, at_bounds): no second solve is made once a force is saturated.

Measured (4 mm cantilever mesh, 6 mm arm, 2 / 5 ms steps; shared CPU, times indicative; wall time includes building the scene):

Case QP (SOFA) Repeated solve, SOFA backend Speed Cantilever, 2 degrees 0.2699 N (angle error 1.4e-4 rad), 2 runs, 90 steps, 1.2 s 0.2716 N (error 8.6e-5 rad), 5 equilibria, 693 steps, 9.1 s 7.5x Cantilever, tip x = 2 mm 0.5575 N (tip 1.9977 mm), 1 run, 60 steps, 0.9 s 0.5509 N (tip 1.9767 mm), 6 equilibria, 868 steps, 10.0 s 11x Same, 8 mm with at most 0.7 N 0.7 N, tip 2.49 mm, bounded_best - - Arm, tip x 3.994 mm and z 118.515 mm 0.4497 / 0.1500 N (true 0.45 / 0.15 N), errors 0.02 um / 0.3 um, 1 run, 2.8 s 0.4464 / 0.1488 N (0.8% low, converged, tip errors 20 um and 12 nm), 13 equilibria, 2689 steps, 47 s; before the cable fix it was stalled, 0.245 / 0.234 N, 28 equilibria unsettled, 336 s 17x Bending tube (2 mm mesh, 1279 points), tip x = -0.28681 mm (what 4 kPa gives) 3999.0 Pa (true 4000, 0.03%; tip error 0.09 um), 3 runs, 110 steps of 2 ms, 32 s 4000.3 Pa, 7 equilibria, 824 steps, 225 s 7x PneuNet (1.5 mm mesh, 4936 points), tip z = 5.3077 mm (what 5 kPa gives, 10 ms steps) 4997.7 Pa (true 5000, 0.05%; tip error 1.5 um), 2 runs, 40 steps, 96 s not run (the explicit backend needs minutes per equilibrium at this size) - Bending tube, tip x = -1 mm with at most 2 kPa 2000 Pa, tip -0.1231 mm, bounded_best - - Bending tube, tilt 0.013947 rad (what 4 kPa gives) 4000.02 Pa (0.0005%; angle error 9e-8 rad), 4 runs (one on the wrong side, +x), 38 s; 3 runs, 25 s with angle_direction: -x not run (225 s per position target) - Tube with a cable in the thin wall, tip x 2.9624 mm and z 39.4169 mm (4 kPa and 0.2 N) 3983 Pa (0.4%) and 0.19992 N (0.04%), tip errors 0.1 and 0.3 um, 6 runs, 210 steps, 37 s not run (two actuators, minutes per equilibrium) - Same, bend_angle 0.138112 rad and tip z 39.4169 mm 4004.5 Pa (0.11%) and 0.20003 N (0.01%), 5 runs, 220 steps, 42 s - - Same, cable limited to 0.1 N cable 0.1 N, bounded_best - - Stroke cable (300 N/m), tip x 1.14667 mm (what a 1.5 mm stroke gives, 4 mm mesh) stroke 1.4997 mm (0.02%), 1 run, 0.5 s; for the angle target 1.4969 mm (0.2%), 2 runs - - Same, stroke limited to 1 mm stroke 1.0002 mm, tip 0.7693 mm (ordinary backend at a 1 mm stroke: 0.7682 mm), 3 runs, bounded_best - -

The tensions agree to 0.6% (angle target; the two stop at residuals of 0.014 and 0.009 of a 0.01 rad scale, i.e. 0.4% in angle) and 1.2% (position target; the repeated solve stopped 23 um short of the target, and scaling its tension by the ratio of the tips gives 0.5517 N against the QP's 0.5575 N: 1%). The QP's tension, applied as the ordinary backend's explicit cable force, puts the tip within 0.05 mm of the 2 mm target (tested). The arm's targets are the tip MuJoCo reaches at 0.45 / 0.15 N on the same mesh, so the 0.07% agreement is across backends.

The pressure targets are the tips the same model reaches at a held pressure: the bending tube's from the ordinary SOFA backend (explicit follower pressure, 2 ms steps, 59 s), the PneuNet's from a QP run clamped at 5 kPa (the explicit backend is too slow at 1.5 mm; the clamped run was checked against it on the tube). The tube's tip moves only 0.3 mm at 4 kPa (stiff walls), so its scale is 0.01 mm, not the default 1 mm, which a run that never pressurised would satisfy.

Why the arm stalled on the repeated solve (found and fixed). The ordinary SOFA backend used to apply the cable as an explicit follower force, and on the 6 mm arm that did not settle: the tip's x swung by 0.6-1.9 mm peak to peak indefinitely (period 0.39 s, 2.6 Hz, along the mesh diagonal), at every step from 10 ms to 0.25 ms, while MuJoCo settled. Measured on the 6 mm mesh at 0.45 / 0.15 N, Rayleigh beta 0.15 s:

Run Tip x peak to peak, last seconds explicit cable, dt 10 / 5 / 1 / 0.25 ms 0.59 / 0.85 / 1.9 / 3.9 mm (grows as dt shrinks; still growing at 0.25 ms) explicit, no damping, 5 ms 1.8 mm explicit, beta 0.5 / 1.5 s, 5 ms regrows to 0.67 mm / decays (0.012 mm at 3.5 s) cable A alone, B alone, both at half tension (10 ms) settle both cables at twice the tension (10 ms) 1.7 mm released at 2 s (no cable) decays in 1 s force-type CableConstraint (SoftRobots) instead of the force field identical to the explicit run to 4 digits linear (small) or corotational (large, svd) elastic law, same load settles (tip x 1.80, 4.39, 4.74 mm) cable as springs in the implicit system (below), 5 / 2 / 1 ms settles; tip x 4.0025 mm, z 118.514 mm at every step

So it is not the step size (it gets worse as the step shrinks, and extrapolating the positions to the end of the step for the force changes little), not the routing points (the cable's Jacobian is symmetric and positive semi-definite, checked against finite differences), and not the constraint form of the cable (identical). It needs both cables (the S shape) and the hyperelastic force field. The reading that fits all of it, and that the fix below supports (an inference, the hyperelastic tangent was not computed directly), is: the cable is a stabilising lateral stiffness T (I - u u^T) / l per segment, and under the arm's compression (0.6 N against a column whose Euler load is about 0.03 N) it balances the elastic force field's negative geometric stiffness. TetrahedronHyperelasticityFEMForceField has, we infer, that geometric part in its tangent, so the implicit matrix (and with it the Rayleigh beta K damping, and implicit Euler's own numerical damping) is nearly singular or indefinite in the bending mode, with the cable's compensating stiffness missing from it. The slowest modes are then undamped or anti-damped whatever the step: a limit cycle. The corotational field has no geometric stiffness in its tangent and the small-strain one no geometric effect at all, so they settle (but are wrong: 4.39 and 1.80 mm against 3.994 mm).

The backend now puts a tension-controlled cable into the implicit system: springs between the via points (mapped on the mesh) whose rest lengths are reset every step to length - T / k, which gives the force T at the current positions and the tangent T (I - u u^T) / l as stiffness, with a negligible axial k (1% of T per via-point spacing). The arm now settles within 1 s at 5 ms to 1 ms steps (tip x 4.0025 mm, z 118.514 mm; the QP path's tip is 3.994 mm and 118.515 mm, MuJoCo's 3.994 mm: 8.5 um apart in x, and the tension is the same), and the repeated solve on SOFA now converges (table above). Stroke-controlled and anchored cables are still explicit follower forces.

Limits.

  • Same model as the repeated solve, same locking. SOFA's linear tetrahedra lock in bending like MuJoCo's flex: the 4 mm cantilever is too stiff, and the tensions are those of the mesh (see actuation.md). The QP solves the model faster; it does not make the model more accurate.
  • Quasi-static. The forces are the held values at equilibrium; the path and the time to get there depend on the step and the damping. The QP is a per-step solution, not a trajectory plan.
  • The effector. A position (up to three axes) of one point. Angles are reached through that point's goal (the iteration above, a few extra QP runs), not as an orientation constraint of the QP; at most three targets (positions and angles) in all, an angle's direction must be a free axis, and the angle direction is a single sign for all angles. A tilt of an unreachable direction (e.g. +x for a tube that only curls to -x) is detected only when the actuators sit at their lower bound. Output constraints are not built. Fewer targets than actuators is refused (the repeated solve refuses it too).
  • Scope. Cables (tension- or stroke-controlled, no anchors) and pressures, alone or together, on one soft body with a tip / top region; force actuators, rigid bodies, contact, viscoelasticity, prescribed motion and moving mounts are refused or not built. A stroke cable's tendon is the scenario's (stiffness) and the stroke read back assumes the ordinary backend's model, tension = k (L - L0 + s) (an explicit follower force there; the QP has the tension as a constraint force).
  • One equilibrium. As above: the QP follows one branch from the rest state; a snapping structure may have others.
  • Bounds on the forces (tensions, pressures) and, for stroke cables, on the stroke through the iteration above; maxDispVariation / CableActuator's own displacement limits are not used (they would model a rigid tendon, not the series spring).

docs.title: Open decisions
docs.text: Each entry: the question, the options, what I recommend and why, and what I did meanwhile so nothing waits on it. Answer by editing the Decision line (or tell me in the chat); I will then do what the entry says.

docs.title: 1. MuJoCo timing fix: keep or revert
docs.text:
Since the prescribed-motion work, MuJoCo's step is split mj_step1 → explicit forces → mj_step2, and state() recomputes kinematics, because after mj_step MuJoCo's positions are one step stale (the forces and the reported state were a step old). It moves documented MuJoCo numbers by 1.5–3% (nrmse) and one 0.1 ms step in the time of a peak; the committed MuJoCo fits and transfers used the old timing.

  • Keep (recommended). The old timing is a bug (a force computed from last step's positions); the new numbers are the correct ones. Cost: the committed MuJoCo fits/transfers should be re-run when convenient (hours of MuJoCo time, not measured here); nothing else changes.
  • Revert. Hand-edit softsim/backends/mujoco/backend.py (it shares the file with prescribed motion). Keeps old numbers, keeps the bug.

Decision: Keep the fix (my recommendation, applied 2026-11-03 under your "follow your recommendations"). Why: the old timing used last step's positions, a bug. Re-run on 2026-11-03 from a frozen copy of the package: the bending, inflation and PneuNet transfers reproduce the committed numbers (bending unchanged; inflation E 23.66 vs 23.7 kPa, errors 0.5/1.2/2.2% as before; PneuNet body E 91.0 kPa, layer 1.76 MPa, cost 2.9%, checks 3.2% and 4.3%, as before), so the timing fix moves the transfers by less than their rounding and the documented tables stand. The Ecoflex 00-10 drop transfer (transfer_ecoflex_00_10_mujoco.yaml, 40 evaluations, fresh output folder) reproduces the committed run to every digit (E 64.89 kPa, g 0.678, tau 7.82 ms, cost 0.0593, 8.6% / 3.3%), so the numbers in docs/experiments.md are those of the current code. ecoflex_00_10_drop.yaml (fit against the recordings, 50 evaluations) is not re-run.

docs.title: 2. Joint drop + datasheet fit: stop or continue
docs.text:
The 80-evaluation joint fit is nearly flat (E0 190 kPa, g 0.60, τ 0.58 ms, cost 0.108) but not proven converged; at 40 evaluations it clearly was not.

  • Continue to 160 evaluations (80 more evaluations at 60–70 s each on the GPU box, so 1.5–2 h): settles whether the datasheet term and the drop cases are compatible.
  • Stop (recommended). The cost is flat to the third digit; the remaining mismatch (the 20 g first contact 14%) looks structural (the card has one Prony term) rather than unconverged, so more evaluations buy little. A better use of the time is a second Prony term, which changes the card, so it is your call.

Decision: Stop (recommendation applied 2026-11-03). Why: cost flat to the third digit; the residual looks structural (one Prony term). A second Prony term changes the card, so it waits for you.

docs.title: 3. M7 real data for the pneumatic finger (blocks "compare with a real finger")
docs.text:
The brief asks for a PneuNet against real public data with DOI and licence. What I found (Zenodo API, repositories, search, 2026-11-02):

Candidate DOI Licence Has Problem Elgeneidy, Lohse, Jackson (2017), Experimental data – modelling the bending response of soft pneumatic actuators 10.17028/rd.lboro.5509528 CC BY-NC 4.0 bending angle θ [deg] against pressure [psi] and tilt, flex-sensor volts; 1108 rows (training + testing) geometry and printed material are in the paper (Mechatronics 50, 2017, doi 10.1016/j.mechatronics.2017.10.005, open access) which I cannot download: the publisher and the repository mirrors return 403 or a bot challenge. I will not bypass that. Joshi & Paik (2019), Multi-DoF force characterization of soft actuators 10.5281/zenodo.3627901 CC-BY-4.0 pressure, position and force for pulling, tip loading and three-point bending the actuator is a fabric-constrained film bellows (Robertson et al. 2017), not a PneuNet, and neither geometry nor material is in the record Georgopoulou et al. (2021–22) 10.5281/zenodo.5841687, .5841739 CC-BY-4.0 stress–strain and resistance of printed TPS strips strain-sensor data; no pressure–angle pairs Omnidirectional soft sleeve (2026) 10.5281/zenodo.18433594 CC-BY-4.0 bending angle and force files (PDF) a sleeve, not a PneuNet; plots as PDFs
  • Option A (recommended): Elgeneidy. Right quantity (pressure → bending angle) with a published geometry. Needs you to download the paper (open access, https://doi.org/10.1016/j.mechatronics.2017.10.005) into data/raw/ so I can read the dimensions and the printing material and build the finger. The licence is non-commercial: fine for this research use, but the table must not be redistributed in the repository (as with the drop-test videos: referenced by DOI, downloaded by the user; the fit file points at the local copy). The data is also a free-bending angle from a flex-sensor-instrumented printed actuator, so the material is likely a printed elastomer rather than silicone: the card will have to be fitted, not taken from a datasheet.
  • Option B: build a finger of your own and measure it (angle against pressure on camera); gives full control of geometry and material, costs your bench time.
  • Option C: digitise a figure from an open-access paper that gives a full geometry (e.g. a CC-BY MDPI four-chamber design). Weaker: digitised points carry reading error, and I would flag them as such.

Meanwhile: the machinery is done and tested on a twin experiment (softsim fit, docs/experiments.md), and the reference's mesh convergence on the existing PneuNet is measured (docs/actuation.md).

Decision: Option A chosen by recommendation. Status 2026-11-03: the paper is in data/raw/ and the table is downloaded (data/raw/elgeneidy2017/data_open_access.xlsx, md5 45e17500b9c3afbe926262670a08a7ac checked against figshare; gitignored, CC BY-NC 4.0). The paper says the finger is moulded from Ecoflex-50 (SmoothOn), with a paper strain-limiting layer and a flex sensor, but gives NO dimensions: they are in Elgeneidy & Lohse, ASME IDETC 2016 (the Loughborough record is under permanent embargo). The table is a 100 Hz time series: P [psi], flex sensor, tilt phi [deg] (-45, 0, 45) and absolute bending angle theta [deg]; supply 8, 10, 12 psi; internal pressure up to about 7 psi (48 kPa), above the 8 kPa where the thin walls of our PneuNet already balloon. BLOCKED again on the geometry: needs the dimensions of that finger (a copy of the 2016 paper, or the user's own measurement of a finger).

Update 2026-11-03: Option C chosen (the 2016 paper costs money). Candidate: Wang, Zhang, Cai, Tong, Wei, Design, Experimental Validation, and Pressure-Control Simulation of a Modular Pneumatic Soft-Finger Gripper, Actuators 15(9), 488, doi 10.3390/act15090488, CC BY 4.0 (Crossref); PDF in data/raw/actuators-15-00488.pdf. It has: measured chord angle at 5, 10, ..., 40 kPa (Table 5: 5.00, 10.30, 16.90, 23.20, 30.10, 34.40, 36.80, 35.00 deg; one finger, one ascending sequence, no uncertainty stated); Shore A20 silicone (Posilicone) with a third-order Yeoh fit from the same batch (Table 2: C10 0.044163 MPa, C20 5.3071e-4, C30 1.6251e-5, D1 0.226434 /MPa; monotonic uniaxial only); nine chambers, a = 89 mm, h = 10 mm, wall t = 2 mm, chamber width 20 mm, finger width 24 mm, constraint layer c = 3 mm with teeth (3 mm wide, 1 mm high, 2 mm spacing), tip reserve 10 mm; the paper's Abaqus result (Table 4) as a second reference. Chord angle = angle between the initial axis and the root-to-tip line (not the tip rotation our bend_angle reports; a chord metric is needed). The finger hangs vertically in the photos. Open: the total height, the manifold height and the chamber/wall pitch are not stated (a = 89 mm with nine chambers does not match l = 5 mm and t = 2 mm), and Figure 2 is a schematic. The supplement (https://www.mdpi.com/article/10.3390/act15090488/s1) holds the raw tensile data and the Abaqus input files, which fix the geometry. MDPI returns 403 to my fetcher, so the user downloads it. Until then the finger is not built: guessed dimensions would make the comparison meaningless.

docs.title: 4. M8 rod backend: which library
docs.text:
M8 wants a rod (Cosserat) backend for slender bodies, cross-checked against FEM.

  • SOFA BeamAdapter (installed with the v26.06 plugins; no new dependency): fits the existing SOFA backend; Euler–Bernoulli-like beams with fixed stiffness.
  • PyElastica: a real Cosserat rod (shear, twist, dynamics), pip-installable; a new dependency and a new backend to write.
  • Own implementation: most control, most work, and a verification burden (it would need its own analytic checks).

Recommendation: BeamAdapter first, because it is already installed and a cantilever has exact solutions to check it against; PyElastica only if a quantity BeamAdapter cannot give (large shear, twist) is needed.

Decision: SOFA BeamAdapter first (recommendation applied 2026-11-03). Why: already installed, no new dependency, cantilever has exact solutions to check against.

docs.title: 5. Rigid-tendon option for cables
docs.text:
A cable whose tendon stiffness tends to infinity (stroke imposed exactly) is the one case where an implicit SOFA CableConstraint (displacement type) would beat the explicit force, which is unstable for stiff tendons. It changes the cable model (today stiffness must be finite) and is SOFA-only.

  • Add it (config: stiffness: rigid): lets SOFA run stroke-controlled cables at any stiffness; the reference already has a stiff-tendon test to compare with. Cost: about a day, SOFA-only.
  • Skip (recommended for now). No scenario needs it; finite tendon stiffness is the physical case.

Decision: Skip (recommendation applied 2026-11-03). Why: no scenario needs it; finite tendon stiffness is the physical case.

Status 2026-11-03, late: finger built, validation NOT yet passing. Built from the supplement's mesh: shape ribbed_finger (softsim/geometry/soft.py; solid 19,568 mm^3 and cavity 12,400 mm^3 equal the paper's mesh, tests/test_ribbed_finger.py), card posilicone_a20_wang2026, scenario scenarios/actuation/ribbed_finger.yaml, metric chord_angle, data datasets/wang2026_finger.yaml, tool tools/compare_wang_finger.py. First reference runs (fem, 2 mm, teeth omitted): the dynamic ramp failed to converge at ~17 kPa after 24 min; a static probe (steps of 2 kPa) gave chord 10.0 deg at 2 kPa, 18.5 at 4, 26.0 at 6, 32.4 at 8, 37.3 at 10, 41.5 at 14 kPa, then a limit point near 16 kPa (volume doubles). The paper measured 5.0 deg at 5 kPa and 10.3 at 10 kPa and its Abaqus gives 5.12 and 10.92: our finger bends about four times too much. Not explained yet. Candidates: teeth omitted (the floor is 2.6 mm thick with them, not 2), the paper's Root_Face and planar constraint, the pressure's direction/sign, or the solver. The decisive next step: load the paper's OWN mesh (the .inp corner nodes, CC BY) as a mesh file in softsim and run it with the same Yeoh card, which separates my geometry from the solver; then the same mesh with the paper's constraints. Do not report any agreement with the measurements until that is understood.

Update 2026-11-04: the 4x was the missing planar constraint. The paper's .inp holds *Boundary AllNodesPlanar, 3, 3: U3 = 0 on EVERY node (plane strain across the 24 mm width), plus Root_Face, ENCASTRE. Our finger had a free width. With u_y = 0 on all nodes (y is our width axis; z is the height, constraining it removes all bending), same Yeoh card, 2 mm mesh, no teeth, static, chord angle by the paper's definition:

p [kPa] ours measured paper FE 5 5.03 5.00 5.12 10 10.07 10.30 10.92 15 14.92 16.90 17.34 20 19.07 23.20 24.09 30 20.85 34.40 35.25 40 4.51 35.00 35.38

Agreement to 10 kPa (within 2%), then ours falls behind and peaks at 21.7 deg (27.5 kPa) before un-bending. Steps of 2.5 kPa give the same curve, so this is the equilibrium path, not a branch jump. Open: the toothless floor (2 mm instead of an effective 2.6 mm) is the leading suspect for the high-pressure gap (the floor is the strain-limiting layer); being run with teeth at 1.5 mm. The planar constraint is not yet an option of the scenario (the probe sets Problem3D.fixed_dofs by hand: scratch script, not in the repo). Reproduce: build the scene from scenarios/actuation/ribbed_finger.yaml with body.mesh.size=2mm body.geometry.tooth_height=0 mm, set fixed_dofs to 3*node+1 for all nodes, Solid3DSolver(dynamic=False), raise pressures[0] in steps and read chord_angle.

Update 2026-11-04, later: validation passes with teeth. Same setup but teeth included (tooth_height=1 mm, mesh 1.5 mm, planar u_y = 0, static, steps of 5 kPa), chord angle [deg]:

p [kPa] ours measured paper FE 5 5.04 5.00 5.12 10 10.73 10.30 10.92 15 16.99 16.90 17.34 20 23.55 23.20 24.09 25 29.73 30.10 30.45 30 34.42 34.40 35.25 35 36.30 36.80 37.16 40 34.41 35.00 35.38

All eight points are within 0.5 deg of the measurement, and the peak and the fall-off after 35 kPa are reproduced. The toothless floor was the cause of the earlier gap. Still to do: make the planar constraint a scenario option, run through tools/compare_wang_finger.py, mesh convergence (1.5 mm vs 1 mm), a test, and the MuJoCo/SOFA transfers. Reproduce: as in the previous update, with body.mesh.size=1.5mm body.geometry.tooth_height=1 mm.

Update 2026-11-04, end-to-end: the scenario file reproduces the paper. body.plane_strain: y is now a scenario option (reference only; tests/test_plane_strain.py: a plane-strain beam deflects 0.8106 of a free one against 1 - nu^2 = 0.7975, and dropping the held dofs fails the test). The committed scenario, run as is on the reference (softsim run scenarios/actuation/ribbed_finger.yaml --backend fem --set simulation.timestep=10ms, 1.5 mm, dynamic 1 s ramp), read by python tools/compare_wang_finger.py runs/wang/fem_1p5mm --plot (figure docs/media/wang_finger.png): RMS error against the measurements 0.76 deg (the paper's own FE: 0.56 deg), largest error 1.3 deg (30 kPa); the 5 kPa point is 1.15 deg low, the start of the ramp, where the dynamic run lags the static value (static probe: 5.04). Open: mesh convergence (1 mm), transfers to MuJoCo/SOFA (Yeoh must be projected), docs/actuation.md section.

Update 2026-11-04, plane strain on MuJoCo and SOFA. body.plane_strain runs on all three backends. MuJoCo: the scene is lowered to a zero prescribed motion of every free vertex along the axis (SoftBodySpec.lowered). SOFA: the same lowering was tried first and failed the ratio test (tip deflection with the width held / free: 0.17 at nu = 0.45 and 0.14 at nu = 0.3, expected 1 - nu^2 = 0.80), so it is not locking: PartialLinearMovementProjectiveConstraint over every vertex with one held axis made the beam about 7x too stiff (the held axis was exactly 0, the free ones barely moved). SOFA now uses PartialFixedProjectiveConstraint with the axis as fixed direction: 0.85 at 3 mm in the short check, test passes at 2 mm. Caution for later: a many-vertex prescribed region holding one axis on SOFA may over-constrain the same way; tests/test_prescribed.py only covers boundary grips. tests/test_plane_strain.py: reference 0.8106 (+1.6% vs 1 - nu^2), MuJoCo and SOFA within 6% (slow-marked: 2 and 12 min).

Update 2026-11-04, Wang finger on MuJoCo: the transfer does not work at 2 mm, the mesh is the limit. calibrations/transfer_wang_finger_mujoco.yaml (stable Neo-Hookean projection of the Yeoh card, nu 0.45, 2 mm, 0.2 ms; output runs/transfer/wang_finger_mujoco_2mm): best E 242 kPa, cost 0.25 (raw card 0.28); cavity volume NRMSE 0.008 but chord angle NRMSE 0.49, flat across E (cost 0.25-0.45 for E 219-468 kPa; E 137 kPa diverged), so it is not a modulus problem. Mesh test at the fitted E, run as the scenario with the backend overrides: RMS error against the measurements 16.4 deg at 2 mm, 8.1 deg at 1.5 mm, reference 0.76 deg (table from python tools/compare_wang_finger.py runs/wang/mujoco_2mm runs/wang/mujoco_1.5mm runs/wang/fem_1p5mm). The error halves with 25% finer mesh: the 2 mm walls are about one linear tet thick and bend too stiff, and a modulus cannot compensate because the stiffening depends on the load shape. 1.5 mm on MuJoCo takes ~40 min per ramp. A finer mesh (1 mm) is untested and probably too slow. SOFA transfer not run: it uses linear tets too, so the same limit is expected; it was not tested. (compare_wang_finger.py --plot rewrote docs/media/wang_finger.png with the two MuJoCo curves added.)

Update 2026-11-04, Wang finger on SOFA at 1.5 mm. calibrations/transfer_wang_finger_sofa.yaml (stable Neo-Hookean card, nu 0.45, 1.5 mm, 2 ms, 6 evaluations, 51 min, ~9 min per ramp; output runs/transfer/wang_finger_sofa_1p5mm): the unfitted card (E 268 kPa) is the best point, cost 0.18 (chord angle NRMSE 0.25, cavity volume 0.11); E 293k 0.23, 219k 0.27, 370k 0.32, 468k 0.40, 137k diverged at t = 0.75 s. Chambers_5 check 0.16. So the fit finds nothing to gain from E; the remaining error is mesh/element error. Checked against the measurements (python tools/compare_wang_finger.py runs/wang/sofa_1p5mm runs/wang/mujoco_1.5mm runs/wang/fem_1p5mm): RMS error SOFA 1.5 mm 10.2 deg (9.3 deg low at 20 kPa), MuJoCo 1.5 mm 8.1, reference 0.76. So the earlier reading that SOFA is the usable fast backend for this finger was wrong: the NRMSE against the reference (0.25) understated a 10 deg miss, and neither fast backend reproduces the finger at 1.5 mm. Mutation tests on the finger (tests/test_ribbed_finger.py): chord measured from the origin, chord angle against the wrong vector, tooth count +1, floor height doubled each fail a test on an assertion (tooth count 20 vs 19, solid volume 20936 vs 19568 mm3). Full suite: 319 passed, 13 slow deselected.

Update 2026-11-05, mesh convergence of the reference (1 mm vs 1.5 mm). softsim run scenarios/actuation/ribbed_finger.yaml --backend fem --set body.mesh.size=1mm --set simulation.timestep=10ms --set simulation.output_rate=100Hz --out runs/wang/fem_1mm, compared with python tools/compare_wang_finger.py runs/wang/fem_1mm runs/wang/fem_1p5mm. RMS error against the measurements: 0.95 deg at 1 mm, 0.76 deg at 1.5 mm (paper FE 0.56). The two meshes differ by at most 0.9 deg (20-25 kPa, 1 mm lower) and 0.5 deg RMS. So the reference is converged to about 1 deg, which is also the size of its disagreement with the measurements: "0.76 deg" should be read as agreement within the discretisation error, not as a proof that the model is exact. The finer mesh is not closer to the measurements (mid-range ~1 deg low).

Update 2026-11-06, SOFA at 1 mm. Same run as SOFA 1.5 mm at body.mesh.size=1mm (73 min, runs/wang/sofa_1mm, read with python tools/compare_wang_finger.py runs/wang/sofa_1mm runs/wang/sofa_1p5mm runs/wang/fem_1p5mm): 8.14 deg RMS against the measurements, from 10.24 at 1.5 mm; the curve keeps rising to 40 kPa (27.5 deg) and shows no fall-off after 35 kPa. Past the 8 deg line set in the gripper plan, so SOFA stays out of the gripper.

Update 2026-11-06, the reference with the fast backends' card: the mesh claim holds, with a floor added. The 8-16 deg errors above could have been the Neo-Hookean card, not the mesh, so the reference ran that card itself (--set body.material.preset=posilicone_a20_wang2026_nh --set body.material.elastic.youngs_modulus=268000 --set body.material.elastic.poisson_ratio=0.45, 1.5 mm, 10 ms, runs/wang/fem_nh_1p5mm, read with python tools/compare_wang_finger.py runs/wang/fem_nh_1p5mm runs/wang/sofa_1mm runs/wang/fem_1p5mm). Over 5-35 kPa it is 3.18 deg RMS from the measurement, bending too much (+2.8 to +4.6 deg at 10-30 kPa), against 0.79 deg for the Yeoh card and 8.22 deg for SOFA at 1 mm, which bends too little. SOFA is 10.4 deg RMS below the reference on the same card, so the card does not explain SOFA's error: the under-bending is the discretisation, as claimed above. Two things change. A fast backend on this card cannot do better than about 3 deg even with a perfect mesh. And the card has no stiffening at large stretch: past about 35 kPa the reference's bend collapses (28.7 deg at 0.78 s, 12.1 deg at 0.85 s, 38.6 kPa) and Newton stops converging at 0.867 s even at 0.6 ms substeps, so that run ends at 0.85 s; the compare table's 40 kPa row shows the last frame and its overall 8.61 deg should not be read. SOFA's and MuJoCo's lack of a fall-off there is therefore not evidence of accuracy.

docs.title: 6. The reference's static friction creeps, at a rate set by the time step
docs.text:
The fem backend smooths Coulomb friction with IPC's mollifier below a slip of SLIP_TOLERANCE = 1 um per step (softsim/backends/fem/backend.py): below that, friction is mu N (2 y - y^2) with y = slip / 1 um, a spring rather than a stick. A contact held at a fraction r = F / (mu N) of its limit slips y = 1 - sqrt(1 - r) um every step, so it creeps at y x 1 um / dt. Measured on the sliding-block benchmark at r = 0.71 (benchmarks/sticking_block.yaml): 0.233 mm/s at dt 2 ms and 0.117 mm/s at 4 ms (uniform-r prediction 0.233 and 0.116). MuJoCo, known for soft-constraint creep, creeps less on this case (0.13 mm/s); SOFA least. Sliding is unaffected: all three backends are within 0.8-0.94% of exact Coulomb sliding (benchmarks/sliding_block.yaml). The finite-element grasps (docs/gripper.md) hold for seconds with the same smoothing, so part of their sink is this creep.

Done meanwhile (no default changed): contact.slip_speed makes the tolerance a speed (slip_speed x dt, the IPC convention), so the creep is y x slip_speed at any step. Measured, 5 mm block, slip_speed 1e-5 m/s: 0.0052 mm/s at dt 2 ms and 0.0053 mm/s at 4 ms; sliding unchanged (70.45 mm). tests/test_friction.py checks both behaviours.

  • Make slip_speed 1e-5 m/s the default (recommended). Creep 45x lower at dt 2 ms and independent of the step. Cost: the finite-element grasps (about an hour each on the GPU machine) should be re-run, and their numbers in docs/gripper.md may move.
  • Keep the per-step default, and state the creep rate with every finite-element grasp.

Decision: make slip_speed 1e-5 m/s the default (2026-11-11, agreed with you). contact.slip_speed: null restores the old per-step smoothing. Still to do: re-run the finite-element grasps on the GPU machine and update docs/gripper.md.

docs.title: Three-minute gripper demo
docs.text: A script for showing the soft gripper live, on docs/viewer/gripper.html. Every outcome below is rehearsed on the real page by tools/rehearse_gripper_demo.py, and held grasps are checked out to 20 s, so you can talk over them.

docs.title: Before you start
docs.text:
cd ~/personal_projects/softsim
source .venv/bin/activate
python tools/rehearse_gripper_demo.py docs/viewer/gripper.html    # every beat as scripted, about 3 minutes
xdg-open docs/viewer/gripper.html

Leave the page on Play, with Box, 2 fingers, friction 0.80 and mass 10 g, which is how it opens. Check that the Speed readout says more than 1x real time on the machine you will present from. The page needs no network or server.

If the page fails, the desktop version has the same finger and the same sliders: python tools/demo_gripper.py --finger softsim/reduced/wang_finger.json.

docs.title: 0:00 The problem (20 s)
docs.text: Soft robots are hard to simulate. An accurate solver takes hours; a fast one is usually wrong. This gripper is built from a published silicone finger. My own finite-element solver matches the authors' measured bending to 0.76 degrees. That solver is far too slow to touch, so it taught a fast model, and the fast model is what's running here, live, in this browser.

docs.title: 0:20 Pick something up (30 s)
docs.text:
Set Finger pressure to 30 kPa and press Grasp and lift. The fingers close, and the badge goes to Held.

Air pressure bends the fingers. Nothing here is animated: that's physics running in the page. Look at the readout: the grip gives friction enough to carry 0.20 newtons, and this box weighs 0.10.

docs.title: 0:50 Break it on purpose (30 s)
docs.text:
Drag Mass up slowly, about 1 g a second, while pointing at the bar under the readout.

Friction can carry about 20 grams at this pressure, so it should let go right about there.

The badge goes to Dropped at 20 g.

That's the number you get by hand, from grip times friction.

Press Reset, set Mass to 20 g and Finger pressure to 35 kPa, then press Grasp and lift. Held.

More pressure, more grip, and the same box stays up.

docs.title: 1:20 Show the truth (45 s)
docs.text:
Open Truth and press Closed, Off the table, then End.

A fast model is only worth something if you know where it's wrong. Left is the finite-element grasp, which took an hour to compute. Right is the live model, on the same clock. Both pick the box up almost as soon as the palm moves, and both carry it. The grip agrees to 8% while holding. What the fast model can't show is the pad squashing around the box, which you see on the left. I also ran the 30 gram box on the slow solver: the fingertips slide up the box and it stays on the table, which is what the fast model said. That's one check each side of the limit.

Press Play at 1/4 speed if you have the time.

docs.title: 2:05 What it can hold (25 s)
docs.text:
Open Grasp map, and select the cell for 15 g at 30 kPa.

That's 504 grasps from the fast model, which you could never run on the slow solver. Pick a cell and it loads straight into the live demo.

It opens in Play and picks the box up.

docs.title: 2:30 What I'd tell you before you trust it (30 s)
docs.text: None of these grasps is checked against hardware, only against my solver. The solver is what's checked against real measurements. Two finite-element grasps are in, on a coarse mesh, one held and one dropped, so the rest of the map is the fast model's own. It also taught me to be careful what "held" means: my first map stopped two seconds after the lift, and 48 of its 154 held grasps turned out to fall within 20 seconds, so now every grasp has to last 20. What I'd stand behind is the chain: measurements, solver, fast model, with the error at each link written down.

docs.title: Stay away from
docs.text:
• Quoting a payload limit as a property of the gripper. The 20-26 g is this fast model's, and the real four-finger gripper held far more.
  • Calling the map checked. Two finite-element grasps check one boundary, the box at 25 kPa. The cylinder and bottle are unchecked. If someone asks about the earlier no-slip runs, see the gripper notes.
  • Cylinder or bottle at 30 kPa or above. These grip well and then fall within 20 s. If you want a second object, use the cylinder at 10 g, 25 kPa, which stays up for the full 20 s.
  • Three and four fingers as evidence. They are fun to show, but they are extrapolations.
  • Waiting on a held box. It sinks about 0.4 mm/s. That is MuJoCo's soft friction creeping, not a real slip.

docs.title: Likely questions
docs.text:
Why not use SOFA or MuJoCo's soft bodies? On this finger, both were 8° or more off the measurements, against under 1° for my solver. Full MuJoCo flex also ran at about 1/370 of real time.

How good is the fast finger? 5-7% on a tip load left out of the fit, and 9-27% on a load spread along the pads, which is its known weakness.

Why is the grip so small? The finger is very soft: 0.2 N moves its tip about 90 mm. This is a gripper for light things.

Does it work on a real gripper? Not shown, and I know it's weaker than the real one. The authors measured 0.96 N of tip force at 35 kPa, which they never modelled. I ran it blind on my solver and got 0.165 N, about 5.5 times too weak, from the same finger that matches their bending to 0.76 degrees. Releasing the width and stiffening the rubber closes about half of it, and no setting matches both. Where the tip touched their gauge isn't recorded. So the bending is checked and the force isn't, and the gripper's limits inherit that.

docs.title: Design optimisation
docs.text: softsim optimize <job.yaml> tunes design parameters of a scenario (geometry, a cable offset, a material value, any dotted config key) to maximise, minimise or hit a number from the run's summary, optionally under limits on other summary numbers. It reuses the calibration engine's patterns: a YAML job, bounds, a resumable evaluation log, spawned worker processes, a report. Code: softsim/design/optimize.py.

docs.title: A job
docs.text:
scenario: ../scenarios/actuation/cable_cantilever.yaml    # relative to the job file
backend: mujoco                                            # optional
overrides: [body.mesh.size=5mm]                            # applied before the design values
parameters:
  "actuators[0].path[0][0]":                               # dotted key, list indices allowed (also nested)
    initial: 3 mm
    bounds: [0.5 mm, 4.5 mm]
    tie: ["actuators[0].path[1][0]"]                       # more keys that take the same value
objective: {metric: final_bend_angle, target: 0.06 rad}   # or goal: maximize | minimize; `per: <metric>` divides
constraints:                                               # optional; a metric or a design key, min and/or max
  - {metric: cable_stroke, max: 4 mm}
max_evaluations: 30
output: ../runs/design/cantilever_target_angle
  • Parameters: bounds and initial are numbers (SI) or unit strings; mixing dimensions is an error. log: true searches in log space, integer: true rounds (e.g. segments), tie sets further keys to the same value (the cantilever's cable runs from path[0] to path[1], both at offset d). A key that does not exist in the scenario is an error: a typo must not silently optimise nothing.
  • Objective: any key of the scenario's summary (softsim run prints them: final_bend_angle, final_tip_x, cable_stroke, peak_max_radius, ...). goal: maximize|minimize, or target: v (minimise |metric - v|). per: other_metric optimises the ratio (e.g. angle per unit tension).
  • Constraints: bounds on summary metrics (or on design keys).
  • Examples: jobs/cantilever_target_angle.yaml (match a tip angle with the cable offset) and jobs/cable_finger_slots.yaml (slot depth and width of the cable finger, under a stroke limit).

Outputs in output: report.yaml (best design, objective, constraint values, whether the best is feasible, which parameters sit on a bound, evaluations simulated/failed, wall time), history.parquet (every evaluation in order, with every summary metric), best_overrides.txt (the best design as key=value lines for softsim run --set; a nested list index is written as the whole inner list) and evaluations.jsonl.

docs.title: Method
docs.text:
Nelder-Mead (scipy, derivative-free, bounded) in the unit cube of the parameters (log or linear scale), started at initial with a simplex step of 25 % of each range (simplex_step). The initial simplex is evaluated first, in parallel with --jobs; later evaluations are sequential (Nelder-Mead is). No new dependency.

Constraints are exterior penalties, not a constrained solver: cost = f / |f0| + 100 x sum of the relative violations (how far a metric lies beyond its bound, divided by the bound), with f0 the objective at the first evaluation. The penalty is steep but finite, so the simplex can cross an infeasible region. The reported best is chosen among feasible evaluations only; the penalised cost only steers the search. If no evaluation is feasible, the report has feasible: false, a warning, the violated constraints with their violation, and the least-violating design; the CLI prints the warning and exits with status 2. Infeasibility is never hidden. A failed simulation (crash, unstable, non-finite objective) costs 1000 and is counted in failed.

Log and resume: every evaluation is appended to evaluations.jsonl with its full summary. Re-running the job replays them (Nelder-Mead is deterministic), so a stopped job continues, and raising max_evaluations extends a finished one. Entries are keyed by the scenario (its file and the resolved config, extends included), softsim's own code, the overrides (and backend) and the parameter keys, so a code change starts afresh; objective, constraints and bounds are not in the key, since they only re-weigh stored summaries.

docs.title: Checked against known optima
docs.text:
tests/test_optimize.py (MuJoCo, cable cantilever at 6 mm mesh and 0.3 ms steps, about 2 s per simulation; the angle grows monotonically with the cable offset d because the cable puts a moment T d on the beam):

  • maximising the tip angle for d in [1, 4] mm ends at the upper bound (4 mm, at_bounds lists it);
  • matching a 0.05 rad target gives the d that nine bisection steps on the same forward map give, to 20 um (bracket 6 um); the objective reaches the target to 0.2 mrad;
  • a stopped job (5 evaluations) continues to 8 without re-simulating logged points (the number of simulations is counted); an identical rerun simulates nothing; a changed override does not reuse the log;
  • an unreachable constraint (cable stroke >= 1 m) returns feasible: false with the violation; a cap on the angle itself gives a feasible best just below the cap;
  • bad job files (unknown keys, bad or mixed-unit bounds, initial outside bounds, a typo in a design key, missing goal, empty constraint, unknown metric) raise ConfigError with the reason.

Mutation checks: a log that is never read fails the resume test; flipping the maximise sign fails the upper-bound test.

docs.title: Measured examples
docs.text:
Cantilever, target tip angle (jobs/cantilever_target_angle.yaml; MuJoCo, 5 mm mesh, target 0.06 rad): cable offset d = 2.127 mm found in 30 evaluations (26 simulations, 109 s on one core, about 4 s each); the objective reaches 0.060001 rad. The angle at this d on other models (same scenario, measured):

model tip angle at d = 2.127 mm MuJoCo, 5 mm mesh (the one optimised) 0.0600 rad MuJoCo, 2 mm mesh (scenario default) 0.134 rad fem reference, 5 mm mesh 0.198 rad Euler-Bernoulli, T d L / (E I) 0.196 rad

The optimum on the coarse MuJoCo mesh is 3.3 times off the reference: that d bends the real beam to 0.2 rad, not 0.06. This is the locking bias of the limits section below, measured; re-running the job with backend: fem (and a coarser time step) gives the physical d.

Cable finger, slot geometry (jobs/cable_finger_slots.yaml; MuJoCo, 3 mm mesh, --jobs 2): maximise the final bend angle over slot depth in [1, 4] mm and slot width in [1, 5] mm, subject to a cable stroke of at most 4 mm. Best: depth 4.0 mm (the upper bound: deeper slots bend more, and 4.5 mm would cut the tendon's web), width 4.875 mm, bend angle 0.278 rad against 0.160 rad at the starting design (3 mm, 3 mm); the stroke there is 1.84 mm, so the constraint is inactive. 30 evaluations (21 distinct designs, the rest revisits served from the log), 437 s for the last run (earlier evaluations were replayed from a first, stopped run). An earlier version of this job allowed depths up to 6 mm: the scenario refuses a slot deeper than the tendon offset, those evaluations were reported as FAILED with the reason, and the bounds were fixed. The width optimum is not sharp: the bend angle jitters by about 0.01 rad between neighbouring widths (4.0 mm: 0.260, 4.5 mm: 0.271, 4.625 mm: 0.258, 4.75 mm: 0.276, 5.0 mm: 0.270) because each design is re-meshed, so the optimiser sees mesh noise of about 4 % and the width is determined only to about 0.3 mm. Checked on the fem reference (2 mm mesh, 2 ms step, the scenario's 0.2 N; about 20 min each on the laptop):

Design (depth / width) MuJoCo, 3 mm Reference, 2 mm start, 3 / 3 mm 0.160 rad 0.267 rad optimised, 4 / 4.875 mm 0.278 rad 0.488 rad (stroke 2.63 mm, within the 4 mm limit) gain +74% +83%

The ranking transfers: the design MuJoCo chose is better on the reference by a similar (slightly larger) factor, while MuJoCo's absolute angles are about 1.7 times too small (linear tetrahedra lock). Use the fast backend to rank designs, the reference to state how far the winner bends. Reproduce: softsim run scenarios/actuation/cable_finger.yaml --backend fem --set simulation.timestep=2ms --set body.mesh.size=2mm --set body.geometry.slot_depth=4mm --set body.geometry.slot_width=4.875mm.

docs.title: Limits
docs.text:
• The backend's error bar applies to the optimum. The optimiser exploits the simulator, including its errors. MuJoCo's linear tetrahedra lock in bending: the coarse cantilever above bends 0.084 rad where Euler-Bernoulli gives 0.28 rad, so a design tuned to a target angle on MuJoCo is a design for the locked beam, not for the real one (the table above: 3.3 times off). Check the winner on the fem reference (softsim run <scenario> --backend fem --set ... with the best_overrides.txt lines) and re-optimise, or calibrate the backend's effective material first (softsim transfer).
  • Local, deterministic search. Nelder-Mead finds the optimum nearest the start; use several starts for multimodal problems. It stalls on the plateaus of integer parameters (they are rounded), so scan those by hand. Dimensions beyond ~6 parameters need many more evaluations than the default 40.
  • Penalty, not a constrained solver: with a loose max_evaluations the best feasible point can lie slightly inside the true constrained optimum.
  • Geometry must stay valid: a design the mesher or backend refuses is a failed evaluation (cost 1000); keep the bounds inside the shape's valid range (e.g. the slots must not exceed the body).
  • Mesh noise: a design change re-meshes the body, so the objective carries discretisation jitter (about 4 % on the finger); the optimum is not resolved finer than that. Use a mesh fine enough that the jitter is below the differences you care about.
  • Each evaluation is a full simulation; there is no surrogate and no gradient.

docs.title: Soft drop bench
docs.text:
Drop things on the Ecoflex cylinder and watch the impact in slow motion, with the high-speed film's trace beside the live one. It runs on your own machine.

xdg-open docs/viewer/drop.html      # or double-click it: no server, the solver is inside the file

Set height, offset and tilt, then declare the object and the soft body. The fall plays in real time and the impact at about 1/300 of real time, close to the 3000 fps film played at 10 frames per second. Replay a recorded drop uses the film's measured impact speed, offset and spin, restores the filmed settings and overlays its track.

docs.title: What you can declare
docs.text:
Setting Ways to give it Object Shape disc or ball, or the bare cylinder falling on the table Size diameter, and thickness for a disc Weight mass, or a material (its density times the volume; a disc's knob adds no mass this way) Soft body Stiffness a library material, Young's E, shear G, or a datasheet's 100% modulus Other Poisson's ratio, density, relaxing share g and relaxation time τ Size diameter and height

Every value can be typed or dragged. Switching between E, G and 100% modulus keeps the same solid and only changes how it is written: G = E / 2(1 + ν), and 100% modulus = 1.75 G, the engineering stress of an incompressible Neo-Hookean solid at twice its length. The panel shows the resulting E, G, K and masses, and the readout shows the time step, which shrinks as the body stiffens, so stiffer bodies play slower.

Library materials use their initial shear modulus, from slow tests, as a Neo-Hookean solid with no relaxation, and the page's ν rather than the card's. Those cards are softer than the same silicone under impact: Ecoflex 00-10's slow card has G = 12.9 kPa, close to the filmed card's relaxed 47.8 × (1 − 0.691) = 14.8 kPa. Add relaxation by hand for an impact.

A new body size stretches the 40 × 17 mm mesh, so very flat or very tall bodies have elongated elements. There is no Shore hardness input: nothing here checks a Shore-to-modulus conversion.

docs.title: The solver
docs.text:
tools/drop_solver.js is an explicit solver written for this page: linear tetrahedra with nodal averaged pressure, a 3.5 mm mesh (762 nodes, 3240 tetrahedra), penalty contact and a rigid object with six degrees of freedom. It uses the 3D reference's physical card unchanged (Neo-Hookean, E0 = 143.3 kPa, ν = 0.4995, g = 0.691, τ = 2 ms). Nothing is fitted. The page and the checks run the same file.

Two findings shaped it:

  • ν cannot be relaxed. At ν = 0.47 the 50 g impact compresses the core by a quarter and collapses it. The true ν = 0.4995 costs 2-3 µs steps, which slow motion absorbs.
  • Fitting did not help. A grid over E0 and g improved 50 g only by making 20 g worse, so the card stayed as it is.

docs.title: Checks
docs.text:
python tools/check_drop_solver.py
python tools/make_drop_page.py
python tools/check_drop_page.py docs/viewer/drop.html --shots runs/page
pytest tests/test_drop_solver.py
Drop Film peak 3D reference track Page solver RMS gap to film, first contact 20 g 3.74 mm at 3.33 ms 3.85 mm at 3.00 ms 3.37 mm at 2.86 ms 9.2% 50 g 4.31 mm at 3.67 ms 4.31 mm at 3.40 ms 4.83 mm at 3.76 ms 25.1%
  • tests/test_drop_solver.py: stress against the closed-form law, relaxation against the Prony curve, free flight against the parabola, the filmed peaks within 15%, and the heaviest objects survive the filmed height. Mutations of the relaxation, the pressure, the object's gravity and the contact reaction each fail a test.
  • The same file: a declared 100% modulus comes back as the solver's engineering stress at twice the length. Twice the size at the same speed gives twice the indentation and time, and four times the stiffness at twice the speed gives the same indentation in half the time, both within 0.2%. Mutations of each conversion, the mesh axes, the ball's volume and the size and wave speed in the bulk viscosity each fail a test.
  • tools/check_drop_page.py opens the page from disk in headless Chrome, fails on any script error, and compares the filmed drops with the same solver under Node: the peaks agree to 0.001 mm. Two declared drops run through the page's fields and match jobs written by hand from the same numbers to 0.001 mm. Real clicks confirm that changing the declaration keeps E, a typed modulus reaches the solver, and a filmed replay restores the card.

docs.title: Limits
docs.text:
• The rebound is too slow. At 20 ms the film's 50 g weight is about 15 mm above the rest surface and the solver's about 8 mm, so bounce height is not a prediction. The page's trace shows the gap.
  • Only the 20 and 50 g drops at the filmed height and on the filmed body are checked against film. Every other object, body, material, height or tilt is unchecked, and the page says so. The similarity tests show the sizes and stiffness reach the solver correctly, not that those drops match reality.
  • The 500 g film is not reproduced: the solver peaks at 9.0 mm against 4.52 mm, and why is open (experiments.md).
  • 500 g from 80 cm breaks the solver. The page says so and stops.
  • Peak force is filtered over 0.2 ms, because a node landing on the object is a one-step spike. It is 66 N for the 50 g drop, where the film implies 65 N at peak indentation; the two are not the same moment in general.

docs.title: Gymnasium environments (M12, CPU groundwork)
docs.text:
A reach task on any actuation scene as a Gymnasium environment: the action is the actuator values, the observation a list of scenario metrics, the reward a smooth distance to a target. Code: softsim/envs/; tests: tests/test_envs.py. The extra is optional: pip install "softsim[rl]" (gymnasium >= 0.29, scipy). Without it import softsim.envs works and softsim.envs.make_env raises an ImportError that says what to install.

import gymnasium as gym
import softsim.envs

softsim.envs.register_envs()              # registers the ids below (Gymnasium 0.x also does it on `import gymnasium`; 1.x does not)

env = gym.make("softsim/CableBeamReach-v0", randomize=True)
obs, info = env.reset(seed=0)             # redraws the material and the target
obs, reward, terminated, truncated, info = env.step(env.action_space.sample())   # tension in N
id config actions task softsim/CableBeamReach-v0 scenarios/envs/cable_beam_reach.yaml cable tension, 0-0.7 N tip angle (bend_angle) to a target drawn from 0.02-0.07 rad, tolerance 0.004 rad softsim/CableArmReach-v0 scenarios/envs/cable_arm_reach.yaml cables A and B, 0-0.5 N each tip (x, z) to (3.994 mm, 118.515 mm), tolerance 0.4 / 0.3 mm softsim/PneuNetBend-v0 scenarios/envs/pneunet_bend.yaml chamber pressure, 0-25 kPa tip bend angle to a target drawn from 0.1-0.3 rad, tolerance 0.02 rad softsim/ReducedGripperLift-v0 softsim/envs/gripper.py (no YAML) finger pressure 0-40 kPa and palm height 0-0.06 m grasp a box and lift it 0.04 m, hold it to 4 s

Your own: write a YAML next to a scenario (the two files above are the templates) and call softsim.envs.make_env("my_env.yaml", reward_fn=None). The config keys are in the docstring of softsim.envs.env.SoftsimEnv.

docs.title: Pneumatic finger: PneuNetBend-v0
docs.text: The PneuNet of actuation with thicker walls (3 mm walls and layer, 6 mm base, 20 mm high) so that a 3 mm mesh is allowed; the validated 1.5 mm finger takes about 5 s per 20 ms step, which is useless for control. Physics step 5 ms (30 solver iterations), 50 ms per action, 20 actions per episode, Rayleigh damping. This is a coarse stand-in with MuJoCo's values, not the validated finger: settled it bends 0.09 rad at 10 kPa and 0.4 rad at 25 kPa, and it balloons above about 30 kPa, so the pressure bound is 25 kPa. The finger creeps towards equilibrium over ~0.3 s, so the observation is [bend_angle, tip_x, tip_z, d(bend_angle)/dt, pressure, target]: the rate is the velocity the policy needs (observation_rate: in the YAML, any metric). Randomisation: Ecoflex modulus +-20 %.

docs.title: Reduced gripper: ReducedGripperLift-v0
docs.text:
The reduced gripper (softsim.reduced, finger tables softsim/reduced/wang_finger.json) is its own MuJoCo model of link chains, so it is a separate small class, softsim.envs.gripper.ReducedGripperLiftEnv, with the same conventions. It is the fast env: about 150 steps per second of a 50 ms action, 8x real time.

  • Action [pressure Pa, palm height m], both ramped linearly from the previous value over the control period.
  • Observation (7): the held pressure and lift command, the palm's actual rise, the object's rise above the table, its vertical velocity and horizontal offset (x, y) from the palm axis.
  • Reward per step: min(object_rise, 0.04) / 0.04 - 0.05 * pressure / 40 kPa; 80 steps (4 s) then truncation. info["held"] / info["success"] is softsim.scenarios.grasp.is_held on the rise history, evaluated at the end (and every fourth step).
  • Randomisation, on by default (randomize=False fixes the means): object mass 8-20 g and friction 0.7-1.2, uniform, from the reset(seed=) generator; reset(options={"mass": ..., "friction": ...}) fixes them. The object is a box (shape="cylinder" also works). The fitted finger holds this range at 30 kPa or more and slips below 20 kPa; a 50 g box is never held by it, so the range stops at 20 g.
  • The rise can exceed the palm's: curling fingers push the object up. The reward only sees the object.

docs.title: Definitions
docs.text:
• Action: a Box over the listed actuators, in order, in SI (N for a cable tension or a force, m for a stroke, Pa for a pressure; bounds are written with units in the YAML). Values are clipped to the box and applied with Simulation.apply_controls, then held for control_period (e.g. 20 ms = 20 physics steps of 1 ms) while the simulation runs. After a reset every actuator is at its lower bound.
  • Observation: float32 vector: the metrics listed under observation (any scenario metric: tip_x, tip_z, bend_angle, cable_length, ...; SI, radians), then optionally the held actuator values (include_actuators) and the target (include_target). Nothing is normalised: scale it in a wrapper if the learner needs it.
  • Reward: -||(metric - target) / scale|| over the task metrics (default scales 1 mm for lengths, 0.01 rad for angles, set in the YAML), plus success_bonus (default 1) on the step that reaches the target, failure_penalty (default -10) on a numerical failure. reward_fn(env, metrics, target) replaces it.
  • Termination: every task metric within its tolerance of the target (info["success"]), or a backend exception (divergence, solver failure): then info["failure"] holds the message and the last observation is returned. Truncation: after max_steps actions.
  • Info: all scenario metrics, simulation time, target, error, and the drawn material values.

docs.title: Domain randomisation
docs.text:
reset(seed=s) seeds everything random. With randomisation on (randomize=True in gym.make, or no enabled: false in the config) each reset rebuilds the body with a redrawn material and redraws the target:

  • randomize.card_uncertainty: true: parameters drawn from the card's uncertainty with softsim.materials.sampling (the calibrated error bars; needs a card that states them);
  • randomize.ranges: {"elastic.youngs_modulus": {rel: 0.2}} (uniform, +-20 %), {abs: ...} or [low, high], applied on top for what a card does not cover (the example envs use this: their inline materials have no bars).

The drawn values are in info["material"]. A reset with options={"target": [...]} fixes the target and options={"material": False} skips the redraw.

docs.title: Vectorised use
docs.text: gymnasium.vector.SyncVectorEnv([lambda: gym.make(id) for _ in range(n)]) works (tested: batched spaces, per-env seeds, autoreset). It steps the environments one after the other in one process. The batched GPU version (many scenes in one call on MuJoCo Warp/MJX or similar) is M12 proper and needs the GPU machine.

docs.title: Speed and limits
docs.text:
Measured on this laptop (MuJoCo, one process, 2 threads), per step including the physics:
