env physics per step steps/s reset with randomisation CableBeamReach (4 mm mesh, dt 1 ms) 20 ms about 21 0.04 s (the model is rebuilt) CableArmReach (6 mm mesh, dt 0.5 ms) 50 ms about 3.3 0.08 s PneuNetBend (3 mm mesh, dt 5 ms) 50 ms about 7 (0.14 s) 1 s (the model is rebuilt) ReducedGripperLift (1 ms, 50 substeps) 50 ms about 150 3 ms (rebuilt every reset)

That is about 0.4x real time for the beam, 0.16x for the arm, 0.35x for the PneuNet and 8x for the reduced gripper: enough for a controller, tests and small experiments (the gripper even for a few thousand episodes), not for sample-hungry deep RL on the FE-based ones.

  • CPU MuJoCo only. Its values are MuJoCo's, not physical, unless a transferred card is used: on the coarse 4 mm mesh linear tetrahedra lock and the beam reaches 0.089 rad at 0.7 N where Euler-Bernoulli gives 0.28 rad (actuation). A policy trained here learns this model, not the real beam.
  • The environments add Rayleigh damping (equilibrium unchanged) so the beam settles in ~0.1 s and the arm in ~1 s; the arm's response lags the action by that much, so it needs a 2 s episode.
  • Only the first soft body's material is redrawn (randomize.body picks another); zones keep their cards.
  • The default arm target is one reachable point; randomised targets need a reachable set (see inverse control).
  • The PneuNet env is a thick-walled, coarse variant; the gripper env learns the reduced model (finger tables from the reference, no chambers, no local deformation around the object).
  • A controller is a callable on the observation: a proportional-integral one that adds 5 N/rad x error to the tension reaches the beam's 0.05 rad target in 2 steps (tests/test_envs.py).

docs.title: Training baseline
docs.text:
tools/train_baseline.py is a numpy-only cross-entropy method over a linear policy (action = low + (high - low) * sigmoid(W z + b), z the standardised observation), scored by mean return over a few seeded episodes per candidate and compared with uniformly random actions on 20 held-out seeds. It needs no torch; for deep RL use stable-baselines3 or similar on the same ids (optional, not a dependency of softsim).

python tools/train_baseline.py                                       # CableBeamReach-v0
python tools/train_baseline.py --env softsim/ReducedGripperLift-v0 --generations 8 --pop 16 --episodes 3
python tools/train_baseline.py --env softsim/PneuNetBend-v0 --generations 4 --pop 8 --episodes 2 --eval-episodes 8

Measured on this laptop (2 workers, randomisation on, held-out seeds, mean return +- std over episodes):

env random actions CEM linear policy training CableBeamReach (20 episodes) -13.8 +- 23.2 -0.87 +- 1.0 288 episodes, 70 s ReducedGripperLift (20 episodes) -2.4 +- 0.5, held 0 % 44.0 +- 17.8, held 90 % 384 episodes, 223 s PneuNetBend (8 episodes) -20.8 +- 15.1 -3.0 +- 3.1 64 episodes, 197 s

Random actions are a weak reference, and the beam's returns are small because the episode ends at the first step within tolerance. The point is that the envs are learnable and what number to beat, not that a linear policy is good.

docs.title: Experiments: tracking and calibration
docs.text:
softsim track datasets/czopek2026_ecoflex_drop.yaml --jobs 5        # about 3 min; data/processed/<dataset>/
softsim calibrate calibrations/ecoflex_00_10_drop.yaml --jobs 3      # about 4 min; runs/calibration/...

docs.title: Dataset description
docs.text: datasets/czopek2026_ecoflex_drop.yaml records the DOI, licence, camera, specimen and, per case, the zip archive, the scenario config and how the weight looks. Frames are read directly from the zips (FrameSource); nothing is extracted or redistributed.

docs.title: Tracking (softsim/experiments/video/)
docs.text:
Segmentation. The backdrop is saturated green with no red, and shadows on it stay red-free. A per-pixel reference background (the median of the first frames) separates three classes:

  • the translucent specimen: red present, bluish;
  • brass weights: red present, neutral;
  • black weights: much darker than the background behind them.

Scale and camera. The specimen's resting silhouette width equals its diameter, giving about 5.5 px/mm. Its silhouette height, H·cos e + D·sin e, gives a camera elevation of e ≈ 17–20°. Vertical motion therefore scales by cos e.

Weight motion. The weight is followed as a rigid body (x, y and in-plane rotation) by incremental ECC alignment of its upper part, frame to frame. The upper part keeps the specimen and the weight's shadow out of the mask. The weights rotate strongly during impact (the 20 g seats with about 10° of rocking, the 100 g rolls about 100°), and a translation-only template loses them. The tracked point is the silhouette centroid, which is close to the centre of mass.

Contact. Contact is the first frame where the centre of mass departs from a local free-fall parabola by more than 0.5 px (about 0.1 mm). The same rule is applied to simulations (compare.simulated_indentation).

Compared quantity. indentation_rel is the centre-of-mass displacement since contact, relative to the specimen base.

docs.title: Findings about the recordings
docs.text:
Case Impact speed Offset Spin Usable? 20 g (brass) 2.67 m/s +6 mm 317 °/s yes; lands slightly tilted and rocks while seating 50 g (brass) 2.47 m/s 0 mm 48 °/s yes for the first contact; tumbles off afterwards 100 g (black, no knob) 2.47 m/s +14 mm 27 °/s no: hits the specimen edge and rolls off 200 g (black) 2.62 m/s −13 mm −59 °/s no: tilted edge impact 500 g (black) 2.65 m/s −6 mm ~0 first contact only; see below
  • Frame rate is 2999.3 fps (overlay timestamps). Impact speeds are 2–10% below the nominal 2.73 m/s, so simulations use the measured value per case.
  • Local free-fall fit. Just before contact the tracker fits a free quadratic to the weight's height. Its apparent acceleration comes out at only 3–4 m/s², but over the 8 ms fit window that is a difference of about 1 px from free fall. M3 blamed perspective; that is not established (the specimen's hop, below, decelerates faster than g). It doesn't matter for contact detection, and the fitted impact speeds agree with the nominal drop speed.
  • The specimen hops; the table does not move. After impact the specimen rises 8–20 mm and lands again 70–110 ms later. The green cloth it sits on rises next to it (most near the specimen, less 55 mm away, with ripples spreading out), while the backdrop lighting band stays within ±1 px, so the camera is still. The 200 g specimen visibly tilts and slides in mid-air. The tacky specimen sticks to the cloth and drags it up, which is also why its hop decelerates at 13–20 m/s², faster than g. Correction: M3 read this as the table moving and discarded everything after the first contact; see After the first contact.
  • Out-of-plane tilt can't be measured from a single side view. Simulations get the measured horizontal offset and in-plane spin; tilt stays zero.
  • Rotation is the less precise output. On synthetic sequences the tracker recovers position to about 2% of the motion and rotation to about 20%.
  • Correction to Step 0: the 4 mm preview estimate for 20 g happens to match (3.7 mm). The method was unreliable, though: it used the weight's bottom edge, which the specimen rim hides.

docs.title: Calibration (softsim/experiments/calibrate.py)
docs.text:
calibrations/ecoflex_00_10_drop.yaml fits stable Neo-Hookean E and Rayleigh β (in log space) on MuJoCo to the 20, 50 and 500 g cases at once:

  • Optimizer: a coarse 4×4 grid, then Nelder-Mead, 50 evaluations.
  • Simulations: each case uses its measured impact conditions and a 5 mm mesh.
  • Cost: the mean of RMSE divided by the experimental peak over the first contact phase.
  • Outputs: the fitted preset (with provenance), the evaluation history, report.yaml and plots.
  • Failures and resuming: an unstable parameter set, or one that crashes its worker process outright, gets the maximum per-case cost (10) instead of stopping the run. Each evaluation is appended to <output>/evaluations.jsonl. Re-running the calibration replays those evaluations, so an interrupted multi-hour run resumes where it stopped. Changing max_evaluations, grid, bounds or initial values keeps them. The log does not know about code changes: delete it after changing simulation code. The history also records each case's maximum ground penetration, which flags contact artefacts.

Result: E = 54.8 kPa and β = 0.31 ms. This is preset ecoflex_00_10_drop_fit. E is lower than the 91 kPa datasheet-derived starting estimate, and very close to the datasheet's 100% modulus (55 kPa).

Case Peak exp Peak, preset (91 kPa) Peak, fitted t_peak exp / fitted NRMSE fitted 20 g 3.74 mm 1.40 mm 3.32 mm 3.3 / 3.2 ms 15% 50 g 4.31 mm 2.16 mm 4.20 mm 3.7 / 3.6 ms 3% 500 g 4.52 mm 8.01 mm 10.97 mm 2.7 / 6.6 ms 113% 100 g, 200 g edge impacts, not fitted

docs.title: What this does and does not show
docs.text:
• For light weights the model works. For 20 g and 50 g (local indentation by a weight smaller than the specimen), a Neo-Hookean solid with one Rayleigh damping coefficient reproduces the whole first contact (loading, peak and unloading) within 3–15%.
  • For the 500 g weight it fails. That weight is wider than the specimen and compresses its whole face. In the recording it stops within 4.5 mm in 2.7 ms, while the model needs about 11 mm and 6.6 ms. No single (E, β) fits both regimes. The measured peak indentation is almost independent of mass (3.7 → 4.5 mm for 25× the energy). Candidate explanations, none verified:
  • rate-dependent stiffening of the silicone, which Rayleigh damping can't represent;
  • stronger large-strain stiffening than Neo-Hookean;
  • near-incompressibility under full-face confinement (the model uses ν = 0.45);
  • energy absorbed by the compliant table, which is measurable here but not modelled.

M4 tested the material-law and compressibility candidates on SOFA; see below. - The fit depends on the mesh. With the fitted values, the 20 g peak goes 3.32 → 3.55 → 3.79 mm as the mesh refines from 5 to 3.5 to 2.5 mm. Use the preset with specimen.mesh.size=5mm, or refit at the target resolution. - 50 g after first contact isn't modelled. In reality the weight tumbles off after the first contact, so later times shouldn't be compared.

docs.title: Fitting any scenario to a measured table (softsim fit)
docs.text:
softsim calibrate is built around the drop test's tracked videos. softsim fit is the scenario-neutral version: any observable column of any scenario against a measured table, registered with its source. A fit file is a transfer file (config, backend, overrides, parameters, checks, max_evaluations, output, see softsim/transfer.py) whose reference: is replaced by data: (softsim/experiments/fit.py has the full description):

data:
  source: {name: ..., doi: 10.xxxx/..., licence: CC-BY-4.0, file: ../data/processed/x/table.csv}
  kind: curve                      # y against a simulated x (a quasi-static ramp), or series: y(t)
  filter: {tilt: 0}                # rows with these column values
  x: {column: p_kPa, scale: 1000, sim: cavity_pressure}
  y: {column: theta_deg, scale: 0.0174533, sim: bend_angle}
  relative_to: first               # compare changes from the first sample (zero offsets in the data)

source must give name, doi, licence and file, so a number in a report can be traced. The error is the NRMSE of the transfer (RMS difference over the largest measured change); the report adds the data's own noise floor (the scatter at repeated x over the same range), because a fit cannot be better than that. The fitted card is kind: physical on the reference (--backend fem), effective on the linear-tet backends, and it names the measurement in its provenance.

Check (a twin experiment, tests/test_fit.py): the "measurement" is the sphere's pressure-volume curve at a hidden E = 45 kPa. Fitting from 25 kPa gives back 45.18 kPa from the clean curve (0.4%), and 46.6 kPa from the same curve with 1% noise (3.5%, a cost of 0.018, about the noise). A wrong modulus costs more than 10 times the right one on a time series, and four mutants of the code (dropped unit scale, dropped baseline, whole run instead of the loading branch, ignored filter) are caught. This tests the machinery against a known answer; it says nothing about a real actuator. That needs a measurement with a known geometry and material.

docs.title: Backends and material models (M4)
docs.text:
Same cases, cost and procedure on the SOFA backend, which offers more material laws. The question: can a different material law reproduce 500 g together with 20 and 50 g? Both SOFA fits use a 5 mm mesh and dt = 0.05 ms (0.1 ms diverges for 500 g) and took about 1 h and 2.7 h on 8 cores.

Fit Parameters Cost 20 g 50 g 500 g peak / t_peak (exp 4.52 mm / 2.7 ms) MuJoCo, stable NH (ecoflex_00_10_drop_fit) E 54.8 kPa, ν 0.45, β 0.31 ms 0.44 15% 3% 11.0 mm / 6.6 ms SOFA, stable NH (calibration) E 105 kPa, ν 0.45, β 0.89 ms 0.54 49% 37% 8.3 mm / 5.7 ms SOFA, one-term Ogden (ecoflex_00_10_drop_fit_sofa_ogden) μ 22.9 kPa, α 1.20, K 200 kPa, β 0.28 ms 0.24 3% 11% 9.0 mm / 5.3 ms

(Percentages are NRMSE over the first contact phase. Reproduce the figures with python tools/make_model_comparison.py.)

What M4 shows:

  • No material law fits 500 g. Each fit leaves 500 g about twice too deep and twice too slow. The SOFA stable-NH fit is a compromise that fits nothing: it stiffens to help 500 g and then misses 20 and 50 g by 37–49%.
  • Large-strain stiffening isn't the explanation. The Ogden fit chooses α ≈ 1.2, less stiffening than Neo-Hookean (α = 2), and fits 20 and 50 g within 3–11%, the best of the three. The M3 candidate "stronger large-strain stiffening" is ruled out for this data.
  • Same model, different backend, different parameters. Stable NH on MuJoCo and SOFA ends at E = 55 vs 105 kPa (compliant vs hard contact, integrator damping; see sofa.md). Fitted values are effective parameters of a backend + mesh + model combination.
  • Compressibility matters for the full-face impact. At peak, the SOFA fits lose 27% (Ogden) and 36% (stable NH) of the specimen's volume. Silicone is practically incompressible, so ν = 0.45–0.47 is wrong here; under local indentation the material can flow aside and ν matters much less. Single runs of the Ogden fit with a higher bulk modulus (not refitted):
Bulk modulus (ν) 20 g peak (exp 3.74) 500 g peak (exp 4.52) 500 g t_peak (exp 2.7) 200 kPa (0.466), fitted 3.82 mm 8.96 mm 5.3 ms 1 MPa (0.493) 3.54 mm 7.65 mm 5.2 ms 5 MPa (0.499) 3.31 mm 6.54 mm 4.6 ms

Near-incompressibility closes about 45% of the 500 g peak gap while 20 g stiffens 12%, partly linear-tetrahedron locking. A joint refit with the bulk modulus free is prepared but not run yet (ecoflex_00_10_drop_sofa_ogden_bulk.yaml, about 3–4 h; repeat at a 3.5 mm mesh to separate locking from material). - The remaining gap (500 g still about 45% too deep and 70% too slow at ν ≈ 0.5) points to what no tested model has: rate-dependent stiffening (Prony viscoelasticity; Rayleigh β can't represent it) and/or the compliant table. - SOFA contact failed at extreme rim flaring (fixed). In the Ogden 500 g run the specimen's rim spreads to 45 mm radius and, from 7.6 ms (after the peak at 5.3 ms), rim vertices passed up to 8.5 mm through the ground. No element inverts. The cause was the intersection's alarm distance (0.4 mm) against the rim's 0.6 mm per step when it snaps back onto the ground; the backend now widens it to the fastest vertex's travel (backends/sofa.md: 2.83 mm to 0.006 mm at 8.8 ms, peak unchanged). The 500 g peak and timing were before this and are reproduced (9.0 mm / 5.3 ms); the fit's stored 500 g NRMSE (58%) included the artefact, and re-simulated without it the 500 g NRMSE is 79% (2026-11-12). The Ogden fit's cost of 0.24 above was minimised with the artefact in its 500 g term. - Re-simulating these fits needs their own setup. They were made (28-29 Oct) before the measured 11° in-plane landing tilt of the 500 g drop was applied to every re-simulation (31 Oct); with the tilt, both SOFA fits blow up at 5 mm / 0.05 ms (8.3-8.4 ms, a real instability, not the speed guard) and the figures were left without 500 g. Their calibration files now say tilt: false, and tools/make_model_comparison.py re-simulates each fit as it was fitted. Whether SOFA survives the tilted impact at a finer mesh or step is open.

docs.title: After the first contact: tack and the hopping specimen
docs.text:
M3 and M4 compared only the first ~8 ms, because M3 had read the later motion as the table moving. That was wrong (see the findings above): the specimen itself hops. The whole first 100 ms is usable data, and it shows that the simulations got the physics after the first contact wrong. Without any adhesion, the simulated 20 g weight flies off at 1.2 m/s and rises 70 mm. The real one never leaves the specimen.

What the recordings show:

  • 20 g: the weight sticks. It comes off the compressed material at 1.0–1.2 m/s relative to the base, as fast as in the simulation, and then stops within about 1 mm and stays there for 90 ms while rocking. Momentum says why: 20 g × 1.0 m/s ≈ 42 g × 0.45 m/s, and weight plus specimen then hop together at about 0.45 m/s (7.6 mm apex). The weight is stuck to the tacky Ecoflex and pulls the whole specimen off the cloth.
  • 50 g: the weight peels off. With 2.5× the momentum, the bond can't hold the weight. It separates while rotating (a peel from one edge) at about 1 m/s relative to the specimen, the same as the simulation up to 22 ms. After that it tumbles away from the camera and lands on the table behind the specimen (it lies still there from ~210 ms). Its image height then mixes height with depth, so the side view can't measure its rebound. The specimen still hops 8 mm.
  • 500 g: the weight lifts the specimen with it by 20 mm, and separates only around 70–100 ms.
  • The cloth comes along. The green cloth next to the specimen rises with it and ripples, and the hop decelerates at 13–20 m/s², faster than g: the specimen sticks to the cloth too.

Model. Two scene elements, both general features of softsim:

  • Adhesion (material.adhesion: {strength, range}), an exponential cohesive law for the normal traction between the soft surface and what it touches (t = σ (g/δ) e^(1 − g/δ); work of separation e·σ·δ). Bonds form on contact and break beyond 6δ. Verified against analytic equilibria on MuJoCo and SOFA (tests/test_adhesion.py).
  • A compliant support (support: in the drop test): a carrier plate under the specimen that can lift off the table against a spring and damper. It is a lumped stand-in for the cloth, and its parameters are effective ones.

Fit (calibrations/ecoflex_00_10_drop_adhesion_support.yaml, MuJoCo, 5 mm mesh). Compared quantities:

  • 20 g: weight position relative to the specimen base and specimen lift over 0–100 ms;
  • 50 g: relative position over 0–15 ms (later, the flipping weight's centroid is not its centre of mass) and specimen lift over 0–100 ms.

500 g is not used (below).

Only the tack and support are fitted; the bulk material stays at its M3 first-contact values (preset ecoflex_00_10_drop_fit_tacky; softsim sweep scenarios/drop_test/sweeps/fitted_tack_support.yaml runs all five weights with it):

Fitted value tack strength σ 14.6 kPa tack range δ 0.29 mm (work of separation e·σ·δ ≈ 11.6 J/m²) support stiffness, damping, mass 33 N/m, 0.35 N·s/m, 45 g Case Observable Without tack (rigid table) With tack + support 20 g weight rel. to base, 0–100 ms flies off (−75 mm at 100 ms) stays seated; NRMSE 25% 20 g specimen hop 6.2 mm, too slow 7.0 mm (exp. 7.8), lands at ~80 ms; NRMSE 12% 50 g weight rel. to base, 0–15 ms NRMSE 6% (first contact and separation) 50 g specimen hop 29 mm 8 mm (exp. 9); NRMSE 11%

Total cost 0.133 (90 evaluations, flat from about the 55th), against 0.48 at the first initial guess.

What to make of it:

  • Tack, not dissipation, is why the simulations flew too high. In the MuJoCo model the weight already leaves the compressed specimen at the measured speed. What was missing is that it stays stuck.
  • The parameters are effective, and tied to the mesh. The tack is a cohesive law whose process zone (~4 mm) the 5 mm mesh doesn't resolve. On a 3.5 mm mesh the same values let the 20 g weight peel off. The support is a lumped stand-in for a cloth that sticks, stretches and ripples, so 45 g and 33 N/m are not the cloth's mass and stiffness.
  • Checked: halving the timestep changes the errors by less than 0.01.
  • The cloth pulls back harder than gravity (13–20 m/s² in the recordings). The fit captures that through the spring, which is why the simulated hop is about 10% too low but lands on time.
  • 500 g is outside this model (below). With its first contact 2.4× too deep, the weight rebounds too fast for any bond and tears off.

docs.title: Every weight, whole bounce (validation)
docs.text:
python tools/validate_drop_bounces.py (about 1 min on 8 cores) runs all five weights with each recording's measured impact for 200 ms. It compares the first contact, the weight's rebound (its height above its contact height) and the specimen's hop (runs/bounce_validation/metrics.csv, figure docs/media/bounce_validation.png). It covers the two MuJoCo models above and, since 2026-10-31, the MuJoCo and SOFA transfers of the physical card, plus the 3D reference's first contacts.

  • The transfers reproduce the first contact best: 6–8% at 20 g, 8–14% at 50 g.
  • They have no tack, so the weight then flies 38 mm high instead of staying seated.
  • They diverge where their strong relaxation lets heavy weights crush the specimen: MuJoCo from 100 g, SOFA at 500 g.

(Those numbers are for the transfers of the earlier physical card, 143 kPa / 0.69 / 2 ms, run on 2026-10-31. With the joint card below (2026-11-02), the table's first-contact NRMSE against the recordings is 13% (MuJoCo) and 4% (SOFA) at 20 g and 6% and 5% at 50 g; the 3D reference itself gives 14% and 3%. The weight now rises 72 (MuJoCo) and 64 mm (SOFA) at 20 g, still with no tack. MuJoCo diverges only at 500 g, like SOFA: its 200 g run completes. The run was done with the MuJoCo timing fix of that day, see below.)

python tools/make_comparison_media.py writes docs/media/compare_wXXX.gif: for each weight, the recording next to the MuJoCo tack-and-support model, with the same scale and view angle.

Case First peak mm (t ms) Weight max rise mm Specimen hop mm (t ms) Specimen landed ms 20 g experiment 3.7 (3.3) 9.1 7.8 (33) 73 rigid, no tack 3.3 (3.0) 71 6.2 (44) 83 tack + support 3.5 (3.2) 7.5 7.0 (41) 74 50 g experiment 4.3 (3.7) 10.1 (to 15 ms) 9.2 (48) 79 rigid, no tack 4.3 (3.6) 10.8 29 (85) 161 tack + support 4.5 (3.8) 9.2 7.8 (44) 78 100 g (edge) experiment rolls off the rim falls 25 mm beside it 11.4 (48) 94 tack + support 8.1 (6.1) 48 (bounces up) 0.1 200 g (edge) experiment 4.5 (3.3) 42 18.9 (50) 108 tack + support 8.7 (4.6) 96 0.3 500 g experiment 4.5 (2.7) 31 21.8 (66) after 200 tack + support 9.0 (5.0) 105 20.1 (62) 111 (same, dropped flat) 10.7 (6.7) 126 10.4 (54) 93

The 100, 200 and 500 g simulations get each recording's measured in-plane tilt at contact (−7.6°, −8.7° and −11.0°; tools/measure_tilts.py, softsim.experiments.video.tilt). It is measured from the straight side edges of the dark weights' silhouettes 15 frames before contact, with 0.5–1.6 px residuals and less than 1.3° of spread. The brass weights' reflections and knobs make their edges unusable, so 20 and 50 g stay untilted. The rigid model gives the same as tack + support for 100–500 g within a few mm. All weight numbers after 15 ms are unusable for 50 g: the weight flips.

  • 20 g and 50 g are reproduced over the whole bounce: hop height within 10–15%, landing time within 2 ms, and the 20 g weight stays seated. That is what the tack and the support were fitted to.
  • 100, 200 and 500 g all fail. In every simulation the weight rebounds 45–130 mm and leaves the specimen behind. The real heavy weights rise only 30–40 mm (or roll off) and carry the specimen up 11–22 mm with them. Two of the three are not comparable impacts, though: the simulations drop every weight flat, and the heavy weights don't land flat.
  • 200 g comes down strongly tilted: its bottom face is visible from the camera above. It digs in with its edge and keeps rotating, so its shallow 4.5 mm "first contact" is an edge impact, not evidence of a stiffer material.
  • 100 g lands 14 mm off centre and tilted. It rolls off the rim, falls 25 mm beside the specimen and still drags the specimen up 11 mm.
  • 500 g lands least tilted: 11° in the image plane, rotating only 2° in the first 20 ms, with an unknown out-of-plane tilt.
    • Applying the measured tilt brings the specimen's hop from 10 to 20 mm (measured 21.8 mm) and its first contact from 10.7 to 9.0 mm.
    • It still stops at 4.5 mm in 2.7 ms in the recording.
    • Its rise height means an upward speed of about 0.8 m/s (restitution about 0.3), against about 1.4 m/s simulated, so the real impact is still stiffer and more lossy than the model.
    • The tack doesn't change it.
  • Next: compare the heavy weights only with the measured attitude. The in-plane tilt can be measured. The out-of-plane tilt needs either a second view or a 3D fit in which it is a free parameter. Until then, the material question rests on the flat impacts (20 and 50 g) and on 500 g (below).

docs.title: The 500 g first contact
docs.text:
The 500 g weight stops within 4.5 mm in 2.7 ms. No simulation so far gets close: every material law, both backends and a near-incompressible bulk modulus leave it at 6.5–11 mm and 4.6–6.6 ms (M4). Three checks so far:

  • The tracking is right. Tracking the top edge of the weight's knob against the plain backdrop, independently of the tracker, gives the same motion within 0.5–1 mm. The weight travels almost freely for the first ~1 ms, then decelerates at ~1750 m/s² (~900 N), and comes back up at ~0.85 m/s.
  • It lands tilted, which explains part of it. Before impact the weight is tilted by 11° in the image plane (side-edge fits, see the bounce validation). The simulation with that tilt peaks at 9.0 mm at 5.0 ms instead of 10.7 mm at 6.7 ms: closer, but not close.
  • No elastomer explanation fits. As a linear spring, the stop needs ~170 kN/m, an effective modulus above 1 MPa, against ~55 kPa from the light weights. That is 19× the 50 g case's stiffness, with a shorter time to peak than 20 g despite 25× the mass. No string or guide is visible above the weight.

  • It is not a modelling artefact of the tetrahedral backends. The locking-free axisymmetric reference (reference_fem.md) is nearly incompressible (ν = 0.4995) with sticking contact on both faces, so it has none of the suspects: locking, volume loss, friction slip. It still peaks at 8.1 mm (E = 100 kPa) and 6.4 mm (E = 200 kPa), against the measured 4.5 mm. Statically, sticking faces stiffen 26% compression only 1.7× over frictionless.

  • Rate dependence does not explain it either. This was tested with Prony viscoelasticity on MuJoCo: 48 combinations of instantaneous modulus E0 = 100–800 kPa, relaxing fraction g = 0.5–0.95 and τ = 0.3–3 ms, each case with its measured impact. Every material that stops 500 g near the measured depth stops 50 g at a quarter of its measured depth. For example, E0 = 800 kPa, g = 0.5, τ = 1 ms gives 3.85 mm at 2.9 ms for 500 g (measured 4.52 mm at 2.7 ms) but 1.10 mm at 1.1 ms for 50 g (measured 4.31 mm at 3.7 ms). Both weights hit at the same speed, so their strain rates are similar, and no linear viscoelastic spectrum can stiffen one and not the other. (Materials with a soft long-term modulus made MuJoCo diverge under 500 g; the trend is clear without them.)

  • It does not land flat. The frame montages show the weight squashing the specimen into a wedge, and it rotates only 2° in the first 20 ms. Its side edges give an 11° in-plane tilt (the earlier 7° estimate is superseded). With that tilt, MuJoCo's first contact goes from 10.7 to 9.0 mm and the specimen's hop from 10 to 20 mm (measured 21.8 mm).
  • Out-of-plane tilt does not explain it. That tilt can't be seen from one view, so it was swept on MuJoCo (python tools/sweep_out_of_plane_tilt.py, first-contact fit card, measured impact and in-plane tilt):
Out-of-plane tilt 0° 5° 10° 15° 20° measured First contact [mm] 9.08 8.69 8.42 8.04 7.53 4.52 Time of peak [ms] 4.8 4.6 4.4 4.2 4.0 2.67

Even 20°, more than the side view could hide, takes off only 17% of a 2× gap. The MuJoCo transfer of the physical card (Prony g = 0.94) inverts elements under 500 g and can't be used for this case.

  • The force the film implies. The force on the weight at its peak indentation is m·(a + g), with the deceleration a taken from a parabola through the tracked indentation (±0.8 ms around the peak):
Weight Peak indentation Time of peak Deceleration at peak Force at peak 20 g 3.74 mm 3.33 ms 750 m/s² 15 N 50 g 4.31 mm 3.67 ms 1285 m/s² 65 N 200 g (tilted) 4.47 mm 3.33 ms 615 m/s² 125 N 500 g 4.52 mm 2.67 ms 1572 m/s² 791 N

The tracked decelerations hardly depend on the mass, which spans 25×. 50 and 500 g hit at the same speed and reach nearly the same indentation: 4.3 against 4.5 mm, in 3.7 against 2.7 ms. The 500 g recording needs 12× the force. This is not model-free, and it does not rule the specimen out. The two weights do not deform the specimen the same way: the 50 g weight is 27 mm wide and indents a 40 mm face, the 500 g weight is 43 mm wide and compresses all of it, so the same depth need not mean the same force. What stands is the simulations above: full-face runs on the reference still stop at 6.4-8.1 mm.

The cause is still unknown. The candidates left are the material under full-face confinement, the setup and the measurement:

  • what is under the specimen (cloth and table compliance, a stiffer support under heavy loads);
  • the side view's projection of depth motion: the camera looks down at 18.6°, so a weight moving away from it appears to rise by 0.32× that motion.

500 g is kept out of the fits because no model matches it and the cause is open.

docs.title: What the fitted modulus means
docs.text:
All fits on this page are effective models of a backend, mesh and contact model, not the silicone's material constants. The axisymmetric reference solver (reference_fem.md) cross-checks this:

  • it agrees with MuJoCo's 3.5 mm mesh within 2–5% for static indentation;
  • in the drop, MuJoCo's impact loses energy to friction slip and contact mechanics that the reference doesn't have;
  • on the reference, the first contacts need E ≈ 100–130 kPa plus some damping, consistent with the datasheet (≈ 94 kPa). MuJoCo's 55 kPa compensates for MuJoCo's own losses.

Use the MuJoCo presets with MuJoCo at their mesh size. Take the material's actual modulus from the reference.

docs.title: A physical card on the 3D reference (fem backend)
docs.text:
The 3D locking-free reference (reference_fem.md) runs the drop test with each recording's measured offset, spin and tilt. It answers the material question without the axisymmetric solver's limits: the 20 g weight lands 6 mm off centre and spinning. The card:

  • Neo-Hookean, E0 = 143 kPa, ν = 0.4995;
  • one Prony term, g = 0.69 at τ = 2 ms;
  • sticking contact.

These are the axisymmetric fit's values. Nothing was refitted for 3D.

Case Measured first contact 3D reference, physical card NRMSE (first contact) 20 g (6 mm off centre, 317°/s) 3.74 mm at 3.33 ms 3.94 mm at 3.00 ms 6.6% 50 g 4.31 mm at 3.67 ms 4.41 mm at 3.40 ms 9.9% 500 g (11° in-plane tilt) 4.52 mm at 2.67 ms 7.41 mm at 4.20 ms 60% (over 0–6 ms)

(Each run takes 4–9 minutes on a laptop with a 5 mm quadratic mesh.)

  • One physical, locking-free material reproduces both light weights within 10%. The axisymmetric joint fit's 20 g/50 g conflict (15–20%) was the centred approximation of the off-centre 20 g, not the material.
  • The card describes the silicone at impact rates. Its instantaneous modulus is 143 kPa, relaxing about 70% within a few milliseconds, so the long-term modulus is about 45 kPa. The Marechal et al. tension data give 31 kPa (Neo-Hookean over 0–200%) at 0.23/s. Those data probably understate the modulus, since their strain was measured at the crosshead. So the slow tension test and the relaxed drop card are consistent within that uncertainty, while impacts see a 3× stiffer material.
  • 500 g is not reproduced here either, now without any backend artefact: no locking, no contact losses, the measured tilt, a material that fits the light weights. It stops 1.6× deeper and 1.6× later than recorded. The out-of-plane tilt and the model-free force check above show it isn't the material.
  • Transfer to MuJoCo. The reference runs are saved as tracks (tools/make_reference_tracks.py), and MuJoCo is calibrated against them (calibrations/transfer_ecoflex_00_10_mujoco.yaml, 3 min). At a 5 mm mesh and ν = 0.45, MuJoCo reproduces the physical card with E0 = 66 kPa, g = 0.94, τ = 5.5 ms, within 3.4% (50 g) and 9.7% (20 g) of the reference. Those are MuJoCo's effective values for this card, and its error bar.
  • Transfer to SOFA (calibrations/transfer_ecoflex_00_10_sofa.yaml, 43 min): E0 = 79.6 kPa, g = 0.77, τ = 2.7 ms, within 2.6% (50 g) and 6.8% (20 g). SOFA needs much less extra relaxation than MuJoCo (g 0.77 against 0.94), because MuJoCo loses impact energy on its own through friction slip and numerical damping (backends/mujoco.md).
Card E0 g τ Error vs reference (20 / 50 g) Physical (3D reference) 143 kPa 0.69 2.0 ms – SOFA, 5 mm, ν = 0.45 79.6 kPa 0.77 2.7 ms 6.8% / 2.6% MuJoCo, 5 mm, ν = 0.45 66 kPa 0.94 5.5 ms 9.7% / 3.4% - Refined in 3D (E0, g, τ free, both cases; calibrations/ecoflex_00_10_drop_fem_prony.yaml, 40 evaluations, 5.4 h): E0 = 147 kPa, g = 0.70, τ = 2.24 ms. The cost falls only from 0.084 to 0.080 (first contact NRMSE 9.5% for 20 g and 6.4% for 50 g; peak indentation 3.86 vs 3.74 mm and 4.31 vs 4.31 mm). The 3D fit confirms the card: E0 and g move by 3% or less, τ by 12%, all within the spread between the two weights. The card and its transfers keep the values above.

docs.title: Joint fit: the drop and the datasheet (GPU box, 2026-11-02)
docs.text:
The drop-only card relaxes to E∞ = E0 (1 − g) = 44 kPa, about half the ~94 kPa that the datasheet's 100% modulus (55 kPa) implies: impacts alone cannot say how much of the stiffness relaxes within milliseconds. calibrations/ecoflex_00_10_drop_fem_joint.yaml fits the 20 and 50 g drops and that datasheet point together (weight 0.5; the datasheet moduli are approximate: Roels et al. measured 93 kPa against a datasheet 69 kPa for Ecoflex 00-30). The first 40 evaluations ran on the laptop; the next 40 resumed from their log here.

Card E0 g τ E∞ 20 g / 50 g NRMSE Datasheet term Cost Drop only (40 evaluations) 147 kPa 0.70 2.24 ms 44 kPa 9.5% / 6.4% 40–60% off 0.080 Joint, after 40 evaluations 143 kPa 0.53 1.23 ms 68 kPa 13.3% / 5.2% 28% 0.130 Joint, after 80 evaluations 190 kPa 0.60 0.58 ms 76 kPa 14.3% / 2.9% 20% 0.108
  • The datasheet pulls the relaxed modulus up from 44 to 76 kPa (94 kPa implied) at the price of the 20 g first contact (9.5% to 14.3%); the 50 g one improves (peak 4.310 vs 4.314 mm recorded). The card turns stiffer and relaxes faster: 190 kPa for 0.6 ms.
  • Forty evaluations were not enough. At 40 the best point was still the last one and τ was drifting down; the cost fell from 0.130 to 0.108 over the next
  • It is nearly flat at the end (0.1099 at evaluation 70, 0.1080 at 80), but not proven converged.
  • Speed. A 20 g or 50 g evaluation takes 58–69 s on the GPU and 73–83 s on the CPU of this box (the laptop's was ~8 min). Replaying the first logged evaluation reproduces the laptop's numbers to 5e-8 (20 g) and 7e-13 (50 g).

The reference runs of this card (tools/make_reference_tracks.py) are the target of the backend transfers (5 mm mesh, 2 min on MuJoCo, 20 min on SOFA):

Card E0 g τ Error vs reference (20 / 50 g) Joint physical card (3D reference) 190 kPa 0.60 0.58 ms – SOFA, 5 mm, ν = 0.45 86.1 kPa 0.70 2.47 ms 8.5% / 1.6% MuJoCo, 5 mm, ν = 0.45 64.9 kPa 0.68 7.82 ms 8.6% / 3.3%

The transfers again soften the material by 55–66% (linear tetrahedra lock) and change the relaxation. Their peaks: 3.40 and 3.37 mm at 20 g against the reference's 3.85, and 4.34 and 4.50 mm at 50 g against 4.31.

Two things that bit on this run, both fixed. - Stale replays. A calibration's log was keyed by the path of its tracks, not their contents. After the reference tracks were regenerated from the new card, both transfers replayed every evaluation fitted to the old tracks and finished in minutes with a result for the wrong reference. Log entries now record a digest of the track files and are ignored when it differs (tests/test_experiments.py). Logs from before the digest are still trusted. - Calibration on a GPU. --jobs 2 forked its workers after the parent had used CUDA, so every 3D case crashed its worker; JAX also reserved 75% of the GPU per process. Workers are now spawned and memory is allocated on demand.

The MuJoCo numbers above were made after a timing fix in the MuJoCo backend: mj_step computes positions before it integrates, so softsim reported positions one step late and evaluated its explicit forces from them. On the adhesion fit's best point, the fix moves the first-contact NRMSE by 1.5–3% (20 g 0.1822 to 0.1795, 50 g 0.0835 to 0.0808) and the 50 g time of the peak by one step (3.78 to 3.57 ms). The MuJoCo rows of the earlier tables (tack and support, rigid) were fitted with the old timing.

docs.title: Soft gripper
docs.text: A two-finger gripper built from the validated Wang finger, and a fast model of it that runs live on your own machine. The slow reference solver matches the measured finger to about 1°; it teaches a chain of links, and the chain runs faster than real time.

docs.title: Play with it
docs.text:
xdg-open docs/viewer/gripper.html      # or double-click it: no server, the physics is inside the file
python tools/demo_gripper.py --finger softsim/reduced/wang_finger.json    # desktop version (MuJoCo viewer, sliders)

The page runs MuJoCo compiled to WebAssembly in your browser. Play has sliders for pressure, mass and friction, three objects, two to four fingers, and a live readout of grip against weight. Drag the object to push it. Truth replays a recorded finite-element grasp beside the fast finger on the same clock, with a time slider and jumps to the moments that matter. Grasp map shows which grasps hold; selecting a cell loads that grasp into Play. Only the page's fonts come from the network, and it falls back to system fonts offline.

docs.title: The fast finger
docs.text:
softsim/reduced cuts the finger into 8 links, each with a hinge and a slide. Tables in pressure give each link's rest angle and length, read from the reference's free-bend ramp. They are tables, not laws, because the pad stretches by a third at 40 kPa and the bend falls back after 35 kPa. One stiffness per pressure, shared by all hinges, comes from static tip loads on the reference (tools/probe_finger.py). softsim/reduced/wang_finger.json holds the result, and the page and Python read the same tables and the same model text.

Errors of the fitted finger against the reference:

Check Used in the fit Result Free tip against the static shape, 5-35 kPa no 0.3-3.1 mm Tip load, 5, 15, 25, 35 kPa yes 4-7% of the tip's movement Tip load, 20 kPa no 5-7% (3.5-4.7 mm of 53-91 mm) Load spread over the pads, 5-35 kPa no 9-27%

The spread-load error is the model's known weakness: at 20 kPa the chain bends 17-22% too far, so one stiffness for the whole finger is too simple. Contact on the objects here is near the tip, where the tip-load figures apply.

Reproduce (the probes take about an hour on the RTX 3060):

python tools/probe_finger.py --pressures 5 15 20 25 35 --forces 0.1 0.2 --out runs/reduced/probes_static.json
python tools/fit_reduced_finger.py --ramp runs/media/wang/fem.npz --probes runs/reduced/probes_static.json \
    --hold-out 20 --out softsim/reduced/wang_finger.json

runs/media/wang/fem.npz is the free-bend run written by tools/make_actuation_media.py.

docs.title: What it can hold
docs.text:
tools/grasp_map.py runs 504 grasps: three objects, three frictions, eight masses, seven pressures; 107 hold (60 box, 23 cylinder, 24 bottle). Each grasp holds to 20 s. Held means the object ended at least 10 mm above where it started and sank less than 1 mm over the last 0.2 s (softsim.scenarios.grasp.is_held, shared with the finite-element grasps). It is not a share of the lift, because soft fingers can lose much of the lift before the object leaves the table. The finger is very soft (0.2 N moves its tip about 90 mm), so this is a light gripper: the box grips at 0.16 N per finger at 35 kPa, and at friction 0.8 two fingers can carry about 26 g. The map holds 20 g and drops 30 g, as that limit says it should.

Why 20 s. Stopping 2 s after the lift called 154 grasps held. tools/check_long_hold.py runs those on, and only 123 are held at 10 s and 106 at 20 s: 60 of 61 box grasps, 23 of 46 cylinders and 23 of 47 bottles. One bottle grasp the short window rejected holds at 20 s, which makes 107. Even a good box grasp sinks, at 0.40 mm/s for 10 g at 30 kPa, so 20 s also marks down a grasp that creeps below 10 mm: the 30 g box at friction 1.2 and 35 kPa ends at 9.2 mm. That sink is MuJoCo's soft friction creeping rather than the grasp slipping: raising impratio from 10 to 100 cuts it to 0.04 mm/s. The cylinder's fall is not only creep: at impratio 100 it still falls, later.

Three things decided the layout:

  • Palm height 140 mm. At 120 mm the lengthened fingers reach the table at 30-40 kPa and pinch objects at their base, so a cylinder tips over.
  • More pressure is not always better. A 10 g cylinder at friction 0.8 holds at 20 and 25 kPa, and is back on the table by 10 s at 30 and 40 kPa. At 25 kPa and above even a 2 g cylinder falls by 20 s, so weight is not the cause. The cause has not been established.
  • Fingers do not collide with each other in the fast model.
python tools/grasp_map.py --finger softsim/reduced/wang_finger.json --out runs/reduced/grasp_map.json
python tools/make_gripper_page.py --finger softsim/reduced/wang_finger.json --map runs/reduced/grasp_map.json
python tools/check_gripper_page.py docs/viewer/gripper.html --finger softsim/reduced/wang_finger.json --shots runs/page
python tools/grasp_map.py --finger softsim/reduced/wang_finger.json --end 3.5 --out runs/reduced/grasp_map_3p5s.json
python tools/check_long_hold.py runs/reduced/grasp_map_3p5s.json --finger softsim/reduced/wang_finger.json --out runs/reduced/long_hold.json

docs.title: Against the finite-element grasp
docs.text:
The same grasp on the reference: 25 kPa, a 10 g box, a 30 mm lift, Coulomb friction 0.8 on both models. Two meshes: 2 mm and toothless, and the validated 1.5 mm finger with teeth (19 hours). Both ran with the default contact (a slip speed, decisions.md entry 6).

FE, 1.5 mm with teeth, μ 0.8 FE, 2 mm, μ 0.8 Fast finger FE, no-slip (earlier) Palm rise when the box leaves the table 1.3 mm 1.3 mm 0.2 mm 13.9 mm Final rise of the box 29.0 mm 28.9 mm 27.1 mm 17.2 mm Grip before the lift 0.133 N 0.122 N 0.107 N 0.170 N Grip while holding 0.113 N 0.100 N 0.092 N 0.100 N held 1 1 1 1

The two agree on how the grasp works, not only that it holds. The pads stay on the box's sides, the box leaves the table almost at once and follows the palm. Against the 2 mm run the grip is within 8% while holding and 12% before the lift; against the validated 1.5 mm finger the fast finger grips about 19% less (0.092 against 0.113 N while holding, 0.107 against 0.133 N before the lift). The fast finger's friction was not tuned to either run.

The earlier comparison was wrong, and why. The first finite-element grasps ran with no-slip contact while the fast finger ran at 0.8: the backend takes the larger of the silicone card's friction (1.0) and the object's, and from STICK_MU = 1.0 up it sticks, so object.friction had no effect. In those runs the fingertips pressed the box down, peeled off and re-gripped it at its top corners. That was the no-slip contact, not the finger: with friction it does not happen. Real friction is set with the card, body.material.friction.sliding, below 1.

The fast palm also stops 1.15 mm short of its target, sagging on its position actuator; ReducedGripper.palm_rise is the real height.

python tools/run_fe_grasp.py --mass 10 --out runs/grasp/coulomb_10g_2mm.npz --checkpoint runs/grasp/coulomb_10g_2mm.ckpt.npz \
    --set body.mesh.size=2mm --set body.geometry.finger.tooth_height=0 --set body.material.friction.sliding=0.8    # about 5 hours with other jobs running
python tools/plot_fe_grasp.py runs/grasp/coulomb_10g_2mm.npz --finger softsim/reduced/wang_finger.json --out docs/media/gripper_fe_grasp.png
python tools/run_fe_grasp.py --mass 10 --out runs/grasp/coulomb_10g_1p5mm.npz --checkpoint runs/grasp/coulomb_10g_1p5mm.ckpt.npz \
    --set body.material.friction.sliding=0.8    # the validated finger: 19 hours on an i5-13500, alone
python tools/make_gripper_page.py --finger softsim/reduced/wang_finger.json --map runs/reduced/grasp_map.json \
    --truth runs/grasp/coulomb_10g_1p5mm.npz --truth-label "1.5 mm mesh with teeth, friction 0.8"
python tools/check_gripper_page.py docs/viewer/gripper.html --finger softsim/reduced/wang_finger.json --truth runs/grasp/coulomb_10g_1p5mm.npz --shots runs/page

docs.title: The first finite-element drop
docs.text:
The same grasp with a 30 g box, which the map drops. The finite-element fingertips slide up the box's sides to its top corners and the box never leaves the table; the fast finger lifts it 1.5 mm at most and puts it back. Both call it dropped.

Finite element, 2 mm, μ 0.8 Fast finger Final rise of the box 0.001 mm 0.08 mm Grip before the lift 0.122 N 0.108 N Grip while holding (the tips at the corners) 0.074 N 0.092 N held 0 0

The hand check: grip is per finger, so two fingers at μ 0.8 and 0.122 N carry 2 × 0.8 × 0.122 = 0.195 N, which is 19.9 g. The 10 g box is under that and held, the 30 g box over it and dropped, on both models. This is one grasp on each side of the limit, on a coarse mesh, so it checks the map's boundary for the box at 25 kPa, not everywhere.

python tools/run_fe_grasp.py --mass 30 --out runs/grasp/coulomb_30g_2mm.npz --checkpoint runs/grasp/coulomb_30g_2mm.ckpt.npz \
    --set body.mesh.size=2mm --set body.geometry.finger.tooth_height=0 --set body.material.friction.sliding=0.8    # about 2.7 hours
python tools/plot_fe_grasp.py runs/grasp/coulomb_30g_2mm.npz --finger softsim/reduced/wang_finger.json --mass 30 --out docs/media/gripper_fe_drop.png

Mesh error. With friction (μ 0.8, the default slip speed) the 1.5 mm finger with teeth grips 13% harder while holding than the 2 mm toothless one (0.113 against 0.100 N) and 9% harder before the lift (0.133 against 0.122 N); the lift-off (1.3 mm of palm rise), the final rise (29.0 against 28.9 mm) and held are the same. The earlier no-slip pair showed the same 12% (0.112 against 0.100 N). Take about 13% as the uncertainty of a 2 mm grip. It is the teeth and the mesh together, since the two runs differ in both. The 2 mm numbers equal those of the earlier run with the old friction smoothing to the digits shown, so the slip speed does not change this grasp.

The Truth tab draws the finger's side face. Contact is usually mid-width, where the cavity bulges the pad past that face, so a marked node can sit in a gap between the drawn finger and the box. The fast finger there gets the same pressure schedule and is asked for the same palm path, but its palm follows about 6 mm behind during the lift.

docs.title: Checks
docs.text:
• tools/check_gripper_page.py opens the page from disk in headless Chrome, fails on any script error, and runs four scripted grasps in both the page and Python. The largest gap is 0.16 mm, although the page's MuJoCo is an older build (WebAssembly 3.1.16). It ran at about 8x real time with software graphics and two FE runs on the machine.
  • tests/test_reduced_finger.py: tables recover an exact arc, a small tip load matches the hinged cantilever by hand, the fit recovers a known stiffness, MuJoCo agrees with the static balance, and a mass under the friction limit rises while one over it stays. Mutations of the load direction, the spread load, the object's friction and the held metric each fail a test.
  • tools/check_gripper_page.py --truth compares the tab's decoded nodes with the run file (worst 0.005 mm, the storage step) and its readouts with both models. tests/test_truth_data.py checks the packing, the chapters and the schedule.
  • tools/rehearse_gripper_demo.py presses the buttons the demo script names and fails if a beat ends differently, or if Play's lift stops starting at 1.5 s, where the map's does. It found Play lifting 0.6 s early, so a loaded map cell was a different grasp; that is fixed.
  • tests/test_grasp.py: two fingers are exactly two of the finger, they curl inwards, and held and slip mean what they say.

docs.title: Limits
docs.text:
• The 10 g finite-element grasps were re-run with the friction default (a slip speed, decisions.md, entry 6) on 2026-11-13 and give the 2 mm numbers of the earlier run. The 30 g drop above predates it: re-run with the default, the 2 mm 30 g grasp stops converging at t = 1.04 s, during the lift (Newton fails even with 0.6 ms substeps; the checkpoint at sample 104 of 150 is kept, runs/grasp/coulomb_30g_2mm.ckpt.npz). Its dropped-box numbers are therefore from the old smoothing (--set contact.slip_speed=null).
  • Held on the map means held at 20 s, not indefinitely, and every grasp is still creeping then (see above).
  • The map is the fast model's prediction. Two coarse finite-element grasps check it, the box at 25 kPa held at 10 g and dropped at 30 g, as the map says. Every other cell, and the cylinder and bottle entirely, are unchecked.
  • Nothing here reproduces a physical grasp, and the grip is the conservative case. Wang et al. measured a tip force of 0.47, 0.77 and 0.96 N at 20, 30 and 35 kPa (Table 7, not used in any fit here) and showed four fingers holding objects up to 364 g, in single demonstrations with pressure unrecorded. The validated finger with its tip sliding on a gauge pushes 0.085, 0.146 and 0.165 N; with its tip stuck to it, 1.04 N at 20 kPa and 1.19 N at 30 kPa: the measurement lies between, and the paper doesn't record the contact, so the force cannot check the model (docs/actuation.md). The fast finger is fitted to the sliding case: it grips at 0.16 N per finger at 35 kPa and carries about 26 g on two fingers. Its held and dropped limits are the model's, not the real gripper's.
  • The chain does not deform around an object.
  • Two fingers are the fitted case. Three and four fingers on the page are extrapolations, and the validated finger is plane strain, so FE grasps can only be two fingers.
  • In FE grasps the table is a one-way frictionless support under the object's centre of mass (RigidBody3D.floor): it stops the object sinking, but not tipping, and the object cannot slide against it. The reference also has no finger-to-finger contact or self-collision.
  • SOFA is not used: 8.14° RMS on the finger at 1 mm and no browser build (docs/decisions.md).

docs.title: Magnetic soft materials (MRE)
docs.text: softsim models a soft-magnetic elastomer: silicone filled with iron powder, as in magnetorheological elastomer (MRE) grippers. The iron has no magnetisation of its own. The applied field magnetises it, a strip turns to lie along the field, and in a field gradient it is pulled towards the stronger field. The reference solver (backend: fem) runs it; MuJoCo, SOFA and the rod backend refuse it rather than simulate a passive body.

docs.title: Using it
docs.text:
A material card and a field, in any scenario config:

body:
  material:
    density: 2000 kg/m^3
    elastic:
      model: magneto_active
      matrix: {model: neo_hookean, youngs_modulus: 810 kPa, poisson_ratio: 0.49}
      particle_volume_fraction: 0.123   # or susceptibility: 0.45
      along: [1, 0, 0]                  # the strip's length, body frame
      normal: [0, 0, 1]                 # its thickness
      # demagnetization: block          # default; or [N_along, N_normal, N_across]

magnetic_field:
  uniform: [[0 s, [0, 0, 0]], [0.5 s, [20 kA/m, 0, 0]]]   # H, linear between waypoints; or a constant [Hx, Hy, Hz]
  magnets:
    - name: ring
      remanence: 1.23 T
      diameter: 20 mm
      hole: 4.2 mm
      thickness: 5 mm
      position: [0, 0, -12 mm]
      axis: [0, 1, 0]
      path: [[0 s, [0, 0, 0]], [0.2 s, [0, 0, 12 mm]]]    # optional, minimum jerk
      solid: true                                          # optional: the body can touch it
      edge: 0.2 mm                                         # optional: its chamfer (the default)

A solid magnet is also a rigid cylinder of the reference (its outer one), fixed or moving along its path, that the body touches with its own friction. edge is the magnet's chamfer: it rounds the contact surface and softens the field at the rims of the end faces (below).

scenarios/magnetic/mre_strip_buckling.yaml is a complete example (softsim run scenarios/magnetic/mre_strip_buckling.yaml, 12 s).

docs.title: The model
docs.text:
Energy per unit reference volume (softsim/fem/magnetic.py):

w = -mu0 / 2 (chi_a (a.H)^2 + chi_n (n.H)^2 + chi_b (H.H - (a.H)^2 - (n.H)^2))
  • Axes follow the deformation. The strip's axis is a = F a0 and its normal is n = F^-T n0, both normalised, so the energy turns with the material. A shear shows the difference between F and F^-T.
  • Composite susceptibility. chi is given, or comes from the iron's volume fraction by Maxwell Garnett's rule, 3 phi / (1 - phi).
  • Per-axis susceptibility. Each axis takes chi / (1 + N chi), where N is the demagnetising factor of the rectangular block bounding the body at rest. The factor is exact for a block (Aharoni 1998).
  • Field. H is the applied field at the deformed position: a uniform part plus permanent magnets.
  • Each magnet is an axially magnetised cylinder, magnetised uniformly at Br / mu0.
  • Its field is exact outside it (Derby and Olbert's closed form, with Bulirsch's elliptic integral run for a fixed number of steps so JAX can differentiate it).
  • A ring is a disc minus its hole.
  • Inside a magnet, H is B / mu0 - M. Nothing should be there, but contact holds nodes out, not quadrature points. Taking B / mu0 there made a false well just inside the rim, twice as deep as the real field, and it pulled a strip through the magnet's skin.
  • Edges. A sharp-edged magnet's field is infinite on the rims of its end faces (logarithmically). A strip drawn onto the magnet slid into that corner, and Newton failed. Real magnets are chamfered, and edge (0.2 mm, the small end of a chamfer) gives the field one: the elliptic modulus kc, which is zero only on those rims, becomes sqrt(kc^2 + (edge / 2a)^2). The field is then finite there, 1.7% off 1 mm away and 0.6% at 2 mm. On Bernat's rolling strip it lowers the torque by 3.3% (by 1.0% for 0.1 mm). The torque table below uses the exact, sharp field.
  • Derivatives. Newton's gradient and Hessian come from JAX. At each quadrature point they use the field's second-order expansion about where the point is now. Its value and first two derivatives there are the field's, so both are exact. Differentiating the magnets' elliptic integrals twice in reverse instead took 4 MB an element: 41 GB for a 10 800-element finger. The expansion takes 1.0 s a Hessian, at 1.2 GB.

What it leaves out:

  • The field is applied, not solved for. The strip's own field is not computed: the model is first order in chi, with only the demagnetising factors correcting for shape. The factors stay at their rest values as the body bends.
  • Interactions. Bodies do not magnetise one another, and magnets feel no force back.
  • Hard-magnetic particles (NdFeB, magnetised before use): the card's remanent_magnetization M_r [A/m, body frame] adds w_r = -mu0 (F M_r) . H per unit reference volume (Zhao, Kim, Yuk and Zhao, J. Mech. Phys. Solids 124, 2019), the magnetised material carried by the deformation; with susceptibility: 0 the composite is purely hard. Checks: a turned body's energy -mu0 V M_r H cos t, a stretched one's -mu0 V s M_r H (the deformation gradient, not its rotation), and a cantilever magnetised along its length in a field across it, whose tip deflects by Euler-Bernoulli's c L^3 / (3 E I), c = mu0 M_r H A (+1.1% at a 1 mm mesh, converging at second order).
  • Magnetic zones. body.zones may carry their own magneto_active card, or none: the body's magnetic energy is the sum over its elements, each with its own material's susceptibility, remanence, axes and saturation (a zone of a non-magnetic material takes up no field; a non-magnetic body can have magnetic zones). The single-material path is unchanged. Two arms of one body magnetised in opposite directions are two zones whose cards differ in the sign of remanent_magnetization (scenarios/magnetic/hard_magnetic_gripper.yaml). A zone with induced magnetisation (susceptibility > 0) must give its demagnetising factors, demagnetization: [N_along, N_normal, N_across]: block (the body's own bounding block) is refused in a body with zones, because a zone's field is shaped by its neighbours, not by its own block (decision 2026-11-11). A purely hard zone needs no factors. Checks (tests/test_magnetic.py, tests/test_scenario_magnetic.py): a bar of two zones with remanence +M and -M along its length has zero energy in a uniform field along it, at rest, turned and stretched (below 1e-12 of mu0 V M H); with the second zone non-magnetic, exactly half the whole bar's; a turned body with one hard and one soft zone has the sum of the two closed forms (1e-9); the assembled gradient and Hessian equal the single-magnet body's when all zones share a card (1e-12) and agree with central differences of the energy and the gradient when they differ (1e-6); each zone's card reaches the solver over exactly its own elements.
  • Saturation is a tanh law, not a measured curve. With the card's saturation_magnetization M_s set (0 keeps the linear law), the energy is -mu0 M_s^2 / chi_r ln cosh(sqrt(2 chi_r q) / M_s), with -mu0 q the linear energy and chi_r the largest axis susceptibility. Along the easiest axis that is exactly M = M_s tanh(chi H / M_s); the other axes saturate with it, an approximation. Checks (tests/test_magnetic.py): the tanh along the easy axis, the linear law at small fields, |M| <= M_s in any direction, a bar's energy from below to well above saturation, and a saturated piece pulled up a dipole's gradient by mu0 V M dH/dz (3.0 times weaker than the linear law at chi H / M_s = 3). A measured B-H curve would replace the tanh.

docs.title: A hard-magnetic gripper
docs.text:
scenarios/magnetic/hard_magnetic_gripper.yaml is one soft body, a U: a 28 x 4 x 4 mm palm bar clamped at its foot and two 4 x 4 x 40 mm arms on its ends, 20 mm apart (a STEP from scenarios/magnetic/cad/make_u_gripper.py, loaded with mesh_file). The arms are zones of the same 200 kPa elastomer with remanence 100 kA/m along the arm, +z in the left one and -z in the right; the palm is not magnetic. A uniform field along +x turns each moment towards it, so the arms close; reversed, they open. Run it with softsim run scenarios/magnetic/hard_magnetic_gripper.yaml (a 1.5 mm mesh, 2 s, 2 min on 2 threads). Its field ramps to 100 A/m, a small angle for the closed form below.

Measured against the cantilever under a uniform distributed couple c = mu0 M_r H A, whose tip moves c L^3 / (3 E I) (L = 40 mm, 1.005 mm at 100 A/m); static solutions at 100 A/m, both arms:

Mesh Arm bending u''' against c / EI Tip against c L^3 / 3EI Root slope times L, of that 2 mm (2.6k nodes) +7% (left), +10% (right) 1.24, 1.26 1.5 mm +3.4% 1.198 0.162 1 mm (17.5k nodes) +1.4% 1.176 0.75 mm (35.6k nodes) +0.5% 1.168 0.159
  • The arm itself follows the closed form. u''' is the cubic coefficient of the arm's centre line over 10-44 mm (the part away from the palm), which a distributed couple fixes whatever happens at the root. It converges to the closed form, like the 4 x 4 x 60 mm cantilever (+1.1% at 1 mm).
  • The tip does not, and should not. The arm stands on a palm of its own thickness that bends and shears under the arms' couples; the arm's slope at its root times its 40 mm accounts for 0.16 of the closed form, converged with the mesh, so the tip is 17-18% over a clamped-root cantilever's at 0.75-1 mm. A stiffer palm would shrink that term. The test (test_the_arms_of_a_hard_magnetic_gripper_close_by_the_cantilever_closed_form) therefore checks the tip as the cantilever's plus that root slope times the arm, to 5%, and the arm's own bending to 5% at 1.5 mm.
  • Linearity. The tip changes by under 1% against the closed form between 30 and 300 A/m at 1 mm (3 mm at 300 A/m, 7.5% of the arm length).
  • Symmetry. At 1 mm the two arms agree to 0.1%; at 2 mm they differ by 2% (the unstructured mesh is not mirrored).

No object is gripped yet, and nothing here was run for one. Closing on a light rigid object needs a grasp scenario with a rigid body between the arms (scenarios/grasp/box.yaml is the pattern for a box and contact) and the field held after the arms touch it. The arms must travel several millimetres, so the closed form above no longer applies and the field and the contact steps have to be found by running it: a job for the GPU machine, at 1 mm (17.5k nodes) or finer, not for two laptop threads.

Mutations. python tools/mutate_magnetic.py (about 25 min) breaks the model in 32 plausible ways, one at a time, on a copy, and checks that a test fails each time. Before any mutation, it checks that the copy is what gets imported and that the unmutated copy passes. The slips it tries include:

  • a wrong tensor, a dropped factor or a wrong sign;
  • an elliptic integral cut short, or a ring's hole not reversed;
  • the field read at rest or at the step's start;
  • the Hessian lost, or the field's expansion wrong;
  • a solid magnet's size, turn or path wrong.

docs.title: Against Bernat et al.'s MRE gripper
docs.text:
Bernat, Czopek, Superczynska, Gajewski and Marcinkowska (arXiv:2407.13477) built a gripper from 60 x 15 mm MRE strips (iron powder, 1 : 1 by weight) that roll onto axially magnetised ring magnets (20/4.2 x 5 mm, Br 1.21-1.25 T).

Their data. They computed the rolling torque in ANSYS (Fig. 3b) and measured the finger's force (0.70 ± 0.02 N, Fig. 11). tools/digitise_svg_plot.py reads both figures out of the paper's vector files exactly: marker positions, with axes calibrated on the plots' own ticks, so no reading by eye. The result is in datasets/bernat2024_mre_gripper.yaml.

What we compute. tools/mre_rolling_torque.py wraps a meshed strip round the magnet by a prescribed map and takes the torque as the slope of the solver's own magnetic energy. The susceptibility is not in the paper. Ours comes from the recipe alone: 12-14% iron by volume gives chi = 0.41-0.47.

Bands: chi 0.41-0.47 from the recipe. Dotted: the angle at which a strip of that thickness is fully rolled. python tools/mre_rolling_torque.py --plot docs/media/mre_rolling_torque.png, about 1 min on a GPU.

Strip Torque, chi 0.41 Torque, chi 0.47 Ratio to ANSYS (5.15 mN m) chi matching ANSYS Fully rolled 2 mm 3.01 mN m 3.41 mN m 0.58-0.66 0.79 313° 3 mm 3.59 mN m 4.06 mN m 0.70-0.79 0.63 299° 4 mm 3.98 mN m 4.50 mN m 0.77-0.87 0.56 286°

At half the element size the torques move by 0.3% (--size 0.5e-3).

  • Shape. The torque is flat while the strip rolls on, as in ANSYS. It falls to zero once the whole strip is on the rim.
  • Thickness. The ANSYS curve reaches zero at 308.9°. A 60 mm strip is fully rolled at that angle if its mid-surface radius is 11.1 mm, which means a strip about 2.3 mm thick. The paper's text does not say which thickness its simulation used (it gives 2-4 mm). Our 2 mm curve also falls the way ANSYS's does. This is an inference from geometry, not a measurement.
  • Size. For a 2 mm strip, the recipe's chi gives 58-66% of the ANSYS torque. ANSYS's own material matches a chi of 0.79, a relative permeability of 1.8. That is above the dilute Maxwell Garnett estimate, and below the "about 2-5" the paper quotes for MRE in general. Two things could explain part of the gap: the strip's own field beyond its demagnetising factors (which ANSYS solves for and we do not), and whatever B-H curve ANSYS used. Neither is known, so the gap is reported, not fitted away.

The force is not checked yet. The 0.7 N was read with the finger pressed on a gauge, at a contact point the paper does not give.

  • A free end peeled along the rim's tangent. Energy balance gives F = (T - E I / 2 rho) / rho, with rho = R + t / 2: the pull does F rho per angle unrolled, the strip gives back the rolling torque T and releases its bending energy E I / 2 rho (0.37 mN m here). For the 15 x 2 mm strip that is 0.24-0.28 N on our torque and 0.44 N on ANSYS's.
  • Measured. The plateau is higher: 0.66 N for RTV, 0.76-0.83 N for DS and MS. So the gauge must act at a shorter lever, about 7 mm from the magnet's axis on ANSYS's torque ((5.15 - 0.37) mN m / 0.70 N).
  • The clamped finger cannot peel this way. tools/mre_tangent_pull.py wraps a strip clamped at its root half-way round the magnet and pulls its tip along the rim's tangent. It has to be 4 mm wide, narrower than the magnet; see below.
  • The pull does not level off at the 0.119 N energy balance gives that strip. It rises from 0.064 N held to 0.63 N at 1 mm and 1.9 N at 6.2 mm.
  • With the root clamped, the wrap lies between two tangent points that this pull leaves in place, so nothing unrolls.
  • A clamped finger peels only when the push lets its free end swing round. Its force is therefore set by where and which way it is pushed: the missing contact point again.

python tools/mre_tangent_pull.py (about 25 min on a GPU), then python tools/mre_tangent_pull.py --plot runs/mre/peel_4mm_clamped.csv docs/media/mre_tangent_pull.png.

What did not run.

  • Bernat's 15 mm strip. It overhangs the 5 mm magnet by 5 mm a side, and the magnet's poles pull those flaps in at metres per second. A plate estimate gives about 2 mm of flap deflection under that pull. Each step took minutes, and Newton failed at 1.4 ms.
  • A free, frictionless strip held only by its tip. The magnet slid it sideways towards a rim edge, and Newton failed.
  • A strip released from a gap. It hits the magnet at metres per second within half a millisecond (about 1e4 m/s²), and Newton fails at the impact even with 0.125 ms steps. The real finger does not snap shut from a gap: it already lies on its magnet and rolls on or off as the magnet moves.

Simulating the closed finger against a gauge needs:

  • the gauge's contact point and direction;
  • the strip's thickness profile;
  • the magnets' position in the closed state;
  • if possible, a B-H curve of the composite (saturation would also tame the flaps).

docs.title: Limits
docs.text:
• Reduced. The strip's own field is not solved; demagnetising factors from the body's rest block. Saturation is an isotropic tanh law, off by default (saturation_magnetization: 0); no card has a measured value yet.
  • Hard-magnetic particles: checked, not yet validated. remanent_magnetization [A/m, body frame] adds Zhao et al.'s (2019) energy -mu0 (F M_r) . H; checked against a turned and a stretched body's energy and a cantilever's tip deflection (tests/test_magnetic.py), not yet against a measured hard-magnetic robot.
  • One magnetic body. Several magnetic zones of it are allowed (above), but no field on a moving or rotating mount: move the magnets along their path instead. A zone's induced magnetisation needs explicit demagnetising factors.
  • Solid magnets are full cylinders. A ring's contact solid is its outer disc, so nothing enters the hole; the contact rounds its edges by the magnet's edge, as its field does.

docs.title: Material library (generated)
docs.text: Physical material cards fitted to public test data by tools/make_material_library.py; do not edit by hand. Use a card by name, e.g. material: ecoflex_00_30_roels2025. Every card carries its data's strain range (validity), fit uncertainty and references; softsim material show <card> prints them.

docs.title: Roels et al. 2025 (preferred)
docs.text:
Tension and compression, several specimens each, and a 3-hour compression relaxation per material (doi:10.1002/aisy.202500699, data doi:10.5281/zenodo.14983287, CC-BY-4.0).

  • Fit: the law is fitted to tension and compression together, so these cards hold in compression too.
  • Prony series: from the relaxation hold, 1 s to 3 h. These silicones relax only 2–6% there.
  • Fast relaxation (impacts): measured for Ecoflex 00-30 and 00-50 by Croquette et al. 2026 (guided elastic waves, checked against a rheometer; arXiv:2604.27722), and added as Prony branches over 1 Hz–2 kHz without changing the response at the test rate. "Impact stiffening" is the small-strain shear storage modulus at 1 kHz over that at the test rate (0.06 Hz).
  • The other cards have no fast-rate data. Impacts on them will be too soft and too bouncy. For comparison, the Ecoflex 00-10 drop card (experiments.md) relaxes about 70% within milliseconds.
  • μ0 is the initial shear modulus at the test rate.
  • The first second of each relaxation recording is a strain overshoot seen through a lagging load signal, and is left out.
