ros2 service call /softsim/action softsim_interfaces/srv/RunAction \
  "{action: drop, arguments: '{mass: 0.1, height: 0.3}'}"
ros2 topic echo /softsim/metrics/indentation

docs.title: Closed-loop controller node
docs.text: controller_node runs a surrogate controller on top of the simulation node: it subscribes to /softsim/metrics/<output> and ~/target/<output> (Float64) and publishes /softsim/actuators/<name>/command every period seconds. Run it with use_sim_time:=true. Parameters: surrogate, outputs, period, ki, mode, damping, max_correction, sim_namespace. Not yet run against a ROS installation.

docs.title: Timing
docs.text: The simulation runs slower than real time (about 0.005–0.02× for the drop test, depending on mesh). The node steps as fast as it can and publishes simulated time on /clock, so RViz (use_sim_time: true) shows it in slow motion. Consumers should use use_sim_time. The node's own timers use the steady clock, so it never waits on the clock it publishes.

docs.title: Tests
docs.text: python -m pytest ros2/softsim_ros/test -p no:launch_testing -p no:launch_ros   # ROS sourced, venv active

docs.title: Reduced-order surrogates for real-time control (M11)
docs.text:
A repeated equilibrium solve (control.md) takes tens of seconds: every iteration settles a simulation. A controller running at 50 Hz cannot wait for that. softsim surrogate samples the equilibrium map once, fits a smooth model of it, and softsim inverse --method surrogate then answers in milliseconds. Code: softsim/control/surrogate.py; tests: tests/test_surrogate.py.

softsim surrogate jobs/surrogate_cable_cantilever.yaml      # sample, fit, validate -> runs/surrogate/.../surrogate.json
softsim inverse jobs/inverse_cable_cantilever_surrogate.yaml --method surrogate
softsim surrogate jobs/surrogate_cable_arm.yaml             # two cables, tip x and z
softsim inverse jobs/inverse_cable_arm_surrogate.yaml --method surrogate

docs.title: Method
docs.text:
1. Design of experiments. inputs (name: [lower, upper], with units) are sampled on a seeded design: the corners of the box (up to 4 inputs; so the bounds are interpolated, not extrapolated) plus a Latin hypercube (design: lhs), or a regular grid. holdout: m adds m more points from another seeded hypercube that the fit never sees.
  2. Samples. Each point is brought to equilibrium by the same Equilibrium object softsim inverse uses (constant actuators, stiffness-proportional settling damping, settled when the outputs stop moving; settle_* keys and scales are those of the inverse job) and the chosen outputs (any column of the scenario: tip_x, tip_z, bend_angle, ...) are recorded. Every sample is appended to samples.jsonl in the output folder, keyed by the resolved scenario (extends included), overrides, backend, settling options, softsim's code hash and the sample's inputs: a stopped job resumes, a rerun simulates nothing, a changed scenario or code does not reuse stale samples.
  3. Fit. model: poly (total-degree polynomial in the inputs scaled to [-1, 1], least squares; degree: auto picks the degree with the lowest k-fold error, at most 0.7 terms per sample) or model: rbf (cubic radial basis with a linear tail). numpy only.
  4. Validation (held out, never the fit residual). cv: k-fold cross-validation over the fitting samples (folds); holdout: error of the model fitted without the extra points. RMS and max, in SI units and relative to the output's range over the samples. The saved model is then refitted on all points.
  5. The file. surrogate.json holds inputs (name, SI unit, bounds), outputs (name, unit, range), the model (exponents and coefficients, or centres and weights), validation, scenario_hash, code_hash and the sample key. It needs nothing but numpy; for a polynomial, with z = 2 (x - lower) / (upper - lower) - 1:
import json, numpy as np
s = json.load(open("surrogate.json")); m = s["model"]
lo = np.array([i["lower"] for i in s["inputs"]]); hi = np.array([i["upper"] for i in s["inputs"]])
def predict(x):                                           # x in SI, in the order of s["inputs"]
    z = 2 * (np.asarray(x) - lo) / (hi - lo) - 1
    return np.array(m["coefficients"]) @ np.prod(z ** np.array(m["exponents"]), axis=1)

(softsim.control.surrogate.Surrogate.load(path).predict(x) does the same for polynomial and RBF models and refuses inputs outside the sampled box unless extrapolate=True.)

docs.title: The inverse on the surrogate
docs.text: softsim inverse job.yaml --method surrogate --surrogate file.json (or a surrogate: key in the job) solves the same scaled least-squares problem as the repeated solve on the surrogate, with scipy.optimize.least_squares from the box centre and 7 seeded random starts (starts). The job's actuators bounds tighten the surrogate's box; inputs not solved for go in fixed. verify: true runs one forward equilibrium (the job's config, overrides, settling options; refused if the scenario hash differs from the surrogate's) at the solution and reports the true error and how far the surrogate was off. The status is converged, bounded_best or stalled as for the repeated solve.

docs.title: Measured (MuJoCo; the machine was shared, times are indicative)
docs.text:
Cable cantilever, 4 mm mesh, tension 0 to 0.7 N, outputs bend_angle, tip_x, tip_z: 8 samples plus 4 held out, cubic polynomial, 56 s of simulation.

Held-out error RMS Max Relative to range bend_angle 1.8e-7 rad 2.3e-7 rad 3e-6 tip_x 7e-9 m 8e-9 m 4e-6

Two-cable arm (jobs/inverse_cable_arm.yaml settings), 0 to 0.5 N per cable, 20 samples plus 6 held out, cubic polynomial (10 terms), 225 s of simulation:

Held-out error RMS Max Relative to range tip_x 21 um 36 um 0.12% tip_z 1.1 um 1.7 um 0.05%

Inverse via the surrogate against the repeated solve and the truth:

Case Tension Error at the verifying simulation Solve time Cantilever, 2 degrees: surrogate 0.2709 N 3.2e-7 rad 26 ms same, repeated solve (5 simulations) 0.2716 N 8.7e-5 rad 22 s Arm, targets from 0.45 / 0.15 N: surrogate 0.4500 / 0.1500 N 0.53 um in x, 0.18 um in z 38 ms same, repeated solve (13 simulations) 0.4479 / 0.1487 N 22 um in x, 7.5 um in z 57 s

The surrogate finds the known arm tensions to 0.01%, closer than the repeated solve, whose answer is limited by its own stopping tolerance. The speed-up of a solve is ~850x (cantilever) and ~1500x (arm); one evaluation of the model is ~40 us in Python. It is paid for with the samples: 56 s (cantilever) and 225 s (arm), the cost of 3 and 4 repeated solves, so a surrogate pays off from the fourth target on.

Linear dynamic model (optional, dynamics:). DMD with control, s_{k+1} = A s_k + B (u_k - u0), with s the outputs minus their rest value and one earlier sample stacked (delay: 1, which gives it a velocity), fitted by least squares on constant-input step responses from rest (3 training steps, inputs from a seeded hypercube) and checked by open-loop rollout on 2 held-out steps. Cantilever, 0.3 s: held-out rollout RMS 0.37% of the travel for bend_angle (2.7e-4 rad), 0.5% for tip_x, 1.1% for tip_z. The state is the outputs, not the full state; it models the damped step response the settling damping produces, not the free vibration.

docs.title: Closed-loop control on the surrogate
docs.text:
softsim/control/controller.py (tests: tests/test_controller.py) turns the file into a controller you call once per control period, with no ROS and no simulator in it:

from softsim.control.controller import Controller

ctl = Controller.from_json("surrogate.json", dt=0.02, ki=6.0, outputs=["bend_angle"])   # 50 Hz
ctl.reset()
u = ctl.step(measured={"bend_angle": 0.0}, target={"bend_angle": 0.05})    # SI, in the order of ctl.inputs
  • Feedforward. The actuation that puts the target at equilibrium on the surrogate: bounded least squares, warm-started from the last solution (a multi-start solve only if that is poor); about 0.1 ms per step.
  • Feedback. An integral correction in actuator space, v += ki dt (J^T J + lambda^2 I)^-1 J^T e in scaled coordinates (J the surrogate's Jacobian at the applied actuation, e = target - measured; damped least squares, so two cables that move the tip alike do not blow up). Anti-windup by clamping: feedforward + v stays inside the bounds (the surrogate's box, or tighter bounds=), and v inside max_correction of the range, so an unreachable target winds nothing up (tested: after 400 saturated steps the controller is back on a reachable target in the same number of steps as from rest). mode="ff" switches the feedback off.
  • MPC-lite (mode="mpc", needs dynamics: in the surrogate job). An offset-free step on the DMD model: the state is built from the last two measured outputs, the one-step prediction error is held over the horizon as a disturbance, and a bounded linear least-squares problem over horizon periods (tracking error plus move_weight times the moves) gives the first actuation. dt must equal the model's sample period. Tested on a linear plant 15 % off the model (converges to 1e-5 of the target, within bounds); not evaluated on MuJoCo, because the stored models sample at the physics step (1 ms), not at a control rate (set dynamics.sample_every to the control period to try it), and a 3-step DMD fit is coarse.

Measured on MuJoCo (tools/eval_controller.py cantilever|arm, shared machine). The surrogates are the two above (jobs/surrogate_cable_cantilever.yaml, jobs/surrogate_cable_arm.yaml, nominal body); the plant is the same scenario with the Gymnasium environments' settings and a deliberate mismatch. Cantilever: 4 mm mesh, 1 ms step, 50 Hz, bend-angle steps 0 to 0.03, to 0.06, to 0.04 rad, 2 s each, and a ramp 0.02 to 0.06 rad over 4 s. Arm: 6 mm mesh, 0.5 ms step, 20 Hz, tip steps of 4 to 8 mm, 3 s each, and a 5 s ramp between two of them. Settling time: the last time the error is outside 5 % of the step; steady-state error: mean of the last 20 % of the hold (the norm over the outputs); ramp error: mean tracking error over the second half of the ramp.

Plant Settling (s), 3 steps Steady-state error Ramp error cantilever, nominal feedforward 0.04 / 0.02 / 0.02 < 1e-7 rad 2.0e-5 rad feedback 0.16 / 0.18 / 0.18 < 1e-7 rad 1.4e-4 rad cantilever, E +20 % feedforward never 5.0 / 9.9 / 6.6 mrad (17 to 33 %) 9.1 mrad feedback 0.02 / 0.02 / 0.02 1e-7 rad 8.7e-5 rad cantilever, E -20 % feedforward never 7.4 / 14.7 / 9.9 mrad 13.6 mrad feedback 0.28 / 0.28 / 0.28 < 1e-7 rad 3.5e-4 rad cantilever, 6 mm mesh feedforward never 2.2 / 4.2 / 2.8 mrad 3.9 mrad feedback 0.06 / 0.06 / 0.06 < 1e-7 rad 5.2e-5 rad arm, nominal feedforward 0.40 / 0.45 / 0.55 0.010 / 0.003 / 0.007 mm 0.49 mm feedback 0.45 / 1.65 / 1.70 0.001 / 0.026 / 0.047 mm 0.21 mm arm, E +20 % feedforward never 0.66 / 0.70 / 1.82 mm 1.9 mm feedback never (0.63 mm) / 1.10 / 1.20 0.63 / 0.014 / 0.015 mm 0.13 mm arm, E -20 % feedforward never 0.98 / 1.03 / 2.70 mm 1.6 mm feedback 2.05 / 2.20 / 1.70 0.10 / 0.20 / 0.084 mm 0.37 mm

So a 20 % stiffness error (or a coarser mesh) leaves feedforward 17 to 33 % off on the cantilever and 1 to 3 mm off on the arm, and the integral feedback brings both to the noise floor of the settled simulation (cantilever, 1e-7 rad) or to 0.01 to 0.2 mm (arm, whose 1 Hz first mode and the strong settling damping make it slow: with ki = 3 per second the correction has a time constant of ~0.3 s and a hold of 3 s ends before the E -20 % plant has converged). The first step of the E +20 % arm shows the same effect (0.63 mm left). The controller costs 0.4 to 0.6 ms per step (feedforward alone 0.15 ms), under 3 % of a 20 ms period. Note what feedback costs when the model is right: on the nominal plants it only adds lag (settling 0.16 s against 0.04 s, 1.7 s against 0.5 s), because the integrator reacts to the dynamic lag of the body, which the static map does not know; use a lower ki or mode="ff" when the surrogate is trusted. The gain ki must stay well under the plant's bandwidth (ki dt below ~0.5); raise it only after checking for overshoot.

Limits of the controller. It is only as good as the surrogate's Jacobian (a wrong gain changes the speed, not the final value, but a wrong sign diverges); it tracks quasi-static targets (a ramp is followed with a small lag, a fast reference is not, since the model has no time except in the DMD mode); the surrogate's box is a hard bound; it does not estimate sensor bias or noise (filter measured first); nothing here handles contact or a payload that changes the map. The loop above is simulated with the true state read exactly each period.

ROS 2. ros2/softsim_ros/softsim_ros/controller_node.py (ros2 run softsim_ros controller_node --ros-args -p surrogate:=... -p use_sim_time:=true, ros2.md) wraps the controller: it reads /softsim/metrics/<output> and ~/target/<output>, and publishes /softsim/actuators/<name>/command on a timer. It is a thin wrapper, but it has not been run (no ROS in the development environment): a test only parses it.

docs.title: Limits
docs.text:
• A surrogate inherits the backend. It reproduces MuJoCo's equilibrium map, locking included (the 4 mm mesh is about 3 times too stiff in bending, actuation.md): tensions found are the backend's, not physical ones. Fit it on a transferred card and a checked mesh, or on the reference backend, for physical values.
  • Inside the box only. Predictions outside the sampled bounds are refused; the inverse is bounded by it.
  • Smooth maps. A polynomial cannot follow a kink (the unsigned bend_angle of the arm folds at zero) or a snap; the validation error shows it, so read it. Compare degree and model: rbf by the held-out error.
  • Curse of dimension. The number of terms grows as C(d + p, p); beyond about 4 actuators use rbf or more samples.
  • Equilibria only. The static surrogate has no time; the DMD model is linear, fitted on few steps, and its error grows with the nonlinearity and the distance from the training steps.
  • Reuse. The sample log is keyed to the code hash, so any change to softsim makes the next run resimulate.

docs.title: Validation: predictions on data the model never saw
docs.text:
Fitting a model to data and then showing it matches that data says how well the fit converged, not how good the model is. This page lists only predictions: each result compares a model with data that played no part in building it.

Check Data the model saw Data it predicts Result Drop card → independent tension test the 20 and 50 g drop videos quasi-static tension of Ecoflex 00-10, another lab, optical strain 3–22% up to 100% strain Tension → compression tension specimens compression specimens, same lab 4–17% Compression → tension compression specimens (to 25%) tension specimens to 100% 4.5–20% (Mold Max 32%) Leave one weight out one drop recording the other drop recording weight trajectory 22–28%; the specimen's hop fails (51–93%) Labs against each other – the same product measured by different labs up to 3× apart

Regenerate: python tools/validate_materials.py (sections 2, 3 and 5) and python tools/leave_one_out.py (section 4).

docs.title: 1. A drop-fitted card predicts an independent tension test
docs.text:
The physical Ecoflex 00-10 card (Neo-Hookean, E0 = 143 kPa, Prony g = 0.69 at τ = 2 ms) was fitted only to the first contact of the 20 and 50 g drop videos, on the locking-free 3D reference (experiments.md). Its fully relaxed response is a prediction for a slow tension test.

Shojaeifard and Bacca 2025 (arXiv:2506.05371, Table 1) measured Ecoflex 00-10 in quasi-static tension, with optical strain tracking, three specimens: a one-term Ogden law with E = 34 kPa and α = 2.8. Their deep-indentation tests agree with it (E = 38 kPa).

Nominal stress of each card over theirs:

Stretch 1.25 1.5 2.0 2.5 3.0 Physical card from the drop (relaxed) 1.22 1.13 0.97 0.84 0.74 MuJoCo effective drop fit 1.50 1.38 1.14 0.96 0.81 Datasheet card (ecoflex_00_10) 2.49 2.28 1.90 1.59 1.35 Marechal 2021 card (crosshead strain) 0.85 0.72 0.62 0.58 0.56
  • The drop-fitted card predicts it within 3–22% up to 100% strain.
  • Above that it falls short because Neo-Hookean does not stiffen, and the drops never strain the material that far.
  • The datasheet's 100% modulus (55 kPa) is about 2× too stiff for this lab's material. A joint fit of the drop and that datasheet value was therefore stopped: it would have pulled the card the wrong way.

docs.title: 2. Tension-only cards predict compression
docs.text:
Roels et al. 2025: several tension and compression specimens per material. A card fitted to the tension specimens only (0–100%, law chosen by BIC as in the library) predicts the compression specimens (0 to −25%). Error = RMS / the specimen's largest stress, averaged over specimens:

Material Law Fit (tension) Predicted (compression) Joint fit, compression Dragon Skin 20 Gent 4.7% 13.5% 11.0% Dragon Skin 30 Yeoh 1.0% 12.2% 4.9% Ecoflex 00-20 Arruda–Boyce 10.8% 7.3% 2.0% Ecoflex 00-30 Yeoh 4.1% 5.6% 1.4% Ecoflex 00-50 Yeoh 3.6% 5.5% 1.6% Mold Max 14NV Yeoh 0.8% 3.9% 3.5% Mold Star 30 Yeoh 0.7% 16.7% 5.1%

docs.title: 3. Compression-only cards predict tension
docs.text:
The reverse is harder. 25% compression barely constrains a law's higher-order terms.

Material Law Fit (compression) Predicted (tension, to 100%) With Neo-Hookean Dragon Skin 20 Arruda–Boyce 10.9% 20.6% 19.3% Dragon Skin 30 Arruda–Boyce 4.5% 16.0% 21.2% Ecoflex 00-20 Neo-Hookean 0.8% 11.7% 11.7% Ecoflex 00-30 Mooney–Rivlin 1.4% 4.5% 10.0% Ecoflex 00-50 Neo-Hookean 1.6% 7.8% 7.8% Mold Max 14NV Mooney–Rivlin 3.3% 32.0% 18.9% Mold Star 30 Arruda–Boyce 4.7% 8.5% 26.0%

This check found a bug, now fixed. Yeoh fits to compression alone were marked stable, because stability was checked only over the fitted range (up to a stretch of 1). In tension they diverged (errors of 10⁸% and more). Fits are now checked for stability up to a stretch of at least 2, so such laws are rejected. Every card still records the strain range it was fitted on (validity), and softsim check warns when a run leaves it.

docs.title: 4. Leave one weight out (whole bounce)
docs.text:
The MuJoCo whole-bounce model (stiffness, damping, tack, cloth support: 7 parameters) is refitted to one recording only, from neutral starting values, and then predicts the other recording's first 100 ms (calibrations/loo_ecoflex_00_10_fit_w0x0.yaml, tools/leave_one_out.py).

Error = NRMSE over the first 100 ms: the mean of the weight's trajectory (indentation) and the specimen's hop (specimen_lift).

Fitted on Own recording Predicting the other Fitted on both, same recording 20 g 13% 50 g: 60% (weight 28%, hop 93%) 8% 50 g 15% 20 g: 37% (weight 22%, hop 51%) 18%

The material transfers; the setup model does not. - The material agrees between the folds: E = 45 vs 53 kPa, β = 0.87 vs 1.0 ms (the MuJoCo effective values). Each fold also predicts the other weight's trajectory nearly as well as it fits its own (22–28% against 18–20%), and the first-contact peak within 2% (4.39 vs 4.31 mm, fitted on 20 g) and 23% (2.89 vs 3.74 mm, fitted on 50 g). - The cloth support is not identified by one recording. The folds put its mass at 2 g and 77 g, its damping at 1.25 and 0.32 N s/m, and the tack range at 1.2 and 0.3 mm. Each fits its own hop (8–10%), but predicts the other's poorly (51–93%). - So the support and tack values in the drop cards describe the two recordings together. They aren't properties of the material or the table, and the specimen-hop results in experiments.md hold for these two weights, not as predictions for others.

docs.title: 5. How much do labs disagree?
docs.text:
The same product, measured by different labs (stress ratios as in section 1, against Shojaeifard and Bacca's Ecoflex 00-30: E = 81 kPa, α = 2.4):

Ecoflex 00-30 card Stretch 1.25 1.5 2.0 3.0 Roels et al. 2025 (preferred library card) 1.90 1.79 1.57 1.74 Datasheet card 1.35 1.29 1.16 0.95 Marechal et al. 2021 (crosshead strain) 0.61 0.59 0.56 0.52

Small-strain moduli of Ecoflex 00-30 from five sources: 54 kPa (Marechal), 68 kPa (Croquette et al. 2026, 3μ0), 81 kPa (Shojaeifard and Bacca), about 118 kPa (datasheet 100% modulus, Neo-Hookean) and 166 kPa (Roels).

Batch, cure and test method spread a nominal silicone over a factor of 3. No simulation can be more accurate than that for a part made from an unmeasured batch. For accurate work, measure your own material (one tension test, softsim fit-material). A library card is a starting point with an uncertainty of about ±50%, not a fact.

docs.title: MuJoCo backend: physics notes and limits
docs.text: Verified against MuJoCo 3.17.0, the pinned range (mujoco>=3.17,<3.18). The flex API changes every release, so read the changelog before bumping.

docs.title: What is used
docs.text:
softsim MuJoCo Soft body flexcomp type="direct" dim="3" with our tetrahedral mesh; one 3-dof body per vertex stvk default flex elasticity: Saint Venant–Kirchhoff, linear tetrahedra stable_neo_hookean Stable Neo-Hookean (Smith et al. 2018), MjsFlex.elastic3d = 1 (experimental since 3.15, spec-only, not in MJCF). Classic neo_hookean (ln J energy) is not available and is refused. rayleigh.beta, kelvin_voigt flex damping (stiffness-proportional; Kelvin–Voigt maps to beta = eta / E) prony (on stable_neo_hookean) the flex carries the long-term law (shear modulus × (1 − Σg), bulk unchanged); the Maxwell-branch overstress of every tetrahedron (softsim/materials/viscoelastic.py, needs the fem extra) is applied as explicit vertex forces (xfrc_applied) before every step base: bonded <pin> on the bottom-face vertices Contact soft constraints solref = (timeconst, dampratio), solimp; friction combines by max adhesion (material, ground) external forces (xfrc_applied) on surface vertices and rigid bodies, recomputed before every step from analytic signed distances (softsim/contact/adhesion.py) mount: slider_z slide joint along z with stiffness, damping, springref = 0 (rest = initial pose) Integrator discrete (new in 3.13, Sept 2026, experimental): implicit in position, so flex stiffness has no explicit stability limit

Not supported, and refused: small-strain linear elasticity, Mooney-Rivlin, Yeoh, Ogden, Gent, Arruda–Boyce, mass-proportional damping, magneto-active coupling, negative Poisson's ratio, any integrator other than discrete, and the PGS solver.

docs.title: Measured behaviour (drop test, this repo)
docs.text:
• Material mapping is correct. Under a frictionless 3% uniaxial compression, the result matches δ = m·g·H/(E·A) within 0.7–1.8% for both stable_neo_hookean and stvk (tests/test_drop_test.py::test_static_uniaxial_compression).
  • The timestep is not the accuracy bottleneck. With the contact model held fixed, peak indentation at dt = 0.1 ms and 0.05 ms differs by 0.2–0.7%. Use dt ≤ 0.1 ms for impacts; 0.2 ms is within about 3%.
  • Contact compliance matters as much as the material. Peak indentation for 20 g changes by about 10% between timeconst 0.2 ms and 0.4 ms. Penetration scales with roughly v·timeconst. Keep timeconst fixed in configs (scenario default 0.2 ms) and treat it as a model parameter; auto (= 2·dt) couples it to the timestep.
  • Results are not mesh-converged. Linear tetrahedra at ν = 0.45 lock: peak indentation grows 10–15% per refinement step (5 → 3.5 → 2.5 mm). A calibrated modulus is therefore an effective value for one mesh resolution; fitted presets must record their mesh in provenance. Pushing ν toward Ecoflex's real ~0.49 makes this worse.
  • StVK collapses in compression. With 200 g and 500 g, StVK lets the weight crush through the full 17 mm. Stable Neo-Hookean stays physical (8 and 13 mm in the Step 0 probe) and is the default. Naming: this was called neo_hookean until M4; it is the stable variant, a different energy at large strain from classic Neo-Hookean, so it now has its own model name.
  • The 500 g misfit is not a MuJoCo limitation. Expect the 200–500 g cases to fit worse than 20–50 g. M4 tested this on SOFA: an Ogden fit doesn't reproduce 500 g either, and actually prefers less large-strain stiffening than Neo-Hookean. Compressibility (ν = 0.45) and missing rate dependence matter more; see experiments.md.
  • Native damping is a single Rayleigh beta, a crude proxy for viscoelasticity: the loss factor grows linearly with frequency. Beta and E trade off strongly over a millisecond impact. Prony cards avoid this.
  • Prony viscoelasticity is explicit. Its overstress lags one step, so its stiffness Σg·μ0 must be resolved by the time step (softsim check reports ω·dt). This is no issue at drop-test steps: the limit is about 0.25 ms on a 3 mm mesh. The forces match the homogeneous reference exactly under uniform deformation (tests/test_viscoelastic.py). A 50 g drop with g = 0.6 at τ = 2 ms peaks between the instantaneous and the long-term material, at 5.38 mm on MuJoCo and 5.39 mm on SOFA.
  • Friction changes the impact a lot. 50 g drop, no material damping, 5 mm mesh: peak 4.89, 5.72 and 6.80 mm at sliding friction 1, 0.3 and 0. The bulging specimen slides against the weight and the table, and that matters as much as the modulus.
  • An undamped impact loses energy that a converged solver keeps. See Energy and contact fidelity below. Fitted damping (β) is therefore an effective value on top of MuJoCo's own losses.
  • Mesh stiffness against a converged reference: for a static flat punch (small strain) the 5 mm mesh is 20–60% stiffer than the locking-free reference (reference_fem.md).
  • Peak contact force is not converged. It is a first-contact spike on tiny vertex masses and changes with dt (70–140 N for 20 g). Use indentation, timing, rebound and ground force for calibration.
  • Specimen lift-off. In the free-base configuration the specimen's elastic recoil can launch it off the rigid table after the weight separates (1 mm at 20 g up to 16 mm at 500 g with the uncalibrated preset). It is reported as specimen_lift_off. The real specimens do hop, by 8–20 mm, but for a different reason: the tacky specimen is pulled up by the weight stuck to it, and drags the cloth under it along. Reproducing that needs adhesion and the compliant support (below). Correction history: M3 read the specimen's hop as table motion; that was wrong. See experiments.md.
  • Solver warnings. At large dt on finer meshes, the inner M+K solve can run out of CG iterations (mjWARN_INERTIA). softsim reports this as a backend-warnings finding; raise simulation.iterations or lower dt.
  • Divergence. MuJoCo resets the state itself on NaN; softsim detects this through the bad-qacc/qpos/qvel warning counters and raises StabilityError.

docs.title: Energy and contact fidelity
docs.text:
How much of an impact's energy MuJoCo loses that it shouldn't, measured with purely elastic cards (no damping of any kind) against the locking-free 3D reference (tools/contact_restitution.py, 2026-10-31).

1. Flex elasticity is numerically damped like backward Euler. A free axial vibration of the bonded specimen (no contact, no damping, 6.25 ms period) loses energy per cycle as predicted by a damping ratio ζ ≈ ω·dt/2:

Timestep 100 µs 50 µs 25 µs 12.5 µs Energy lost per cycle 52% 30% 15% 6.5% 1 − exp(−4πζ), ζ = ω·dt/2 47% 27% 15% 7.6%

For the mode you care about (angular frequency ω), pick dt so that ω·dt/2 is well below the material damping you want to model.

2. Impacts: friction slip costs most. A centred 50 g weight hits the drop specimen at 2.7 m/s. Restitution e = rebound speed / impact speed:

Contact Reference (fem) MuJoCo, 5 mm mesh MuJoCo, 3.5 / 2.5 mm Frictionless 0.869 0.791 0.839 / 0.838 Sticking, μ = 1 0.905 0.71–0.75 –
  • Contact settings don't matter. e stays at 0.71–0.75 over damping ratio 1 to 0.05, time constant 0.1–0.2 ms and timestep 50 to 6 µs.
  • Without friction MuJoCo is within 3.5% at meshes of 3.5 mm or finer. At 5 mm, each surface vertex's impact on the weight is plastic, and that costs about 6% more.
  • With friction it loses about twice as much. The reference sticks, which does no work. MuJoCo's soft friction constraint slips while the specimen bulges under the weight, and the slip dissipates.
  • The best available mitigation: contact.cone: elliptic with contact.impratio: 10 (10–100 are equivalent). This raises e from 0.748 to 0.78 at 5 mm. MuJoCo's no-slip solver would remove the slip, but it is not supported with flex under the discrete integrator. The defaults stay pyramidal and 1, which is what every fit in this repository used.

3. Locking: at ν = 0.45 the 5 mm mesh's peak compression is 24% below the reference's (4.9 against 6.5 mm with sticking).

These losses are why MuJoCo's fitted cards are effective. Transfer a physical card (materials.md) rather than using its values directly.

docs.title: Adhesion (tack)
docs.text:
• Model: an exponential cohesive law in the normal direction, t(g) = σ (g/δ) e^(1 − g/δ), acting on the surface area that faces the counterpart. A bond forms on contact and breaks for good beyond 6δ. Work of separation is e·σ·δ per area. See softsim.materials.Adhesion.
  • Explicit. The forces are computed from the state at the start of each step, so the adhesive stiffness e·σ/δ per vertex area must be resolvable: softsim check reports adhesion-stiff (ω·dt > 0.3) and refuses adhesion-unstable (ω·dt > 1). Lower the timestep or raise range.
  • No damping of its own. A body held only by adhesion oscillates on the bond undamped (Rayleigh β damps strain, not rigid motion). The energy still stored in a bond when it breaks is the only loss. Rate-dependent tack is not modelled.
  • Verified (tests/test_adhesion.py): a stiff block held to the ground, and a disc held to a block, under slowly reversed gravity settle at the analytic opening of the traction law within 2%. Above the bond capacity the block tears off. The reported contact force equals the load.
  • Mesh dependence. Tractions are lumped on surface vertices, so the bonded area is resolved at the mesh size (a 12 mm disc on a 5 mm mesh bonds about 10% too much area). More importantly, peeling is only mesh-converged when the cohesive zone, l ≈ E·(e·σ·δ)/σ², spans several elements. For the drop-test fit (σ ≈ 14 kPa, δ = 0.3 mm, E ≈ 73 kPa) that is about 4 mm, less than the 5 mm mesh. On 5 mm the bond acts all-or-nothing; on 3.5 mm it peels and lets the 20 g weight go. Fitted tack parameters are therefore effective values for the mesh they were fitted on, like the fitted moduli.

docs.title: Performance
docs.text: 762-vertex cylinder (3.5 mm mesh), dt = 0.1 ms, one CPU core: about 0.005× real time, so a 250 ms drop takes about 50 s. The 5 mm mesh is about 3× faster. Sweeps run in parallel processes (--jobs). No GPU is used or needed.

docs.title: Rod backend: slender bodies as beams
docs.text:
--backend rod runs a scenario's slender soft body as a chain of beams on SOFA's BeamAdapter (softsim/backends/rod/). Needs the SOFA install of sofa.md; no GPU. The same YAML that runs on fem, mujoco and sofa runs on rod, and softsim transfer can compare them:

softsim run scenarios/actuation/cable_arm.yaml --backend rod

docs.title: Model
docs.text:
• Reduction (reduce.py, pure numpy). The body must be a column along its z axis, clamped on its z-min face (fixed: [base]) and at least 4 times longer than wide. Frames sit on planes z = const, one per mesh layer. Per beam the tetrahedra of the slab give, with each element's own modulus (so material zones, layers and stiff disks enter exactly), the extensional stiffness EA, the bending stiffnesses EI_x, EI_y about the stiffness-weighted centroid (the neutral axis moves off the geometric centre in a layered section; the exact quadratic tetrahedron integrals are used) and the mass per length.
  • To BeamAdapter. Three stiffnesses meet three unknowns: a rectangle lY = sqrt(12 EI_x / EA), lZ = sqrt(12 EI_y / EA) and a modulus E = EA / (lY lZ) per beam, plus a mass density that reproduces the mass per length. The beam axis is BeamAdapter's x, so the model runs in the cyclic frame (X, Y, Z) = (z, x, y) of the scene and maps back.
  • Mesh from frames. Every mesh vertex keeps its axial position and in-plane offset; its position is the interpolated frame (lerp the position, slerp the rotation) plus the rotated offset, so every region metric of the scenario works unchanged (bend angle, tip position, cable length).
  • Loads. Cables and region forces call the same functions as the 3D backends (cable_forces, cable_length, region_force_weights) on the deformed vertices; the vertex forces reach the frames through the transpose of the vertex map (virtual work: frame k gets (1 - t) f and the moment (1 - t) arm x f), explicitly once per step, as on SOFA's tets. Tension and stroke control both work.

docs.title: What it is, and is not
docs.text:
Geometrically nonlinear (finite rotations of the frames), materially linear: each element counts with its small-strain modulus. Two consequences, both measured below:

  1. A beam bent to 64° follows the exact elastica-like arc (the cable's pure moment gives a circular arc), with the beam shortened by its axial compression, L / (1 + N / EA).
  2. The 3D reference's Neo-Hookean tangent modulus rises under the cable's axial compression, E_t = E (1 + 2N / EA) (the factor in tests/test_cable_arm.py), which a linear rod cannot have: on the cable arm the rod bends about 8% more than the reference, and that is this factor (7.3% plus the reference's own 1.8% below Euler–Bernoulli), not an error of the rod.

Refused with a message: pressure actuators, ground and contact, rigid bodies, moving and rotating mounts, prescribed motion, Prony, zones with their own damping, more than one soft body, rotated bodies, bodies shorter than 4 widths, a free body (no clamped end).

Damping: Rayleigh beta only. The solver's mass-proportional alpha does nothing on BeamAdapter's mass (measured: the late amplitude of a free vibration with alpha = 20 /s is that without damping, with beta = 0.01 s it falls by 5x), so a card with alpha is refused. For a quasi-static run use beta (damping: {model: rayleigh, beta: 0.3} on the body and on every zone).

Cable timestep. The explicit cable force is limited like on the 3D backends: the arm at 2 ms is refused by the cable-unstable check; 1 ms runs, the arm's 0.1 ms default is 100 times slower.

docs.title: Evidence (tests/test_rod_reduce.py, tests/test_rod_backend.py, 16 tests)
docs.text:
Case Rod Reference value Where Tip load 5 mN, 10 x 10 x 60 mm 0.8641 mm Euler–Bernoulli 0.864 mm (3D reference 0.866 mm) tip_load_cantilever.yaml Cable cantilever, 0.7 N 0.2777 rad T d L / EI = 0.2772 rad cable_cantilever.yaml Same at 2.8 N (64°) tilt 1.116 rad; tip (30.6, 44.0) mm arc of the compressed beam (30.7, 44.2) mm figure, left Layered section (neutral axis −2.57 mm) 0.2233 rad composite T (d - x_c) L / EI within 1% cable_cantilever_layered.yaml Two-segment arm 0.2298, 0.1221 rad linear piecewise E–B 0.2315, 0.1219 rad (3D reference 0.2119, 0.1074: lower by 1 + 2N/EA and 1.8%) cable_arm.yaml, figure, right

Reproduce the figure with python tools/plot_rod.py (about 2 min).

Mutation tests. Each of these deliberate bugs fails the tests (4, 5, 5, 5, 2 and 6 failures): zone stiffness ignored, the moment sign flipped, the moments dropped, nearest-frame instead of interpolation in the vertex map, EI_x and EI_y swapped, and the cable load dropped.

Speed. The rod runs the arm (1.5 s at 1 ms) in 5.8 s and each 10 mm cantilever in under 2 s on the CPU (500 ms at 2 ms); the MuJoCo arm run took 20 minutes (../actuation.md).

docs.title: SOFA backend: setup, physics notes and limits
docs.text: Verified against the SOFA v26.06.00 Linux binary release built for Python 3.10, with its bundled SofaPython3. It runs on CPU; no GPU is needed.

docs.title: Install
docs.text:
# download and unzip the release, e.g. into ~/.local/opt/sofa
curl -LO https://github.com/sofa-framework/sofa/releases/download/v26.06.00/SOFA_v26.06.00_Linux_Python3.10.zip
mkdir -p ~/.local/opt/sofa && unzip SOFA_v26.06.00_Linux_Python3.10.zip -d ~/.local/opt/sofa
export SOFA_ROOT=~/.local/opt/sofa/SOFA_v26.06.00_Linux        # add to your shell profile
softsim run scenarios/drop_test/cases/w020.yaml --backend sofa --set simulation.timestep=5e-5

softsim finds SofaPython3 through $SOFA_ROOT. Without it, the SOFA tests skip and softsim check still reports what SOFA would support.

docs.title: Scene
docs.text:
softsim SOFA Soft body TetrahedronSetTopologyContainer, MechanicalObject, lumped MeshMatrixMass, EulerImplicitSolver, SparseLDLSolver linear TetrahedronFEMForceField method="small" stvk, neo_hookean, stable_neo_hookean TetrahedronHyperelasticityFEMForceField, ParameterSet [μ, λ] mooney_rivlin same force field, [C10, C01, bulk] ogden (one term) same force field, [μ·α, α, bulk] (SOFA writes the term as μ₁/α²) Tension-controlled cable springs between the via points (StiffSpringForceField on a BarycentricMapping child) whose rest lengths are reset every step to length - T / k: the force is the tension at the current positions and the cable's tangent stiffness T (I - u u^T) / l is in the implicit matrix and the Rayleigh damping (k is 1% of T per via-point spacing, so the axial stiffness is negligible). An explicit follower force (a ConstantForceField, as before; identical numbers to the force-type CableConstraint) swung the two-cable arm in a limit cycle, 0.6-3.9 mm peak to peak at every step from 10 ms to 0.25 ms, because the elastic law's geometric stiffness is implicit and the cable stiffness that balances it was not (control.md). Stroke-controlled and anchored cables, pressure and region forces are still ConstantForceFields Rayleigh α, β; Kelvin-Voigt EulerImplicitSolver rayleighMass/rayleighStiffness (Kelvin-Voigt: β = η/E). α is checked against a free-falling body with linear drag (v' = g − αv): the velocity matches the implicit-Euler recurrence v ← (v + g dt)/(1 + α dt) to 1e-12 and the continuous solution to 1% at every step (first order in dt), 0.1% at the end (tests/test_sofa_backend.py). One damping per body: the solver owns it, and a force field's own rayleighStiffness has no effect on the elastic force fields (measured), so zones with their own damping are refused prony the force field carries the long-term law; the Maxwell-branch overstress (softsim/materials/viscoelastic.py, the same code as on MuJoCo) goes through a ConstantForceField updated before every step. SOFA's own MJEDTetrahedralForceField (SofaMJEDFEM) is not used: it relaxes the whole stress including the volumetric part, and its laws use non-isochoric invariants (its Mooney-Rivlin has a stress at rest) base: bonded FixedProjectiveConstraint Rigid body Rigid3d DOF at the centre of mass, UniformMass with inertia, triangulated parts (RigidMapping) Contact FreeMotionAnimationLoop, BlockGaussSeidelConstraintSolver, MinProximityIntersection, frictional Lagrange contact

Refused: Yeoh, Gent, Arruda–Boyce, multi-term Ogden, torsional and rolling friction, self-collision, magneto-active coupling. A card with one of these laws can be projected onto one SOFA has (softsim material project).

docs.title: Verified
docs.text:
• Material mappings. All of linear, neo_hookean, stable_neo_hookean, mooney_rivlin and ogden are checked against analytic 1% uniaxial compression with forces applied directly to nodes (no contact), within 4% (tests/test_sofa_backend.py). Mooney-Rivlin's energy function in the SOFA sources has an integer division (pow(J, -2/3) evaluates to J⁰), but its forces were checked: zero stress at rest and the standard stiffness μ = 2(C10 + C01).
  • Timestep. For the 20 g drop, dt = 0.1 ms and 0.05 ms agree within 2%. The 500 g full-face impact diverges at 0.1 ms (a rim vertex blows up at about 6 ms), and is stable at 0.05 ms. It can still diverge at 0.05 ms with stiff, heavily damped parameter sets (E = 100 kPa, β = 4 ms).
  • Blow-up guard. A diverging FEM state floods the constraint solver with contacts, and SOFA segfaults while allocating the compliance matrix before any NaN shows up. The backend therefore stops stepping once any vertex or rigid body moves faster than SOFTSIM_SOFA_MAX_SPEED (default 100 m/s) and reports the run as diverged (StabilityError), like a NaN.

docs.title: Known limits
docs.text:
• Speed. About 0.001× real time for the drop test on a 5 mm mesh: a 22 ms impact takes 30 s, or 90 s at dt = 0.05 ms. MuJoCo is about 10× faster.
  • Line-line collision is off for soft bodies. It's about 3× faster, and the drop test result didn't change.
  • Frictionless plate test (explained: friction). The old "7% stiff, too much spreading" comes from a plate that was not frictionless: SOFA applies the scene's largest coefficient to every pair, so a 0.8 on any body, the ground or the plate sticks the plate to the specimen's top face and the ground. A weighted plate on a cylinder (R 20 mm, H 17 mm, stable Neo-Hookean 50 kPa, ν 0.45, 2% load, rim measured as the mean radius), contact against the same load as nodal forces on the same mesh (tests/test_sofa_backend.py, 8 mm mesh):
Friction on the ground and plate Compression, contact / no contact Rim spreading, contact / no contact 0 1.108 / 1.101 (+0.6%) 1.012% / 1.011% (rim radius change) 0.01 0.996 of the no-contact one 0.988 0.05 0.976 0.959 0.2 0.898 0.838 0.8 0.670 (-33%) 0.48% (half)

(Rows 0.01 to 0.2 are contact over no contact; the 0.8 row is at 8 mm for both, with 6 mm giving 0.765 and ground only, plate only and both identical.) So the 7% corresponds to a coefficient of about 0.1, and friction on either of the pair acts. At 0 the defaults already agree to 0.6% (0.4% at 6 mm), so the other suspects need no fix: the contact distance (0.1 mm per surface, 1.2% of 17 mm at most, and below the 0.6% seen), solver tolerance and iterations (defaults, converged), mesh coarseness (6 and 8 mm agree), and the analytic reference's boundary (free-slip faces on both sides; the no-contact FEM sits 1% above the analytic rim spreading of 0.91% at either mesh, the discretisation and not the contact). Keep one friction coefficient per scene on SOFA. - Frictionless impacts: compare with every pair frictionless. With purely elastic cards, the centred 50 g drop at 2.7 m/s against the locking-free 3D reference (tools/contact_restitution.py; restitution e = rebound speed / impact speed):

Contact Reference SOFA, 5 mm MuJoCo, 5 mm Sticking, μ = 1 0.905 0.794 0.73–0.75 Every pair frictionless 0.823, peak 7.53 mm 0.795 (−3.4%), peak 6.45 mm (−14%) – Specimen and ground frictionless, the weight at 0.5 0.869 0.650, peak 5.1 mm (not a like-for-like case) 0.791

The last row was long read as "SOFA loses 58% of the energy frictionless". It doesn't: SOFA applies the scene's largest friction coefficient to every pair, so the weight's 0.5 also acted between specimen and ground, where the reference and MuJoCo (friction per pair) had none. With every pair frictionless SOFA loses 3.4% more than the reference, and its peak is 14% shallow, the linear tetrahedra's stiffness at 5 mm. Halving the step (0.784) or tightening the constraint tolerance to 1e-9 does not change that. Keep one friction coefficient per scene on SOFA. With sticking friction SOFA loses less than MuJoCo. That is why its transfer of the physical card needs less extra relaxation (g 0.77 against 0.94, experiments.md). - Rim flare through the ground (fixed: the alarm distance follows the per-step travel). In the 500 g drop with the fitted Ogden material the specimen's top rim rolls under the specimen, and then snaps back onto the ground at about 12 m/s: 0.6 mm per 50 µs step, while the intersection's alarm distance was 0.4 mm. A point farther than the alarm distance from the ground at the start of a step gets no contact, ends it below the surface, and MinProximityIntersection's normal then points away from the far side and keeps it there: one vertex (a surface vertex that was on the top face at rest) went 2.8 mm through at 8.3 ms (8.5 mm by 22 ms), with no inverted element. Measured on the 5 mm mesh, 8.8 ms (the artefact does not appear at 5.5 mm and coarser, and does not in a head-on drop of a block at 6 m/s per 0.5 ms steps):

Run Deepest vertex through the ground Peak compression Before (alarm 0.4 mm) 2.83 mm 13.13 mm Alarm 1.5 mm 0.005 mm 13.16 mm Time step 25 µs (0.3 mm per step) 0.002 mm 13.17 mm Constraint solver 1000 iterations, tolerance 1e-10 8.13 mm (worse) 13.19 mm Every pair frictionless 0.002 mm (no rim snap: the trajectory differs, peak 16.08 mm) 16.08 mm Alarm = max(0.4 mm, contact distance + fastest vertex speed × dt) 0.006 mm 13.14 mm

The solver's limits are not the cause (above), nor is the ground or the collision models: the ground is a 30 m triangle the rim cannot leave (the specimen reaches 42 mm), and every surface vertex carries a point and a triangle model. The backend now sets the alarm distance at each step from the fastest vertex speed (SofaBackend._alarm; SOFTSIM_SOFA_ADAPTIVE_ALARM=0 restores the fixed distance, SOFTSIM_SOFA_ALARM_FACTOR scales the travel, default 1). It costs 12% more CPU time in this run (a factor 2, which fixes it as well, 60%). Below 6 m/s at 50 µs the nominal 0.4 mm applies and nothing changes. ground_penetration in calibration histories still records any left. - One friction coefficient (the largest in the scene) applies to all pairs; softsim check and every run warn (single-friction) when the scene's coefficients differ. MuJoCo's contact compliance settings (contact.timeconst, dampratio, solimp) don't apply here: SOFA contacts are hard constraints. simulation.integrator and solver are MuJoCo settings and are ignored. - Contact forces come from momentum balance per body: net force only, at the centre of mass, with no centre of pressure or torque. - Ground. The ground is one large triangle. A shared triangle edge under the specimen let the vertex sitting exactly on it slip through (0.5 mm penetration) before this was fixed. - Fitted parameters are backend-specific. With the same E, β and mesh, SOFA and MuJoCo differ by about 30% in peak indentation for the 20 g drop, and the stable-NH drop-test fits end at E = 105 kPa (SOFA) vs 55 kPa (MuJoCo). The SOFA fits and their comparison are in experiments.md; preset ecoflex_00_10_drop_fit_sofa_ogden is the SOFA one-term Ogden fit. The differences are hard vs compliant contact and integrator damping (MuJoCo's contact alone adds about 0.5 mm of penetration). Calibrate per backend.

docs.title: Rods (BeamAdapter)
docs.text: softsim.backends.sofa.rod is the bare clamped cantilever on BeamAdapter that the rod backend grew from (F L^3 / (3 E I) to 0.2%, tests/test_rod_sofa.py). The scene backend is --backend rod: see rod.md.

docs.title: Drop test
docs.text: A rigid weight falls onto a soft specimen resting on a table (softsim/scenarios/drop_test.py, configs in scenarios/drop_test/).

docs.title: Reference dataset
docs.text:
Czopek P., Superczynska P., Marcinkowska A., Gajewski P., Bernat J., Records of falling mass on Ecoflex 00-10 cylinder, Zenodo, doi:10.5281/zenodo.23185808, CC-BY-4.0.

  • Specimen: Ecoflex 00-10 cylinder, D 40 mm, H 17 mm, 19.49 g. That implies 912–917 kg/m³ against 1040 kg/m³ on the datasheet. The measured mass is used, and the mismatch is reported as a finding.
  • Drop: from 38 cm, so the impact speed is about 2.73 m/s (air drag neglected).
  • Weights:
Weight Diameter Height Notes 20 g 22.5 mm 5.6 mm brass 50 g 27 mm 9.9 mm brass 100 g 32 mm 18 mm black, no knob; hits the specimen edge 200 g 40 mm 24 mm black; tilted edge impact 500 g 43 mm 38 mm black, mushroom knob, wider than the specimen

docs.title: What we measured from the data (Step 0)
docs.text:
• Frame rate is 2999.3 fps. The overlay frame/017866 … T=<s> gives 200 frames in 66.68 ms, and the zip frames are consecutive camera frames. The zips contain 800×800 RGB TIFFs (698 / 1106 / 786 / 1156 / 1506 frames for 20–500 g); the mp4 previews are the same frames, lossy, played at 12 fps.
  • Scale is about 5.3 px/mm (about 0.19 mm/px). The camera is slightly elevated, so the top face is visible and the weight's bottom edge is partly hidden. Track the weight's top edge or knob instead (it is rigid, so it moves the same distance).
  • 20 g preview, rough tracking: contact to peak takes about 7–9 frames (2.3–3 ms), peak indentation is about 4 mm, then the weight rebounds about 5 mm and settles.
  • 500 g contact sheet: the weight lands tilted, bounces, then topples off the cylinder. The specimen leaves the table about 60 ms after contact. (M3 wrongly attributed this to the table moving; the specimen does hop, pulling up the cloth it sticks to. See experiments.md.)
  • Full tracking results (contact, impact speed, offset, spin, support motion) are in experiments.md.

docs.title: Scenario
docs.text:
The simulation starts with the weight's lowest point drop.gap (0.5 mm) above the specimen, moving at the free-fall speed for the remaining height. Parameters: weight preset or custom body, drop height or initial speed, xy offset, tilt about x and y, and initial angular velocity. The specimen can be base: free (on the table, with friction) or base: bonded (bottom face pinned).

Support (optional). With support.enabled: true the specimen sits on a thin carrier plate (default 80 × 80 × 2 mm, 5 g) that can lift off the table against a spring and damper (support.stiffness, support.damping). It is a lumped model of the cloth in the recordings, which the tacky specimen drags up when it hops. It needs a backend with mount: slider_z (MuJoCo). Give the specimen material an adhesion so it sticks to the plate and the weight:

support: {enabled: true, stiffness: 32.9 N/m, damping: 0.346 N*s/m, mass: 45.3 g}
specimen:
  material: ecoflex_00_10_drop_fit_tacky   # the drop fit plus fitted tack: strength 14.6 kPa, range 0.29 mm

These are the values fitted to the recordings (see experiments.md); sweeps/fitted_tack_support.yaml runs all five weights with them.

Metric Meaning indentation undeformed contact surface minus the weight's bottom-centre height compression downward displacement of the specimen's top-centre vertex bulge_diameter twice the maximum radial vertex distance specimen_min_z, specimen_max_z lift-off and top height contact_force_z specimen on weight (negative while adhesion pulls) ground_force_z ground (or support plate) on specimen support_z support plate height (with support.enabled) weight_z, weight_vz, weight_tilt weight state

Summary: peak_indentation, t_to_peak, first_contact_duration, rebound_speed, restitution, peak_ground_force, max_bulge_diameter, specimen_lift_off, final_indentation, settling_time.

Action drop(preset=, mass=, height=, offset=, tilt=) rebuilds the scene and drops again.

docs.title: M1 results: uncalibrated (superseded by M3 calibration)
docs.text:
These use the ecoflex_00_10 preset (stable Neo-Hookean, E = 91 kPa from the datasheet, ν = 0.45, Rayleigh β = 2 ms placeholder), a 3.5 mm mesh, dt = 0.1 ms, contact timeconst 0.2 ms, 250 ms per run (softsim sweep scenarios/drop_test/sweeps/all_weights.yaml --jobs 5):

Weight Peak indentation [mm] t to peak [ms] 1st contact [ms] Rebound [m/s] e Peak ground force [N] Max bulge Ø [mm] Lift-off [mm] Wall [s] 20 g 1.97 2.0 5.0 0.49 0.18 36 42.0 1.3 68 50 g 3.45 3.0 7.0 0.69 0.25 57 43.7 3.3 66 100 g 4.72 3.6 8.0 0.83 0.30 87 46.0 7.0 63 200 g 6.53 4.4 10.2 0.97 0.36 148 48.7 11.0 53 500 g 10.29 6.4 14.6 1.17 0.43 291 53.6 16.1 47

(Five runs in parallel on 8 cores; a single run takes about 40–50 s.)

Compared with the 20 g preview, the model is too stiff: about 2 mm against about 4 mm of peak indentation. It is also too elastic: it rebounds at 0.49 m/s against roughly 0.3 m/s estimated from the rebound height. The restitution rising with mass is a signature of Rayleigh damping (heavier weights mean slower impacts, which are damped less). Whether real Ecoflex shows this is a key question for the M3 comparison. M3 calibration (experiments.md) fits E = 54.8 kPa and β = 0.31 ms (preset ecoflex_00_10_drop_fit, 5 mm mesh). That matches the 20 g and 50 g first impacts within 3–15%, but not the 500 g, which in reality is far stiffer and faster than Neo-Hookean + Rayleigh allows. The 100 g and 200 g recordings are off-centre edge impacts and can't be used. M4 repeated the fit on SOFA with an Ogden material: 20 and 50 g within 3–11%, 500 g still not reproduced (experiments.md).

docs.title: Tutorial: an actuated body and its transfer to MuJoCo
1. A cable-bent beam
docs.text:
scenarios/actuation/cable_cantilever.yaml is a 10 x 10 x 60 mm beam clamped at its base, with a cable 3 mm off its axis pulled to 0.7 N. A cable puts a pure moment on the beam, so Euler-Bernoulli gives the tip angle exactly: 0.270 rad.

softsim run scenarios/actuation/cable_cantilever.yaml --backend mujoco
softsim run scenarios/actuation/cable_cantilever.yaml --backend fem --set simulation.timestep=2ms

summary.yaml has final_bend_angle. The reference lands within 1% of the beam theory. MuJoCo bends about 30% less at this 2 mm mesh, because linear tetrahedra lock in bending. That isn't a bug in either backend: it's the error bar of linear tetrahedra at this resolution, and the benchmark table states it.

Actuators are YAML entries with a schedule. From Python, a controller can drive them in closed loop instead. It's called before every output interval and returns the actuator values; here a PI loop holds the tip at 0.1 rad:

from softsim import Simulation

sim = Simulation("scenarios/actuation/cable_cantilever.yaml",
                 ["body.mesh.size=2.5mm", "simulation.duration=600ms",
                  "body.material.damping={model: rayleigh, alpha: 0, beta: 2 ms}"])
state = {"integral": 0.0}

def controller(s):
    error = 0.1 - s.metrics()["bend_angle"]
    state["integral"] += error * 1e-3          # output interval: 1 ms
    return {"cable": max(0.0, 0.5 * error + 40.0 * state["integral"])}

result = sim.run(controller=controller)

docs.title: 2. A pneumatic finger
docs.text:
scenarios/actuation/pneunet.yaml is a PneuNet finger: chambers, a channel and a stiffer strain-limiting layer (a material zone), inflated 0-8 kPa. The same finger can be read from CAD: scenarios/actuation/pneunet_from_step.yaml loads cad/pneunet.step and finds the cavity on its own.

softsim run scenarios/actuation/pneunet.yaml --backend mujoco          # about 6 minutes
softsim export scenarios/actuation/pneunet.yaml --cad finger.step      # the parametric shape as STEP

docs.title: 3. Transfer: make MuJoCo agree with the reference
docs.text:
MuJoCo at 1.5 mm bends this finger 24% less than the locking-free reference. softsim transfer fits the effective moduli that make MuJoCo reproduce the reference, then checks them on load cases it never saw:

softsim transfer calibrations/transfer_pneunet_mujoco.yaml       # about 2.5 hours on a laptop

The result for that file: body 114 → 91 kPa, layer 1 → 1.76 MPa, error 17.7% → 2.9%, and on the unseen cases 3.2% (11 kPa) and 4.3% (a 4-chamber finger). The fitted card is written with kind: effective and the backend, mesh and element it belongs to, so it isn't mistaken for a material constant.

docs.title: Tutorial: change a material
docs.text: A material is a card: a constitutive law with its constants, optional rate dependence (Prony series), friction and tack, plus where the numbers come from. The full format is in materials.

docs.title: Look at a card
docs.text:
softsim materials                          # every preset that is visible
softsim material show ecoflex_00_30        # moduli, wave speed, stable time step per mesh size, stresses
softsim material plot ecoflex_00_30 dragon_skin_10 --tests uniaxial,simple_shear   # needs the fem extra

docs.title: Change it in YAML
docs.text:
Use a preset by name, or a preset with some values changed, or write the card inline:

body:
  material: ecoflex_00_30
  # or: material: {preset: ecoflex_00_30, elastic: {youngs_modulus: 60 kPa}}
  # or: material: {density: 1070 kg/m^3, elastic: {model: yeoh, c10: 12 kPa, c20: 0.5 kPa, c30: 0, poisson_ratio: 0.49}}

docs.title: Change it from the command line
docs.text:
--set takes dotted keys, list indices and units:

softsim run scenarios/actuation/cable_cantilever.yaml \
    --set body.material.elastic.youngs_modulus="400 kPa" --set body.mesh.size=2.5mm
softsim params scenarios/actuation/cable_cantilever.yaml | grep material

docs.title: Change it from Python
docs.text:
from softsim import Simulation
from softsim.materials import load_material

card = load_material("ecoflex_00_30", overrides=["elastic.youngs_modulus=60 kPa"])

sim = Simulation("scenarios/drop_test/cases/w020.yaml")
sim.set_material("specimen", {"preset": "ecoflex_00_10", "elastic": {"youngs_modulus": "40 kPa"}})
sim.set_material("specimen", None, ["elastic.youngs_modulus=45 kPa"])   # change single values

From ROS 2, the set_material service takes the same overrides (ROS 2).

docs.title: A law the backend doesn't have
docs.text:
MuJoCo has (stable) Neo-Hookean and StVK only. A Yeoh card on MuJoCo is refused, with a hint: project the card onto a law the backend has, over the strain range you need, and the projection error is recorded in the new card:

softsim material project ecoflex_00_30_roels2025 --to neo_hookean --out eco30_nh.yaml

docs.title: Fit your own card
docs.text:
From tension or compression data registered as a dataset (add a dataset):

softsim fetch datasets/roels2025_elastomers.yaml                 # downloads and checks the archives
softsim fit-material datasets/roels2025_elastomers.yaml ecoflex_00_30 --strain-min=-0.25 --strain-max 1.5

It fits several laws, ranks them by AIC/BIC, and writes cards with uncertainty and validity ranges.

docs.title: Tutorial: a first drop simulation
docs.text: A 20 g brass weight falls 38 cm onto an Ecoflex 00-10 cylinder (40 mm across, 17 mm tall). This is the first case of the Czopek et al. drop dataset (drop test scenario); you don't need the dataset to run the simulation.

docs.title: 1. Check the scene before running it
docs.text:
softsim check scenarios/drop_test/cases/w020.yaml

This prints the mesh (vertices, tetrahedra, quality), the physics findings (is the contact stiff enough for the impact speed? is the time step stable? does the material lock?) and whether the chosen backend supports everything the scene needs. Warnings are worth reading; errors stop a run.

docs.title: 2. Run it
docs.text:
softsim run scenarios/drop_test/cases/w020.yaml --duration 0.05

--duration shortens the run to the first 50 ms (the impact takes about 5 ms). The output goes to runs/drop_test_w020_<timestamp>/:

File Content config.yaml the fully resolved config: re-run it with softsim run <dir>/config.yaml timeseries.parquet one row per output sample: weight_z, weight_vz, indentation, contact_force_z, ... summary.yaml scalars (peak_indentation, rebound_speed, restitution, ...), the check findings, versions, wall time

docs.title: 3. Change something
docs.text:
Any value in the YAML can be changed from the command line with --set, units included:

softsim run scenarios/drop_test/cases/w020.yaml --duration 0.05 \
    --set drop.height="20 cm" --set specimen.mesh.size="5 mm"
softsim params scenarios/drop_test/cases/w020.yaml      # every key you can set, with unit and range

docs.title: 4. From Python
docs.text:
from softsim import Simulation

sim = Simulation("scenarios/drop_test/cases/w020.yaml", ["simulation.duration=50ms"])
result = sim.run()
print(result.summary["peak_indentation"])           # m
ts = result.timeseries                               # a pandas DataFrame
print(ts[["t", "weight_z"]].head())

docs.title: 5. Other backends
docs.text:
softsim run scenarios/drop_test/cases/w020.yaml --duration 0.012 --backend fem    # the 3D reference: slow, exact
softsim run scenarios/drop_test/cases/w020.yaml --duration 0.05 --backend sofa    # needs SOFA_ROOT

The same material card gives different answers on MuJoCo and on the reference, because linear tetrahedra lock and MuJoCo's contact loses energy. Experiments shows which models reproduce the real recordings and by how much, and materials explains how a card is carried to a fast backend with a stated error bar.
